title: U.S. surrogate for Chinese billionaire says she trusted agency, as questions arise
summary: The CEO of the surrogacy agency Patriot Conceptions says he was unaware billionaire Xu Bo was building a massive family.
story: A surrogate carrying a child for Chinese billionaire Xu Bo — a man reported to have over 100 children — said she trusted her agency to "protect surrogates." Now, the business practices of California-based Patriot Conceptions and its CEO are facing fresh scrutiny.

Stanford University's Hoover Institution, where the company's CEO Haotian Bai formerly served as a fellow, cut ties with him last week, shortly after a CBS Sunday Morning investigation featuring the surrogate put a spotlight on loopholes and accusations of questionable practices in the commercial surrogacy industry. A subsequent story in the New York Post looked at Bai's background.

"He is no longer affiliated with the Hoover Institution," the institution said on its website. "In light of recent media reports, it is clear that Mr. Bai misled the Institution on the nature of his businesses."
During his 2024-25 fellowship, Bai focused on veterans' access to in vitro fertilization. He frequently advertises his surrogacy agency as veteran-founded.
Bai said in a 2019 court declaration, filed in a dispute with a former business partner, that he served in the U.S. Army in Afghanistan until 2017 and that he'd been diagnosed with PTSD.

A U.S. Army spokesperson confirmed to CBS News that Bai served as a chemical operations specialist from November 2013 to October 2017. However, the Army said that while he assisted with units that were preparing to deploy, he never deployed himself.
"He had no deployments and left the Army in the rank of specialist," said Christopher Surridge, a U.S. Army spokesperson.

After leaving the military, Bai co-founded another surrogacy agency in 2018. He ended up in a court battle with his co-founder a year later. The case was later voluntarily dismissed. Bai founded Patriot Conceptions in 2019

The Hoover Institution said it would conduct "a full internal review" of the application process for the Veteran Fellowship Program. CBS News reached out to Patriot Conceptions, and in a written response, Bai said he went through "a normal application process as a U.S. Army veteran for a Hoover Institution fellowship in 2023 and was selected through what appeared to be their usual channels and protocols to be a fellow." The statement said there was "no point at which Mr Bai 'misled' the Hoover Institution about his research or his intentions."
Bai's surrogacy agency caters to international clients, who make up 40% of its business — with an emphasis on intended parents from China.
The U.S. is the only developed country where commercial surrogacy is widely legal, attracting foreign nationals who don't have the option in their country, with a large percentage coming from China.

It remains unclear how Patriot Conceptions initially agreed to provide a surrogate for Xu Bo, a video game executive who is well known in China. Patriot Conceptions partnered with a global surrogacy agency representing the intended father.

The surrogate, whom CBS News is calling Judy to protect her identity, said she first learned who the intended parent was on the night before her embryo transfer in April, after traveling from her home state to California for the procedure.
Documents obtained by CBS News showed that the intended father was Xu, who has boasted online about his desire to father large numbers of children.

A single mother, Judy said she decided to become a surrogate because she wanted to use the payment to create a better life for herself and her daughter. She said she also liked the idea of helping someone build a family — but added that she never imagined it would be that large.
"You don't think to ask … 'Oh, do they have, like, over 100 babies already?'" she said in an interview.

In an earlier phone conversation with CBS News, Bai asked whether Judy's surrogacy records had been offered for sale on the dark web. CBS News obtained the records from whistleblowers concerned about irregularities in the surrogacy industry.
During the call, Bai dismissed media reports detailing the scale of Xu's family.

Xu, a reclusive billionaire who is rarely seen in public, made his fortune as founder of Guangzhou Duoyi Network, one of China's largest mobile game companies. The Wall Street Journal first reported on the number of children Xu is said to have fathered via surrogacy, as well as other Chinese billionaires building mega-families.

His company said in a December statement that Xu had 12 children born in the U.S. via surrogates, but acknowledged a larger overall total: "Regarding the rumors about the number of children … the actual number is only a little over one hundred."

Six months later, Xu posted a photo of young children seated in rows alongside a statement: "Mr. Xu Bo believes in the philosophy that more children bring more blessings, and he wishes for all his words and actions to benefit the long-term development of the Chinese nation."
CBS News reached out to Xu directly and through representatives but received no response.

Addressing media coverage in a recent statement, Xu wrote: "Overseas media outlets have previously produced numerous misinterpretations and unfriendly reports about China, as a Chinese citizen safeguarding China's interests, Xu stands on the same side as the Chinese government and avoids granting interviews to overseas media unless necessary."

Following the publication of the CBS News report on Sept. 13, Patriot Conceptions said the firm's employees had encouraged Judy to terminate her contract after public reports about the size of Xu's family surfaced in December.
A statement issued by Patriot Conceptions stated that "it did not know the wider scale of Xu's family described in later public reporting." Patriot Conceptions declined to be interviewed on camera.

Judy disputed this account, stating that the agency "never" advised her to terminate the agreement. She said agency representatives visited her hotel room following her embryo transfer in April to bring her "flowers and snacks."
Judy said the agency told her after she matched that the intended parent was a "single father looking to expand their family."
"I felt like I trusted this agency to kind of protect surrogates and match them with people with good intentions," Judy said.
Judy said when the agency mentioned a large family, she was picturing something from a movie.
"'[The] Sound of Music.' Do you know that movie? My immediate first thought, 'Oh, that would be really cute,' like a family of 10 kids," she said.

title: Netanyahu says it's too early to determine motive in cockpit stabbing
summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu indicated to CBS News that the motive of the Flydubai co-pilot accused of stabbing his fellow pilot on a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv is still unknown.
story: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu indicated to CBS News on Wednesday that the motive of the co-pilot accused of stabbing his fellow pilot on a passenger jet bound from Dubai to Tel Aviv was still unknown.
"I don't think it was a hijacking," Netanyahu told "CBS Evening News" anchor Tony Dokoupil.

"I think it looks like a suicide attempt simply because of what this hero Yaniv described when he went in," Netanyahu speculated, referring to Yaniv Hayoun, one of the passengers on the FlyDubai flight who has been credited with entering the cockpit and helping to subdue the attacker.

"This guy was trying to jam the equipment between the two flight seats, the pilot seats," Netanyahu said of the co-pilot, whose identity has not been revealed. "He wasn't sitting in the pilot seat trying to stabilize the plane, he was trying to jam the equipment."

Speaking Thursday to Fox News, Netanyahu said Israel knew the co-pilot had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination," based on "personal information" gathered during ongoing questioning. He did not offer any further information on the alleged indoctrination, but added to Fox that the attacker was "suicidal," and that after he was subdued by other crew members and passengers, he shouted: "Kill me, kill me!"
According to Israeli officials, on Wednesday morning local time, the FlyDubai jet was about two hours into its flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv when the co-pilot stabbed the captain.
Per data analyzed by CBS News partner network BBC News, the plane then plunged about 17,000 feet, climbed 5,000 feet, and then fell another 7,000 feet before stabilizing.

Israeli officials and passengers said the captain, an Indian national, was able to fight off his co-pilot and unlock the cockpit door. Witnesses recounted how a group of passengers and crew members then stormed the cockpit and subdued the co-pilot.

Two off-duty pilots then took control of the plane and made an emergency landing at an airport in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. There were 174 people on board, Israeli officials said. Most of the passengers later boarded a replacement FlyDubai plane and were flown to Ben Gurion International Airport, arriving Wednesday night.

An Omani official confirmed to CBS News that the attacker, whose name has not been released, was born in Oman and holds Omani citizenship, but the Omani government has not publicly confirmed his nationality.
Netanyahu told CBS News he was being interrogated in Saudi Arabia.
"He'll be, I assume, moved very quickly to Dubai," Netanyahu told CBS News, adding that Israeli authorities will "join the interrogation and find out what happened there exactly."

A senior Israeli official told CBS News' Dov Lieber on Thursday that United Arab Emirates President Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan personally told Netanyahu on Wednesday that he expected Saudi authorities to transfer the pilot to the UAE for questioning.
Asked if he thought the incident could have stemmed from a mental health issue and not an act of terrorism, Netanyahu said, "it could be, I don't know, we'll find out soon."

"We've had signs that Iran, and particularly through its proxies, was intending to heighten terrorist attacks against Israel and Israeli nationals abroad," Netanyahu added. "But I think it's too early to say whether there was Iranian collusion here. I think we'll find out, won't take a long time."

No definitive motive for the stabbing has been determined by authorities. An Israeli security official previously told CBS News that investigators were looking into the possibility that the incident could have been an attempted Sept. 11-style terror attack.

"At this early stage, the underlying reasons and motives behind this event are unknown and remain subject to a formal investigation," FlyDubai said in its own statement. It urged "all parties to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts."

title: Passengers recount terrifying attempted hijack of Dubai-to-Israel flight
summary: Passenger Ron Levi tells CBS News the attempted hijack of a Dubai-to-Israel flight was "the scariest thing possible."
story: Passenger accounts paint a chaotic and terrifying picture of the alleged attempted hijacking of FlyDubai Flight 1073 on Wednesday. The flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said one pilot stabbed his counterpart and tried to crash the Boeing 737 Max 8 aircraft.

"As they were approaching Israel, one of the pilots stabbed the other pilot, and apparently attempted to crash the plane with everyone on board," Netanyahu said in a video statement, lauding passengers he said had helped to "neutralize the pilot."
Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz called it "an attempted jihadist terror attack."
"It was the most frightening experience we've ever had in our lives," passenger Ron Levi told CBS News on Wednesday.
Two U.S. officials told CBS News that four people with dual U.S.-Israeli citizenship were aboard the flight.
Here's what we know about how the suspected terror attack unfolded, based on accounts from Levi and other passengers.
"Worse than a free-fall"

"The flight was going well, we were two hours in," Levi told CBS News' Dov Lieber, speaking from Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, where the plane made its safe emergency landing, piloted by an off-duty flight crew member who happened to be on board.
"All of a sudden, what we thought was turbulence started," said Levi. It kept getting stronger, and "we realized it's not something regular."
"I would say much worse than a free-fall," he said, describing how the plane "started turning all sideways and going up and down in all different kinds of directions, for a pretty long time."
"It's very hard to even to estimate if this was 30 seconds or a minute or more than that … it was just the scariest thing possible."
Levi was sitting in a row of seats with his family, "just holding each other's hands and saying that we love them and just hoping for the best."
"And then shouting started from the front of the plane," he recalled. He saw some people near the front get up.
"Very stressful situation"

Passenger Adam Polo was in row 13, hugging his 6-year-old son while his wife was hugging their 3-year-old daughter. Polo told CBS News he "tried to be cool" for his children and told them, "We will be OK."

"The first couple of minutes was very terrifying; you just feel like you're going to crash, but even after the plane was stabilizing, there was more than an hour where we were in the air without the primary crew members," Polo said.
Polo said he couldn't see much from his seat, but after 15 minutes, he saw a passenger running out of the cockpit covered in blood.
"No one from the crew members told us what was happening," Polo said. "The only ones to give us information was the passengers who stood up with an act of bravery."
Polo, who lives in Israel and was vacationing in Thailand with his family, said everything happened so fast and it was a "very stressful situation."
"I'm a pretty cynical guy, I'm not getting excited easily, but I think it was one of the most exciting moments of my life when the plane touched the ground," Polo said.
"The co-pilot tried to murder the pilot"

Levi said he wasn't close enough to see what happened next, but several other passengers who spoke with Israeli media said one pilot had stabbed the other, details that were also repeated by Netanyahu.
"According to the initial information in our possession, the terrorist's intention was one thing: to crash the plane with all its passengers," said Katz, Israel's defense chief.

Netanyahu said he had spoken with an Israeli passenger who told him that, "somehow, he managed to break into the cockpit together with one of the crew members, and that together they neutralized the pilot who carried out the stabbing while he was attempting to sabotage the aircraft's systems."
Passenger Miryam Shira Ohayon said the plane was "pretty much out of control" when the stabbing took place, she believed somewhere over Jordan.

"The co-pilot tried to murder the pilot and basically carry out a suicide attack on the plane," she told reporters by speakerphone, held up by her mother who was waiting at Ben Gurion Airport near Tel Aviv. "It was really on the way to crashing, and it was simply the resourcefulness of many people who took control of the co-pilot and neutralized him."

Another passenger told The Jerusalem Post that intervening passengers shouted at two off-duty pilots at the back of the plane "to run and take control" of it, and one of them did so after the passengers managed to remove the attacker from the cockpit.
Netanyahu said the person who "managed to stabilize the aircraft" was "another aircrew member who was on the plane."

"All we heard in the back was shouting," said Levi. "We saw that some people were dealing with stuff, and it kept on going like that for, I think, about 10, 20 minutes until … the shakiness [of the plane] relaxed."
"Rumors started coming, and we realized that it wasn't just turbulence," he said. "It was something … a lot worse than that."
"They're heroes," he said of the people who intervened to stop the attacking pilot. "We owe them our lives."
Levi said he saw people covered in blood.
"They're here with us as well now," he told CBS News from the airport in Saudi Arabia. "These were the people I'm talking about who … jumped into the cockpit even and saved the situation."
According to Ohayon, a doctor and others on board helped treat the pilot for unspecified wounds.
"Other than the pilot, there were no injuries, but the bigger fear was really a crash, which is exactly what he was trying to do," she said.
"I just want to go home"
An Israeli security official told CBS News on Wednesday that Israel is investigating whether it was intended to be a Sept. 11-style terror attack, and whether the attacker was working alone.
The pilot was arrested and taken for questioning by Saudi authorities, Netanyahu said, adding that Israel was working to bring the passengers back to Israel safely.
"There's another FlyDubai plane here now," said Levi. "People are a bit reluctant to get on it, naturally. … We want to go home, but we want to do it in a safe way."
Asked how he was processing the incident, Levi replied: "Honestly, I'm not even starting. We're all shaking here … I have no idea. I just want to go home."
The flight landed safely in Tel Aviv around 8 p.m. local time Wednesday. Cheers and chants could be heard as the passengers disembarked.

title: Russia is stockpiling weapons to intensify attacks on Ukraine, analysts say
summary: Russia has been stockpiling "jet-powered drones," a new model of long-range strike drones that fly faster and are harder to intercept.
story: Kyiv — A daytime Russian attack on Ukraine Monday damaged civilian buildings and wounded more than 100 people across the country, according to local authorities.

A drone exploded into the National Academy of Sciences in the heart of Kyiv. Hours later, a second drone damaged a private medical clinic just blocks away. In Dnipro, Ukraine's fourth-largest city, emergency crews rushed to evacuate wounded civilians from a business center also hit in broad daylight.
And yet, the attack could have been much worse.

Ukraine's Air Force said Russia used 124 attack drones from 6:30 a.m. to 6:30 p.m. on Monday — much fewer than in previous barrages this year, which have regularly included more than 500 drones and 50 missiles within the same time frame.
Analysts and Ukrainian officials told CBS News that Russia is stockpiling weapons so that it can launch intensified late-autumn and winter barrages.

During Monday's attack, Russia used primarily "jet-powered drones," a new model of long-range strike drones that fly faster and are harder to intercept. Ukraine's Air Force said that 86 of the 124 drones used in the attack were jet-powered.
Since Russia began deploying the new models in June, Ukraine's interception rate against them is 57% — a sharp drop-off from the military's 90% to 95% success in intercepting older models.

Russia has two models of jet-powered drones, the Geran-4 and Geran-5, and has been stockpiling both. Come Back Alive, a Ukrainian military nonprofit, estimates that Russia will produce 1,200 Geran-4 and 800 Geran-5 in September, and projects those numbers to grow each month.
During his speech at the United Nations General Assembly earlier this month, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia has used just 7,700 jet-powered drones in attacks so far this year.

Viktoriia Chekalina, an analyst at the Come Back Alive Initiatives Center, estimates that Russia has stockpiled 450 to 700 units of the older non-jet-powered drones, the newer jet-powered models and dummy, non-explosive drones known as "Banderols" during each Russian attack this spring and summer.

"Despite the capacity to launch 600-1,000 units in a single massive attack, only about 150-300 drones were actually used," Chekalina told CBS News, explaining that attacks this autumn and winter "could reach around 1,500 units per one raid."

Because Russia has found success striking targets with relatively small barrages of jet-powered drones, it has also managed to save up its cruise and ballistic missiles, which are vastly more expensive and difficult to manufacture.

In the early spring and summer, Russia's attacks on Kyiv included barrages of over 70 cruise and ballistic missiles multiple times per month, according to estimates released by Ukraine's Air Force. In August, Ukraine stopped publicly releasing the numbers of missiles Russia used in each attack, but military analysts told CBS News that there was a drop-off in the number of mass-missile barrages in August and September.

Over this period, Russia has also increased its production of cruise and ballistic missiles. Chekalina said Russia has surpassed its missile production targets by 110% to 120% and estimated that it had stockpiled 130 ballistic missiles by August.

Solutions to countering Russia's ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones remain elusive. Ukraine continues to run dangerously low on American-made PAC-3 ballistic interceptors. And in an address this week, Zelenskyy said that while new defenses against jet-powered drones are being tested, they are not yet ready to be scaled, raising concerns that Ukraine may remain vulnerable heading into winter.

"Russia's goal during winter campaign will be complex: they will focus on attacking electrical and heating infrastructure as they are critical for civilians," Chekalina said. "At the same time, they will use turbojet drones along with missiles on local businesses, warehouses, and other targets."

title: U.S. military lays groundwork for potential action around Cuba
summary: Some units would "possibly [be] needed in 90-120 days," according to an internal Army message reviewed by CBS News.
story: Washington — The U.S. Army Reserve is examining whether it can provide the military's Southern Command with police forces, medical personnel and other support units within the next four months, according to an internal Army message reviewed by CBS News.

Though the message makes no reference to Cuba, the request is for continued military planning aimed at Cuba, according to multiple U.S. officials who spoke to CBS News under condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly.

There is no indication in the document that any units have received deployment orders. But the planning comes as the Trump administration puts intense economic pressure on Cuba and urges the island nation to make political reforms.

The message does not identify how many troops would be needed in the Southern Command's region, which covers Central and South America, including the Caribbean. It also does not specify where the forces could be sent or what operation they would support.

The document reviewed by CBS News says Army Reserve headquarters is seeking feedback from subordinate commands on the possible availability of six types of formations that would fall under the authority of U.S. Southern Command. The units would "possibly [be] needed in 90-120 days," according to the message, which directs commands to provide feedback to Army Reserve headquarters by Sept. 25.

Among the units is a combat sustainment support battalion that specializes in coordinating logistics such as transportation, maintenance, fuel and supply needs, along with an engineer battalion. The document also seeks an expeditionary sustainment command that would oversee logistics across a theater of operations.

The document generated last week also calls for a medical brigade to command and coordinate medical units, as well as a forward resuscitative and surgical detachment to provide emergency surgery and trauma care closer to U.S. forces. Finally, the document seeks a military police brigade — these units typically oversee military police forces responsible for security, detention and other law enforcement missions.
Contacted by CBS News, the Army Reserve did not respond before publication.

A spokesperson for U.S. Southern Command said: "Due to operational security concerns, we do not disclose details or comment on U.S. operational movements or potential deployment timelines associated with current or future operations, contingencies, or planning. However, U.S. Southern Command continuously coordinates with the Joint Force to assess a range of potential requirements across its [area of responsibility] in support of assigned missions."
On Saturday, President Trump told reporters at the White House he doesn't believe the U.S. will need the military and that "Cuba and us will make a deal."
"Cuba is failing very badly. We want to help Cuba. We want to open Cuba up to our people," he said. "We have great Cuban Americans who want to go back. We want to open Cuba up to our people."

Earlier this year, American forces conducted reconnaissance operations on the seafloor and maritime approaches surrounding the Cuban island, multiple U.S. military personnel told CBS News. Separately, U.S. airpower components were placed on heightened readiness and directed to pre-stage personnel for potential deployment. Those plans, however, did not come to fruition. CBS News is withholding certain details from publication that could potentially put U.S. service members at risk.

CBS News reported in May that U.S. intelligence officials were assessing how Cuba would respond to possible U.S. military action, as the Trump administration accused Havana of strengthening ties with Russia, China and Iran. The intelligence community's 2026 annual threat assessment largely portrays Cuba as an enabling environment for larger geopolitical competitors, rather than as an independent strategic threat.

In July, CBS News reported that American military planners had examined a range of options for possible action against the island, including an Army-led air assault involving thousands of U.S. soldiers to be carried out by the 101st Airborne Division, the only unit trained for such a task.
U.S. officials who spoke to CBS News stressed in July that the briefings were not an indication that the president or the Pentagon had decided to go forward with an operation.

Since reentering office, Mr. Trump has asserted a more muscular U.S. role in the Western Hemisphere under what officials have dubbed the "Donroe Doctrine," a Trump-era corollary to the Monroe Doctrine focused on limiting foreign adversaries and other perceived threats in the region.

In April, American and Ecuadorian troops launched a joint mission aimed at dismantling a suspected criminal hub operated by a narco-terrorist organization. On Thursday, U.S. troops and agents with the Drug Enforcement Administration assisted Ecuadorian authorities in arresting more than 30 members affiliated with Mexico's Jalisco New Generation Cartel.

Since September, the U.S. military has killed more than 230 people in 70 strikes in the Caribbean Sea and eastern Pacific Ocean. The operations are a stark contrast to the U.S. military's historical role of maritime drug interdiction and arrest. Some legal experts have said the strikes amount to illegal extrajudicial killings because U.S. forces are prohibited from intentionally targeting civilians or individuals suspected of criminal activity, unless they meet the legal standard governing the use of military force.

For Cuba, the Trump administration imposed sanctions on Cuban entities and officials, including military research and development enterprises tied to the country's nickel industry ahead of the U.N. General Assembly this week.

In New York, Mr. Trump told the U.N. General Assembly that his administration was seeking a "fundamental change" on the island and predicted Cuba's communist government "will fall" and declared that "freedom will be coming to Cuba." The Cuban delegation walked out during his remarks.

Mr. Trump also said Secretary of State Marco Rubio was "deep into negotiations" with Havana and vowed that the United States would not allow foreign adversaries to establish a strengthening foothold "on our own doorstep."

Those remarks follow months of increasingly explicit statements from Mr. Trump about Cuba. Meanwhile, Cuban President Miguel Díaz-Canel has vowed to counter any U.S. attack, and has accused the U.S. of "aggression" and "economic warfare" by blocking oil imports to Cuba.
Earlier this year, Mr. Trump told reporters in the Oval Office that he believed he would have "the honor of taking Cuba."
"Taking Cuba in some form, yeah," he said in mid-March. "Taking Cuba. I mean, whether I free it, take it — I think I could do anything I want with it, if you want to know the truth."
Later that month, Mr. Trump said bluntly: "Cuba's going to be next."

title: The story behind the first CIA officers in Afghanistan after 9/11
summary: Twenty-five years ago, a Soviet-designed helicopter crossed the mountains of Afghanistan with the first CIA officers sent into the country after 9/11, the opening move in what would later become America's longest war.
story: Twenty-five years ago, a Soviet-designed helicopter crossed the mountains of Afghanistan carrying the first CIA officers sent into the country after the attacks on Sept. 11, 2001, marking the opening move in the U.S. response that would soon become America's longest war.

The seven-man CIA team, code-named JAWBREAKER, landed in the Panjshir Valley on Sept. 26, 2001, just 15 days after the attacks, carrying millions of dollars in cash intended to help enlist and equip Afghan allies. Their mission was to gather intelligence and prepare the ground for the looming U.S. campaign against al-Qaeda and the Taliban — including by shoring up ties with the Northern Alliance, whose military leader, Ahmad Shah Massoud, had been assassinated by al-Qaeda operatives just two days before 9/11.
The Mi-17 that carried them there is now on display at CIA headquarters in Langley, Virginia, where it has undergone an extensive restoration ahead of the anniversary.
Former CIA officer David Tyson followed JAWBREAKER into Afghanistan weeks later as a member of Team Alpha, and remembers flying aboard the same aircraft before the war.
"It was shaking a lot, fuel was leaking, very noisy, and I didn't know if it was airworthy," Tyson told CBS News in an interview, "but I was assured by the pilots it was a good bird."
A helicopter built to blend in
The CIA acquired the Mi-17 in the 1990s, calculating that its Soviet origins would be an advantage in the region.
"The Northern Alliance and the Taliban both used Mi-17s," CIA historian Rob Byer told CBS News. "They're Russian helicopters and kind of the pickup truck of helicopters in that region."
"The big reason we got an Mi-17 rather than flying in a Blackhawk is because it blends in," Byer said. "And when you're going behind enemy lines, you'd like to blend in as much as you can."
It could also handle the punishing altitude. To reach the Panjshir Valley, JAWBREAKER had to cross the Anjuman Pass, which rises roughly 14,500 feet above sea level.
"The Mi-17 is one of the few helicopters that can actually make it over that pass," Byer said.

The aircraft had no transponder to identify it to American warplanes, leaving its crew to improvise. They painted "USA" and an American flag across the tops of its stabilizers, visible to friendly pilots overhead but concealed from enemy eyes on the ground. With no blue paint available, the crew left the flag unfinished. And in a reminder of the attacks that had brought them there, they gave the helicopter the call sign "9-11-01."
The Mi-17 would go on to fly more than 300 missions in Afghanistan, remaining in service until 2012.
Team Alpha goes to war

Tyson was a CIA case officer based in Central Asia who was steeped in local languages, including Uzbek, Turkmen and Russian. On Sept. 11, 2001, he was on a flight to the United Kingdom for a meeting related to the CIA's efforts to recover Stinger missiles that had remained in Afghanistan, many of which were sent there in a U.S.-backed initiative during the Soviet war.
Soon after he landed, he began planning his return, realizing his expertise would likely take him to Afghanistan.
"I knew that I would be involved given my languages and experience and so forth and where I was based in Central Asia," Tyson recalled.

On Oct. 17, less than three weeks after JAWBREAKER arrived in the Panjshir Valley, Tyson and the rest of Team Alpha were inserted into a different part of northern Afghanistan, becoming the first Americans sent behind Taliban lines. Their mission was to work with forces commanded by Uzbek leader Abdul Rashid Dostum as part of the campaign against the Taliban and al-Qaeda.
"This was something we hadn't done before," Tyson said, describing a mission that involved working with local forces to "basically prosecute a war."

His principal role was intelligence and liaison work. He worked closely with Dostum's Uzbek-speaking forces, helping his team understand the people and environment around them. The Americans traveled with Afghan fighters on horseback through the mountains, sometimes riding as long as 14 hours a day.

"The horses were not friendly," Tyson recalled. "They were stallions, they fought between each other, they bit us, they kicked us, they tried to knock us off. And the gear, the kit, the saddles were basically wooden frames with carpets thrown on them."

By late November, Taliban forces had collapsed across much of northern Afghanistan. Hundreds of foreign fighters had surrendered and were taken to Qala-i-Jangi, a sprawling 19th-century fortress near Mazar-e-Sharif.
On Nov. 25, Tyson and fellow CIA officer Johnny Micheal "Mike" Spann entered Qala-i-Jangi, where their initial task was to determine who the prisoners were and where they came from.

"For the most part, they were responding and identifying themselves as al-Qaeda members, people who had given oath of allegiance to bin Laden," Tyson said. Among the prisoners was John Walker Lindh, a California native who moved to the region in 2000 and joined the Taliban.
Hours into their mission, the prisoners rose up.
"There were explosions, gunfire, and a lot of yelling," Tyson recalled. "I started seeing things in what I would call slow motion," he said. "Things were moving slowly, but almost automatically."
At a certain point he heard Spann call his name, and began moving toward his partner through the fighting.

"I remember seeing his … silhouette or body on the ground," Tyson said. "I believe Mike was already dead when I got to him and I was able to shoot the men on top of him and took Mike's rifle from him."
Spann, 32, became the first American killed in combat in Afghanistan. His was the 79th star carved into the CIA's Memorial Wall.

Tyson fought his way to safety with Spann's rifle, which he continued using for the rest of his deployment. It is now displayed in the CIA Museum, alongside the pair of boots Tyson wore throughout his deployment. Tyson's then-8-year-old son later dubbed them "Dad's lucky boots."
"That rifle saved my life, I think, among other things," Tyson said. "It's very fitting, I think, that that rifle's in the museum. Again, it reminds us of Mike and who he was."
Restoring a piece of CIA history

After its final operational mission in 2012, the Mi-17 was brought to CIA headquarters in 2018. Its fuel lines and other components were removed and it was installed outside amid rocks meant to resemble the Afghan landscape.
Years of exposure to the elements took a toll. "The paint had faded greatly due to the sun and a few critters were getting inside as well," Byer said.

Over the past year, the CIA sealed openings in the aircraft and repainted it to more closely resemble how it looked in 2001. The green was deliberately made slightly more vivid, Byer said, so exposure to the sun will eventually fade it to the intended shade.

The restoration also brought back "607," the call sign of the Afghan pilot who flew the first mission. Painted on both sides of the Mi-17 in 2001, the number helped it pass as a Northern Alliance aircraft while signaling to allied pilots that it was friendly.
For Tyson, the artifacts preserve a much more personal history.

"As Mike would say, he wanted to be on the tip of the spear," Tyson said. "He was that, and he is today. He will be that forever. And for me to be part of that was just something that obviously I won't forget."
Tyson said he still thinks about Spann and his sacrifice on "a daily basis."
"I'd like to think he helps guide me through things," he added.

Tyson and Spann's widow, Shannon Spann DeBruyn, are now among those involved with Badger Six, a nonprofit created in 2022 and named after Spann's call sign to assist the Afghan fighters who worked alongside Team Alpha, as well as their families. The organization says it currently supports about 35 families with assistance ranging from food and medicine to relocation and resettlement support.

For Tyson, that work is part of a mission that did not end when the United States withdrew from Afghanistan in 2021 as the Taliban reclaimed power, leaving some of the Afghan partners who had fought alongside Americans behind and vulnerable to Taliban reprisals. Asked whether he feels an obligation to help where governments have not, Tyson answered simply, "Sure, yeah. That's what people do. That's what we do."

title: Country star Luke Combs says he’s 'down 30 pounds' during elk hunting trip
summary: Luke Combs revealed his 30-pound weight loss during an elk hunting trip, saying getting healthy has been his main goal as a father of three sons.
story: Luke Combs thanked fans for donating what they could to hurricane relief efforts.
Country music star Luke Combs is celebrating an impressive 30-pound weight loss during a recent hunting trip in Utah.
Earlier this week, Combs appeared in a vlog posted on the Leupold Optics YouTube page.
"I’ve been looking forward to this for a long time," Combs said at the start of the video, before revealing his weight loss.
"I'm down 30 pounds since last time. You probably can't tell because the camera adds 30 pounds, but I am down a little bit from last time."
LUKE COMBS SAYS ‘WHO THE F--- CARES’ IF CHOOSING FAMILY TIME OVER INDUSTRY PARTIES COSTS HIM AWARDS
Luke Combs has lost 30 pounds since he went on a hunting trip last year. He was photographed here in 2025. (Erika Goldring/Getty Images)
The "Fast Car" singer said getting healthy has been his "main goal."

"But this has been one of the big motivators for me. To come here, you know, I got up and down with the guys in New Mexico last year enough to get by, but I can always be better. I just really wanted to be able to hold my own out here and not half-a-- anything. I want to earn it," Combs continued.
Luke Combs went on a recent hunting trip in Utah. (USA Today Network via Reuters Connect)
In the vlog, Combs noted that his main goal for the hunting trip was to shoot, preferably with a bow, and tag a mature elk.
At the end of the vlog, the country music star was not able to kill an elk with a bow but was successful with a rifle.
In 2022, Combs sat down for an interview with Apple Music and revealed having kids was a big factor for him in getting his weight down.

title: Wynonna Judd says she and sister Ashley aren't speaking as family pain resurfaces
summary: Wynonna Judd reveals she and sister Ashley Judd aren't speaking right now as she prepares to release her deeply personal new country music album.
story: Wynonna Judd told Fox News Digital, her and her mom Naomi Judd's shared love of music helped them "bypass the bullcrap" and build a close relationship.
Wynonna Judd is finally telling her story – even the parts that may be painful for her family to hear.
The country star revealed she and sister Ashley Judd aren’t speaking right now, explaining that the two are not "connected" at the moment and focusing on their separate lives.
"We’re taking a break, which all families can relate to," she told People. "She’s doing her thing, and I’m doing mine."
KELLY OSBOURNE DRAWS A LINE WITH ESTRANGED SISTER AIMEE: 'I DON'T WANT YOU IN MY LIFE'

Wynonna Judd revealed she and sister Ashley Judd are currently not speaking, saying the two are "taking a break" while focusing on their separate lives. (Jim Smeal/Ron Galella Collection via Getty Images)

Wynonna Judd shared the personal update while discussing her new album, "The Hard Truth," which explores her complicated relationship with late mother Naomi Judd, long-held family secrets and her journey through anger and forgiveness. (Russell Einhorn/Liaison Agency)

The revelation comes as Wynonna prepares to release her deeply personal new album Oct. 2, a project that prompted her to confront the complicated relationship she shared with her late mother, Naomi Judd, long-held family secrets and the anger and forgiveness she has wrestled with over the years.

"I feel like this is the most honest and vulnerable I’ve ever been," she told the outlet about writing "The Hard Truth." "It’s there for everyone to hear. So there are some days I think, ‘Oh my God, what have I done?’ And then other days I think, ‘There comes a point in your life when you are ready to tell your testimony.’"
Wynonna co-wrote the album alongside her husband, Cactus Moser. The music producer encouraged her to be vulnerable.

"I knew it was going to be cathartic," he told the outlet.

Wynonna gained fame as one-half of the mother-daughter duo The Judds, whose close harmonies and roots-driven sound helped define country music in the 1980s. Between 1984 and 1991, they scored 20 Top 10 country hits, including 14 No. 1 singles, and won five Grammy Awards, nine CMA Awards and seven ACM Awards.
But behind The Judds’ remarkable success was a mother-daughter relationship Wynonna described as filled with both deep love and turmoil.

Part of that complicated dynamic, Wynonna said, stemmed from the struggles her mother faced behind the scenes – and the secrets she felt compelled to keep. Naomi struggled with severe depression for years before her death by suicide in April 2022 at age 76.
"My mother had an illness, she had a disease. I kept the secret, and I was devastated by that," Wynonna explained.

title: 'Yellowstone' star Neal McDonough refuses to watch hit series for ‘painful’ reason
summary: Neal McDonough played Malcolm Beck on "Yellowstone" but has never seen the show, calling his method acting memories "traumatic and painful."
story: The actor explained that his wife gave him an ultimatum when it came to his drinking, which ultimately got him to stop.
Neal McDonough may be known as one of the most ruthless villains in the "Yellowstone" universe, but there's one thing the actor himself has never done: watched the show.
McDonough, 60, portrayed ruthless businessman Malcolm Beck on the hit Taylor Sheridan series, appearing in six episodes during Season 2.
But reliving the performance is something McDonough admitted he avoids.
JEFF BRIDGES NEARLY PLAYED JOHN DUTTON BEFORE KEVIN COSTNER LANDED 'YELLOWSTONE' ROLE
Neal McDonough said he has never watched his performance on "Yellowstone." (Jesse Grant/Getty Images for A+E Networks )
"I've never seen it. You know, I don't watch any of my stuff," McDonough said on the "Arroyo Grande" podcast.
He went on to explain why he refuses to watch himself on screen.

"As a method actor, I can tell you if I look at a frame – that's why I don't watch any of my stuff. If I look at a frame of a show from 20 years ago, I know exactly the thought I was thinking. I know the song I was thinking about. I know where I was going. So going back to me sometimes can be really kind of traumatic and painful," he shared.
Even attending his own movie premieres doesn't necessarily mean he'll watch the finished product.

Neal McDonough attends "The Last Rodeo" red carpet premiere on May 12, 2025, in Fort Worth, Texas. (Omar Vega/Getty Images)

"I'll go to premieres of our films, and I'll do the red carpet. [His wife] Ruvé and I will walk in, out the exit, grab a nice dinner someplace, go to the party after. ‘How'd you like the movie?' 'It was great. It was awesome. I loved it.’ I just don't like to watch myself," he said.
And McDonough isn't losing sleep over whether he delivered in a particular scene.

"I was there on the day," he said. "I know I did a great job because God gave me a talent. I'm terrible at pounding nails. I'm not very good at telling jokes. But as Ruvé said, ‘Man, you can act.’ And so I don't need to look to see if it was good or not. They keep on hiring me, right? If they keep on hiring, I must be doing something right."

His decision to avoid watching "Yellowstone" comes years after a painful chapter in McDonough's life that left him questioning whether his Hollywood career was over.

McDonough has claimed that he was fired from ABC's "Scoundrels" in 2010 after refusing to perform intimate scenes with a female co-star, saying the decision effectively derailed his career and left him struggling financially and personally.

"What time is the bar open? That was generally my thought process back then," he explained to Fox News Digital in May. "It was, you know, fired from a show because I wouldn't kiss a woman. No one would hire me because they thought I was this religious nut bag, which is that I love my wife so much. And no one can understand it, no one could understand it."
McDonough has also spoken openly about his struggles with alcohol during that period.
He said he "was always a drinker," but "it became a bad problem" after he said Hollywood had blackballed him.

title: ‘Double Lives of Suburban Wives’ star's staggering $550K month after leaving teaching for adult content
summary: Brianna Coppage reveals her best month earned $550,000 in adult content, dwarfing her former teacher salary after losing her school position.
story: Former high school English teacher Brianna Coppage tells Fox News Digital she earns more in one month than she made in a year teaching and explains why she would "never" return to the classroom.
Brianna Coppage may have lost her teaching career, but she certainly didn't take a pay cut.

The "Double Lives of Suburban Wives" star told Fox News Digital that her adult-content business has transformed her family's finances, revealing that her most successful month brought in a staggering $550,000.
"Oh, my best month was 550,000," Brianna told Fox News Digital.
‘DOUBLE LIVES’ STAR REVEALS STAGGERING $550K MONTH AFTER LEAVING TEACHING CAREER

The figure marks a dramatic departure from her former life as an English teacher at St. Clair High School in Franklin County, Missouri. In 2023, Coppage was placed on administrative leave after her adult-content work was discovered. She later resigned from her position.
Asked whether she now makes more in a single month than she previously earned in an entire year as a teacher, Brianna didn't hesitate.
"Yes," she said.
'DOUBLE LIVES' STAR SAYS BEING KICKED OUT OF CHURCH OVER ADULT CONTENT CAREER DIDN'T SHAKE HER FAITH
And despite the controversy that followed the end of her teaching career, Brianna said she wouldn't go back even if given the opportunity.
"Never. Never," she told Fox News Digital when asked whether she would accept her teaching job back tomorrow.
"Yeah, just the lifestyle and the time and being able to just be in control of myself and in my business," she continued. "It's changed my family's life and just everything for the better."

Brianna is one of the women featured on TLC's "Double Lives of Suburban Wives," which follows six couples in the St. Louis area navigating marriage, parenthood and suburban life while maintaining careers creating adult content.

According to TLC, what began as a financial pivot for Brianna and her husband, Phillip, quickly became a lucrative business. But that success came with consequences when Brianna's online career was publicly exposed and she lost her teaching job.

Brianna told Fox News Digital that she still struggles with whether losing her career was justified.

"I think… it's a difficult concept to even wrap my mind around," she said. "So obviously like professions have a level of professionalism, but also they couldn't cite anything that I technically broke."
"So was I really doing anything wrong? I don't know," she continued. "I think it's on a basis of morality."
Brianna also pushed back on what she described as a misconception surrounding her former employment.
"There was no like morality clause, which is a lot of… there's a misconception about that, that I signed something or a clause, a morality clause," she said. "There wasn't one. So I don't know."
While losing her teaching career forced Brianna onto a different professional path, she said the financial impact of her new work has been life-changing.
Brianna Coppage said working alongside husband Phillip has brought financial success while also testing boundaries within their marriage. (TLC)
"My family was able to pay off all of our debts. I paid off my student loans," she told Fox News Digital. "So I stopped putting groceries on credit cards."
"Like yeah, it just is so freeing, and I don't know, it's been life-changing."

That financial freedom is one of the central tensions explored on "Double Lives of Suburban Wives," where the women weigh the benefits of their unconventional careers against the judgment and loss of privacy that can accompany them.
For Brianna, the cost has been significant.

"I think the greatest thing it has cost me is the privacy, the lack of privacy," she told Fox News Digital.
Being thrust into the public eye has sometimes left her feeling as though people forget there's a person behind the headlines.
"And being in the public eye, it's like, I'm not a human anymore," Brianna said. "I'm not normal just like everybody else when truly I am. Like we are human beings too."
But when weighing that loss against what her new career has made possible for her family, Brianna said the benefits extend far beyond her income.
"I think the greatest thing it has afforded is just memories and time with my family that I wouldn't trade for the world," she said.
‘DOUBLE LIVES’ STAR OPENS UP ABOUT MARRIAGE ‘BETRAYAL’ AFTER ADULT-CONTENT CAREER CHANGES HER LIFE
Brianna said her own upbringing has shaped how she views the opportunities she can now provide for her children.
"Like growing up, I grew up fairly poor. And I mean family vacations and letting my kids experience things that I never would have is really priceless."
But despite the financial success and freedom Brianna says the career has given her family, she stopped short of saying she would encourage her daughter to follow the same path.

Asked how she would respond if her daughter came to her as an adult and said she wanted to pursue the same kind of work, Brianna said her first priority would be making sure she understood what she was getting into.
DREA DE MATTEO SAYS ONLYFANS BECAME ‘POLITICAL STATEMENT’ AFTER FINANCIAL STRUGGLES THREATENED HER HOME
Promotional artwork for TLC's "Double Lives of Suburban Wives." (TLC)

Still, she said she would offer her daughter the same acceptance she wants from others.
"But also just as I want people to love me and respect me and not judge me, I would give her that same…  that same love and respect."
Her success hasn't eliminated the complications that come with mixing marriage and business.

Brianna and Phillip's relationship became another major storyline on "Double Lives of Suburban Wives," with viewers watching the couple confront trust and boundary issues while simultaneously juggling life as parents and business partners.

She added that she was glad viewers were seeing some of those difficulties rather than an artificially polished version of their marriage.

title: Piers Morgan questions Princess Diana’s brother’s explosive claims about King Charles after error about him
summary: Piers Morgan argues that Charles Spencer's memoir mistake undermines explosive claims about King Charles III's reaction to Princess Diana's death.
story: Piers Morgan argues an inaccurate account about him raises questions about Charles Spencer's recollections of conversations following Princess Dianas death.
Piers Morgan says Charles Spencer's public apology isn't enough.

The British broadcaster told Fox News Digital he is still pursuing legal action over what he calls defamatory passages in Spencer's memoir, "Swan Song: Diana, My Sister," even after Spencer acknowledged a factual error and apologized.

"He's published an egregious defamatory lie about me, and that lie remains in copies of the book being sold all over the world, including the United States," Morgan told Fox News Digital. "Although he's rushed out an apology and admitted that it was completely untrue what he said about me, he hasn't removed it from the book."
KING CHARLES, PRINCE WILLIAM 'FURIOUS' AS PRINCESS DIANA'S BROTHER UNLEASHES EXPLOSIVE CLAIMS: EXPERTS

Piers Morgan, left, told Fox News Digital he is still pursuing legal action against Charles Spencer, right, Princess Diana's brother, following the publication of "Swan Song." (Yui Mok/PA Images via Getty Images; Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

"My legal team has been in touch with him and his publishers demanding that they remove the book from sale and reissue the book without the offending pages," Morgan said. "It's not just a one-off reference. We're talking about several pages here."
Spencer denied that Morgan had sued him, prompting Morgan to release correspondence from his lawyers showing they had contacted Spencer and his publisher, The Sun reported.

Copies of Charles Spencer's book about his sister, Diana, Princess of Wales, are displayed on its publication day at Foyles on Charing Cross Road in London, England, on Sept. 22, 2026. The book, "Swan Song: Diana, My Sister," recounts Earl Spencer's childhood with Diana. King Charles is quoted in the book as saying, "We'll forget her soon enough." (In Pictures via Getty Images)
Morgan wants any damages paid to The King's Trust, a youth charity King Charles III founded in 1976 as the Prince of Wales.
WATCH: PIERS MORGAN CHALLENGES CHARLES SPENCER'S CLAIMS ABOUT KING CHARLES
Fox News Digital reached out to Penguin Press, the U.S. publisher of "Swan Song," and Althorp for comment.

The book incorrectly identifies Morgan as the editor of the Daily Mirror when Mirror Group newspapers published photographs of Diana exercising in a gym in November 1993, People magazine reported. According to the outlet, Morgan was working at The Sun at the time and didn't become editor of the Daily Mirror until 1995.
Princess Diana leaves a press conference at the Hilton Hotel in London on Dec. 3, 1993. (Getty Images)
Spencer acknowledged the error but stood by his recollection that Morgan was "surly and annoyed" when Spencer called Morgan to tell him he was not welcome at Diana's 1997 funeral.
Charles Spencer, Princess Diana's brother, attends a reception celebrating the "Diana: A Celebration" exhibit at the National Constitution Center in Philadelphia on Oct. 1, 2009. (Getty Images)

"Earl Spencer's account of his conversation with Piers Morgan is accurate," read a statement published by People magazine. "Mr. Morgan was surly and annoyed when Earl Spencer called personally to tell him that he was not welcome at his sister's funeral."
Daily Mirror editor Piers Morgan sits in his office at Canary Wharf, London, on Dec. 14, 1998. (Getty Images)

"The book then records Earl Spencer's assumption that Mr. Morgan's response was because he was editor of the Daily Mirror when the Mirror Group had published highly intrusive photographs of Princess Diana at the gym," the statement continued.

Charles Spencer has apologized to Piers Morgan for a factual error in his new memoir, "Swan Song: Diana, My Sister." However, he stands by his account of their phone conversation in 1997. (Jordan Pettitt/PA Images)
"As a historian, accuracy is important to Earl Spencer. He therefore wishes to clarify that his assumption was incorrect. Earl Spencer apologizes to Mr. Morgan for this error."
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
"Swan Song: Diana, My Sister," written by Charles Spencer, is displayed at a bookstore in London, United Kingdom, on Sept. 22, 2026. (Anadolu via Getty Images)

People reported that the passage will be corrected in the second edition of "Swan Song." Spencer has not withdrawn his account of the conversation itself, only his mistaken assumption that Morgan was editor of the Daily Mirror at the time.
Morgan said the error casts doubt on the accuracy of other claims in the memoir, including Spencer's account of what King Charles allegedly said after Diana's death.

Britain's Prince Charles kisses Lady Sarah McCorquodale while her sister Lady Jane Fellows looks on at RAF Northolt Airport near London on Aug. 31, 1997, after the arrival of Charles and the casket containing the body of his former wife, Diana, Princess of Wales. Diana died in a car crash in Paris earlier that morning. (AFP via Getty Images)

"He's claiming to be a historian," Morgan said. "He says he's written this as a work of historical record to set the record straight about his sister, Princess Diana, one of the most talked-about people, obviously, of modern times. But he makes incredibly incendiary allegations against our now-king, Prince Charles, in which he claims that within hours of Diana dying, he spoke to Prince Charles on the phone and Prince Charles sounded as giddy as a lottery winner with excitement that Diana had died."

Prince William and Prince Harry stand with Prince Charles holding a funeral program at Westminster Abbey for the funeral of Diana, Princess of Wales, in London. (Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images)

"It's hard to imagine a more disgusting thing to say," Morgan said. "I don't believe for a moment that Charles was like that. In fact, I had Paul Burrell, Diana's former butler, on my show last week saying that he saw the prince in Paris within hours of Diana dying and the man was a broken man. [He] was utterly grief-stricken. So why this matters about what happened to me is that people have been questioning the accuracy of his memory of these phone calls with King Charles."

Paul Burrell, butler to Diana, Princess of Wales, stands in the background as she makes a three-day visit to Bosnia-Herzegovina to raise awareness about land mines and call for a complete ban on their production, sale and use. The trip was organized by the American-based Landmine Survivors Network. The photo was taken Aug. 10, 1997. (Getty Images)

In the book, Spencer recalled a conversation with then-Prince Charles about whether Diana's sons, Prince William and Prince Harry, then 15 and 12, would walk behind her coffin during the funeral procession. Spencer said a royal aide informed him about the plan and that he opposed it. Charles then called Spencer, leading to what Spencer described as a heated exchange.
Prince Harry, Prince Charles, Earl Spencer and Prince William stand at Westminster Abbey during the funeral service for Diana, Princess of Wales, on Sept. 6, 1997. (Getty Images)

"Prince Charles continued his stream of anger, without me interrupting," Spencer wrote. "Then he stopped. I assumed the pause signaled an effort to bring himself under control, but then he unleashed down the phone what I have always taken to be his pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death. 'Rest assured,' he hissed, 'we'll forget her soon enough!'"

Spencer wrote that he was "so stunned" that he took a few seconds before replying, "I can't believe you just said that," and hanging up.

A Buckingham Palace spokesperson said in a statement, "While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and color memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss."
Prince William and Prince Harry look at floral tributes to Diana, Princess of Wales, outside Kensington Palace in London, England, on Sept. 5, 1997. (WireImage)
A palace spokesperson told Fox News Digital they had no further comment.

"It is not every day you wake up to find you’ve been gaslit by the king," Spencer told the BBC. "It was astonishingly provocative and below the belt because it was essentially trying to say I’d lied without the king being able to deny what I’d said." (Getty Images)
Spencer has stood by the account, telling the BBC, "I'm telling the truth."
Morgan rejected Spencer's account.
Prince Charles and Diana's sisters Lady Sarah McCorquodale and Jane Fellowes are seen here on Aug. 31, 1997, following Princess Diana's death in a car crash. (AFP via Getty Images)

"I can't imagine for a moment [the king] would say that about the mother of his children," Morgan said. "This goes to the heart of the credibility of the book. If he can get something so grotesquely wrong about me over several pages, which is so easy to check and prove he got it wrong, then why should we believe him about anything he says about King Charles? That's why it matters."

"Earl Spencer has apologized to me for his defamatory lies published in his new book, 'Swan Song,' published today," Morgan wrote on X on Sept. 22, 2026. "But I am pursuing legal action against him and his publisher Penguin to have the lies removed, and damages paid to the King’s Trust." (REUTERS/Henry Nicholls)
Morgan also disputes Spencer's recollection of their phone call.

"His account of how he did that and how I was with him is completely untrue," Morgan said. "He says that I was snarling, I was rude, I was all these things. I would simply ask people, how realistic is that? This guy's just lost his sister. Is it likely that I, as a newspaper editor who was very friendly with Diana, friendly with her mother and Earl Spencer's mother, that I would treat a family member in a snarling or rude manner? I don’t think it is."
Diana, Princess of Wales, and her mother, Frances Shand Kydd, are seen here on Sept. 16, 1989. (Getty Images)

"At the end of the call, I said to him that I would like him to pass on my deepest condolences to his mother, who I knew very well. And he said he would do that and thanked me. That's not a snarly, rude conversation."
Diana, Princess of Wales, died in 1997. She was 36. (Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images)

"I put it to people that if he's so wrong about the tone of my conversation with him that week, then why should we believe him when he says that Charles was giddy with excitement?"

story: Fox News' CB Cotton and trial attorney Kelly Hyman join 'Fox News Live' to discuss a proposal for the release of music mogul Sean 'Diddy' Combs from his 50-month prison sentence and more.
Sean "Diddy" Combs may be behind bars, but he has reportedly found a way to bring the perks of his former luxury lifestyle with him.

Combs, who is serving out his 50-month sentence at Fort Dix in New Jersey, has essentially hired a full staff within the prison walls, NBC News reported. Four men living in the same unit as the disgraced music mogul spoke to the outlet about the unusual comforts Combs has secured behind bars.
"He’s a billionaire. People are in awe of him," one of the anonymous sources told the outlet. "Money is power, especially behind bars."

From freshly made beds to cooked meals, clean laundry and Chinese-style massages, Diddy has reportedly turned fellow inmates into a makeshift prison staff.
"This is not some normal s--- you see in jail. This is some rich s---," one of the men told NBC. "It looks crazy, but again, it’s Diddy."
Contraband cellphones, explicit photos, prescription pills and premium booze — Combs’ alleged prison perks reportedly extend well beyond his makeshift staff.

Sources told NBC News the music mogul uses illicit phones to scroll Instagram and view nude and sexually explicit photos sent by an ex-girlfriend. He has also allegedly purchased Remeron, an antidepressant dubbed "rem-roms" behind bars, from other inmates for its mood-boosting effects.

"You can pretty much get anything except a key to the front door and a female," one of the sources said.

In response to the reported claims involving contraband cellphones, drugs and alcohol, FCI Fort Dix acknowledged that keeping prohibited items out of federal prisons remains an ongoing challenge.

"Like all correctional agencies, contraband, particularly cell phones, narcotics, and weapons, remains a constant challenge, and we continue to tackle the problem of contraband being introduced into our facilities," a representative for FCI Fort Dix told Fox News Digital. "Inmates are not permitted to have access to cell phones, and all incarcerated individuals in the Federal Bureau of Prisons (BOP) who are found to violate the ‘Inmate Discipline Program’ policy are subject to sanctions."

"We are fully committed to safeguarding everyone in our custody and to maintaining the safety and security of our correctional staff and surrounding communities," the statement continued. "To this end, we operate under a controlled environment that is both secure and humane. "However, we generally can tell you that allegations of staff misconduct are taken seriously and, consistent with national policy, referred for investigation if warranted," the statement concluded. "Incidents of potential criminal activity or misconduct inside BOP facilities are thoroughly investigated for potential administrative discipline or criminal prosecution."

The musician was sentenced on Oct. 3, 2025 to 50 months behind bars, followed by five years of supervised release and a $500,000 fine. The rapper was transferred to Fort Dix to serve out the rest of his sentence later that month. As of publication, Diddy's release date was set as Jan. 21, 2028.

Diddy's eight-week trial, during which jurors heard dozens of witness testimonies, concluded on July 2, 2025. The rapper was acquitted on the most serious charges against him – sex-trafficking and racketeering.

The "I'll Be Missing You" singer has filed an appeal. Diddy's team claimed the sentence handed down to him was illegal because the judge relied on charges the jury rejected, according to the appeal briefing obtained by Fox News Digital.

title: Dane Cook says brother’s $12M betrayal left him with 'scarlet letter of humiliation'
summary: Dane Cook reveals how his half-brother and business manager stole his fortune, branding him with a "scarlet letter of humiliation" he couldn't shake.
story: Comedian Dane Cook spoke with Fox News Digital about his new documentary which detailed the emotional fallout from his brother Darryl’s theft of millions of dollars, the criminal case and its lasting impact years later.
Dane Cook reflected on the shame he felt while fighting against his family for a fortune that was stolen from underneath his eyes.

After finding success on stage and screen, and during one of the peaks of his career, the comedian discovered that he was essentially broke and his older half-brother, Darryl McCauley — who also served as his business manager — was on the run with a fraction of his fortune.

Cook, 54, exclusively told Fox News Digital that the betrayal not only devastated him financially, but also impacted his mental health as he attempted to reconcile his brother's actions while finally speaking out in the new documentary, "Funny Money: The Dane Cook Story."
JENNIE GARTH ADMITS ‘SCARY’ FINANCIAL SPIRAL AFTER ‘90210’ FAME
Dane Cook detailed how his half-brother, Darryl McCauley, stole millions of dollars from him throughout his career in his new documentary, "Funny Money: The Dane Cook Story." (Michael Tullberg)

McCauley was arrested in 2008 after going on the run with nearly $3 million of his brother's money, only for investigators to discover that Cook's business manager actually stole nearly $12 million over the course of his working relationship with his brother — by hiding it in spaghetti sauce jars.
"It was the scarlet letter of humiliation that I felt like he branded on me," Cook said.
JOHN CANDY'S FAMILY CALLS OUT HOLLYWOOD FOR WEIGHT CRITICISM THE ACTOR ENDURED THROUGHOUT HIS CAREER

"It was like, forget about all the, you know, the criminal, all of it. It's like, he knew I was the kid on the playground with the terrible cystic acne who hated myself and ... self-loathing, and like, a lot of stuff that I guess as adults we feel like it's woe is me, but it was very real to me and it was hard."
Dane Cook's brother, Darryl McCauley, managed his career for years before the comedian discovered theft on a massive scale. (MediaNews Group)

Cook noted that the health and wellness aspect of his entire career was "trying to regulate that and share not only through my comedy, but the back channels of MySpace or the communication of like, 'I'm just like you, but I just did it.'"
"It was the scarlet letter of humiliation that I felt like he branded on me."

"That's happening back channel," he said. "Publicly, I'm the bell of the ball, all the cool stuff that's happening there, but he knew, only he knew that I'd come home every day after school with panic attacks and dreading the next day having to go to school because I was just so scared of people."

He added, "I was so scared to be around other kids."

McCauley pleaded guilty in 2010 to multiple counts of larceny, forgery and embezzlement, while his wife, Erika McCauley, also pleaded guilty to larceny charges. In addition, they were both ordered to pay restitution, a fee which Cook waved against Erika for her participation in the documentary.
Dane Cook found fame as a stand-up comedian, and later pivoted to film and television roles. (Joe Coomber)

"It's like, the money can come and go, and fame can come and go, and that's life. There's so many things that are out of your control," he said. "But that part that he knew about of me was, like man, he let that happen to me."
While Cook resented his brother's action, the comedian also warned that he's "the son of a different dad" as McCauley was his older half-brother.

"I'm the son of George Cook, and he forgot that I am my father's son," Cook declared. "We are conditioned, I think, the DNA of the Cook family is like, we put wins in the win column, and we take our losses and we reconfigure."
"It's like, the money can come and go, and fame can come and go, and that's life. There's so many things that are out of your control."
"We don't sit in them and go, 'Oh, the engine broke,' and tell people we used to have a good engine. That's just not, that's not me. That's not us."
Dane Cook starred alongside Jessica Simpson in the comedy "Employee of the Month." (WireImage)

He added, "I think part of him probably sitting in that courtroom when I read that impact letter was going like, 'Damn, I think he's going to come back stronger from this,' but neither of us knew when at that time, or if."

While Cook isn't sure if he'll ever see any of the money his brother stole or speak to him again, he found support from his sisters and wife Kelsi.

"This documentary wouldn't be here without her," Cook said of his bride of three years. "I wouldn't have a deeper faith ... She's brought faith back into my life in ways that were just absolutely lovely."

title: Tom Cruise's praise of Kate Middleton highlights her 'untouched by scandal' reputation: expert
summary: Tom Cruise's glowing praise of Kate Middleton at the London "Digger" premiere reflects her unique standing in the royal family, experts say.
story: Simon Vigar, author of "The Four Wives of Windsor," praises Kate Middleton’s intelligence and says Prince William trusts the Princess of Wales "absolutely implicitly" for impartial advice.
Tom Cruise's recent effusive praise for Kate Middleton was not just Hollywood flattery, according to royal experts.

The Prince and Princess of Wales, both 44, joined Cruise at the world premiere of the 64-year-old actor's new movie "Digger" in London on Sept. 22. During an interview with "Extra" at the film's Los Angeles premiere on Monday, Cruise raved over the royal couple and shared a particularly glowing assessment of Middleton.

"It was just so fun sitting there watching them watch it and for them to be part of it," Cruise said, via People magazine. "I have so much respect for them, you know, they’re amazing people and how dedicated they are to their country and also… what they give to the world. They’re just beautiful people and fun, very funny."
KATE MIDDLETON’S CAREFULLY PLANNED PATH TO THE THRONE REVEALED AS EXPERT SAYS SHE ‘PLAYED THE LONG GAME’
"She’s got a great sense, incredible sense of humor," Cruise said of Middleton. "I mean, obviously very intelligent and fun."
Tom Cruise recently gushed over Kate Middleton after she and Prince William attended the London premiere of the actor's movie "Digger." (Getty Images for Warner Bros.)
"They’re so charismatic and so elegant," he gushed. "That dress that she was wearing? Stunning."
PRINCE WILLIAM, KATE MIDDLETON FINALLY FEEL FREE TO SHOW AFFECTION IN PUBLIC: EXPERTS
"William did well," Cruise added with a smile. "Way to go, smart choice. Yeah, I gotta give it to William. Way to go. Smart choice."
Cruise's comments quickly made headlines, with royal experts arguing they reflected Middleton's unique standing within the monarchy rather than simply offering another celebrity compliment.
KATE MIDDLETON HAILED AS THE MONARCHY'S 'SAVING GRACE' AFTER CANCER BATTLE TRANSFORMED HER ROYAL ROLE: EXPERTS
Cruise said that William and Kate are "so charismatic and so elegant." (Getty Images for Warner Bros.)

While speaking to Fox News Digital, royal expert Christopher Andersen said that the Hollywood icon's admiration underscores why Middleton has become one of the royal family's greatest assets, pointing to her enduring appeal and scandal-free reputation.

"Do not underestimate the importance of her immense popularity," he said. "Kate Middleton is universally adored, and, unlike most celebrities, is virtually untouched by scandal. Like everybody else on the planet, Tom Cruise certainly wouldn't mind having some of that fairy dust rub off on him."
PRINCE WILLIAM FACES 'WORK-SHY' CRITICISM BUT IS SECRETLY RUNNING MONARCHY LIKE A CEO, EXPERT SAYS
Andersen, who authored the 2026 biography "Kate!: The Courage, Grace, and Power of the Woman Who Will Be Queen," noted that Cruise was also likely drawn to Middleton's beauty and style.
"If she wasn't movie-star gorgeous and stunningly fashionable, I don't think Tom Cruise would be drooling all over her," he said.
Fox News may be compensated for or earn a commission if you buy through our referral links.
"Kate!: The Courage, Grace, and Power of the Woman Who Will Be Queen" by Christopher Andersen is available now. (Gallery Books)
Royal commentator Amanda Matta echoed Andersen's opinion, arguing that Cruise's praise speaks to Kate's central role within the monarchy.

"While this was definitely an easy sound-bite for Cruise to pull out, it also happens to be true," she told Fox News Digital. "I think what Cruise is picking up on with this remark is that Kate is the entire reason the Wales brand works."
PRINCE WILLIAM AND KATE MIDDLETON’S ‘GENUINE LOVE STORY' IS BUILT ON BEING A 'VERY NORMAL FAMILY': AUTHOR
Cruise said that "William did well" by marrying Middleton. (WireImage)

"She wasn’t born into nobility, but that worked in her favor to help the Palace connect with the modern public," Matta continued. "Kate’s grounded humor and elegance are both central to William's public image now, and the public’s warmth toward her is one of the monarchy’s most valuable assets."
Royal commentator Richard Fitzwilliams told Fox News Digital that Cruise's remarks simply reflect the majority of the public's perception of Middleton.
KATE MIDDLETON SCALES UK'S THREE HIGHEST PEAKS IN 24 HOURS WITH A DEEPLY PERSONAL MESSAGE FOR CANCER SURVIVORS

"He’s just saying what most people think," Fitzwilliams said. "She is exquisite, her intelligence, humor and dress sense are part of her personality, which has given them both a worldwide aura as a couple. This is of enormous help to Britain, as soft power is so significant and also to the charities they both do so much for."
Cruise, Middleton, William and David Beckham are pictured at the "Digger" premiere. (Getty Images for Warner Bros.)
Royal experts also told Fox News Digital that Cruise's remarks about Middleton carried extra weight given the action star's decades-long relationship with the British royal family.
KING CHARLES RESPONDS TO CHARLES SPENCER'S CLAIMS ABOUT PRINCESS DIANA IN A RARE STATEMENT

The actor met the late Princess Diana at the 1992 London premiere of "Far and Away" alongside his co-star and then-wife Nicole Kidman. Andersen recalled that he had previously written about their first encounter and the "schoolgirl crush Diana had on Cruise" in his 1998 best-selling book "The Day Diana Died."

"Diana joked that she wouldn't mind if Kidman were out of the way. ‘Nicole kept giving me dagger eyes,’ Diana told a friend, ‘as if to say keep your hands off my handsome husband!’" Andersen remembered.

After their first meeting, Cruise and Diana went on to develop a friendship. In 1995, Cruise invited the princess and her sons, William and Prince Harry, to visit the set of the original "Mission: Impossible" movie at Pinewood Studios outside London.
In 2022, royal expert Neil Sean wrote that Cruise was "devastated" when Diana died in a car accident at the age of 36 in August 1997.
"She was a magical person and really engulfed you with her personality," Cruise told Sean.

Cruise has been linked to the royal family since the early days of his career when he and then-wife Nicole Kidman met Princess Diana at the London premiere of their 1992 movie "Far and Away." (Tim Graham)
KATE MIDDLETON WEARS PRINCESS DIANA'S PEARL BRACELET AT TROOPING THE COLOUR AS CHARLOTTE MIRRORS HER MOTHER
Cruise and Kidman were among the celebrity guests who paid tribute to the late princess at her funeral on Sept. 6, 1997.

William would later forge his own friendship with Cruise, who held a special screening of his 2022 sequel "Top Gun: Maverick" for the prince and Middleton ahead of the movie's release. Cruise invited the royal couple after learning that William, who previously served as a pilot with the Royal Air Force, was a huge fan of the original film. The Prince and Princess of Wales later attended the London premiere of "Top Gun: Maverick" at the invitation of Cruise.
At the time, Cruise told PA News Agency that he and William had "a lot in common," explaining, "We both love England, and we're both aviators. We both love flying."
The actor later appeared in King Charles III's 2023 coronation concert and previously took part in Queen Elizabeth II's Platinum Jubilee celebrations.
"Cruise, perhaps more than most Hollywood stars, has had a fairly up close and personal relationship with the royal family," Andersen noted.
Middleton and William previously joined Cruise at the premiere of "Top Gun: Maverick." (Photo by Dan Kitwood/Getty Images)
Having witnessed both Diana's extraordinary popularity and Middleton's rise within the royal family, Andersen explained he believes Cruise's admiration is well-founded.
