title: States leading nation on the biggest education battles gripping classrooms revealed in first-ever report
summary: The Defending Education report ranks Tennessee first among all 50 states on parental rights, DEI, gender identity and public school policies.
story: Fox News correspondent Alex Hogan reports live from Washington on a U.S. House of Education and Workforce Committee hearing. Lawmakers grill superintendents from Chicago, San Francisco and Loudoun County Public Schools over their districts' gender policies and parental rights. Concerns include school staff's communication with parents about student gender transitions and topics like "Drag Queen Story Hour." The superintendents deny claims of withholding information from parents.

FIRST ON FOX: The escalating battle over what children should be taught in public schools continues to drive America's culture wars, and a new report ranks every state on some of the most contentious issues affecting today's classrooms.

Red states dominated the ranking, which measures all 50 states and Washington, D.C., on issues spanning parental rights, diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI), gender and sexuality, teacher and union policies, and foreign influence, according to Defending Education's first-ever Rankings on Integrity in State Education, released Thursday.
Tennessee claimed the top spot, followed by Alabama, Florida, North Carolina and Iowa, while Washington, D.C., ranked last, followed by Rhode Island, California, Oregon and Illinois.

The rankings do not account for test scores or graduation rates. Instead, the report said it is designed to show how states are approaching hot-button issues as parents demand greater transparency in their children's education.
DOJ LAWSUIT TARGETS ALLEGED SCHOOL ‘SECRET GENDER TRANSITIONS’ POLICIES THAT KEEP PARENTS IN THE DARK
A protester speaks during a rally for safe Centre County public schools in State College, Pennsylvania on April 23, 2023. (Paul Weaver/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)

"For the first time, parents have a single resource to see how their state handles the issues they've voiced concerns about over the last five years, empowering them to evaluate local schools and hold leaders accountable at the ballot box," Paul Runko, senior director of strategic initiatives at Defending Education, said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

Of the report's five categories, the parental rights category ended in a four-way tie, with North Carolina, South Carolina, Tennessee and West Virginia earning the top spot. Each was awarded points for policies that give parents more say over student gender transitions, sex education instruction and whether their children participate in those lessons.

Georgia, Mississippi, North Carolina and South Carolina, all red states, received perfect scores on teacher policies. According to the report, laws governing teacher unions, strikes and collective bargaining, along with work authorization requirements, were key factors in the scoring.
TRUMP ADMINISTRATION PROPOSES STRIPPING TAX-EXEMPT STATUS FROM SCHOOLS USING RACE-BASED PROGRAMS

Presidents of the nation's two largest teachers' unions are Becky Pringle, left, of the National Education Association (NEA), and Randi Weingarten, right, of the American Federation of Teachers (AFT). (Leigh Vogel/Getty Images for March For Our Lives)

Iowa, Missouri and West Virginia topped the report's DEI category after receiving high marks for laws restricting DEI initiatives and other policies related to restorative justice, teacher diversity and antisemitism.

Another major flashpoint in education has been a growing conversation on gender identity and transgender athletes competing in women's sports. The report examined state policies blocking LGBTQ-specific curriculum, restricting transgender athlete participation, and state nondiscrimination and anti-bullying laws related to gender identity, finding Alabama, Florida and Indiana tied for the highest scores.

But the report went further than policies shaping the classroom. Seven red states received perfect scores for laws limiting Chinese government influence in education, including Confucius Institutes, China-backed language and cultural education centers. Alabama, Florida, Indiana, North Carolina, Ohio, Tennessee and Texas aced the category.
In another statement to Fox News Digital, Dr. Terry Stoops, director of government affairs at Defending Education, congratulated the frontrunners.
EXCLUSIVE: HOUSE COMMITTEE PROBES CHICAGO PUBLIC SCHOOLS OVER HIDING 'GENDER AFFIRMATION' FROM PARENTS
Hundreds protest outside a rally held by President Donald Trump at Macomb County Community College in Warren, MI, on April 29, 2025. (Getty Images/Dominic Gwinn)
"If your state is at the top of Defending Education's rankings, congratulations!" he said. "You live in a state with public school policies that prioritize sound academics over shameless antics."
Stoops also blamed elected leaders for the lowest-scoring states, accusing them of having "sacrificed educational excellence at the altar of social justice."
"For parents in bottom-feeder states who value rigor over ridiculousness, the choice is either fight or flight," he said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Despite more blue states embracing DEI and social justice policies, the report said it wants parents to have a clearer picture of where their state stands on education and how those policies could impact their children and future generations.
Kiera McDonald is a Production Assistant for Fox News Digital.

title: Teen's tragic killing by illegal immigrant becomes flashpoint in battle for control of Congress
summary: Sheridan Gorman's parents confronted Rep. Mike Lawler and Democrat Cait Conley over sanctuary city policies during a heated congressional debate.
story: Moderate New York House Republican Rep. Mike Lawler spoke with Fox News Digital about how the tragedy of Sheridan Gorman's killing has affected and motivated his re-election campaign.
A teenage girl's tragic death, allegedly at the hands of an illegal immigrant who was previously deported from the U.S., has now become a political flashpoint in her hometown.

Sheridan Gorman's grieving parents made their heartbreaking plea for change directly to the two candidates running to represent their district in suburban New York during an electoral debate earlier this week. They asked Democrat Cait Conley and incumbent Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., whether they supported ending New York State's law barring local law enforcement from cooperating with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

The 18-year-old Loyola University student was shot and killed while walking with friends late at night near her Chicago college campus in March of this year. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has said the accused, Jose Medina, is a Venezuelan national who came to the U.S. illegally in May 2023 and was released by the prior administration.

He was arrested for shoplifting in Chicago the next month but released again, DHS said. Both Chicago and Illinois are sanctuary jurisdictions, meaning law enforcement there are also barred from cooperating with ICE.
GRIEVING PARENTS OF SLAIN STUDENT SHERIDAN GORMAN SPEAK OUT: 'WE CAN'T LET THIS HAPPEN TO ANOTHER FAMILY'
Jose Medina-Medina is accused of killing Sheridan Gorman. (Sheridan Gorman/Instagram and Cook County Sheriff's Office)
Gorman's killing fast became a rallying cry for supporters of President Donald Trump's crackdown on illegal immigration.

Lawler, who is fighting an uphill battle for a third term representing New York's 17th Congressional District, has also argued it is an example of what could happen more often if Democrats win control on Capitol Hill.

"Look, I've been very clear there should be reforms of ICE. They should wear body cameras. They should not wear masks. They should wear uniforms. They shouldn't be going into places like the Home Depot parking lot. They should be very targeted in what they are doing. And states like New York should be cooperating with them to deport criminal illegal aliens," Lawler told Fox News Digital on Wednesday. "So look, I think the challenge here will be if Democrats win, they will do everything they can to return to the Biden-era of lax immigration policy, lax enforcement, and try to cut off the resources of ICE and [Border Patrol], and I, for one, just will not support that."
DEM CANDIDATE CLEARS CROWDED FIELD TO FACE TRUMP-BACKED INCUMBENT IN NY
His district could be one of the few that decides control of the House for the latter half of President Trump's final term.

Gorman's parents tearfully said during his debate against Conley this week, "The man charged with her murder was here illegally and had previously been arrested for a crime and released under Chicago's sanctuary policies. A simple five-second phone call between local and federal law enforcement would have saved her life."

Madelon Gorman, joined by her parents Tom (L) and Jessica Gorman (R), gets a hug from U.S. Representative Mike Lawler as she arrives to speak about Sheridan Gorman, who was shot and killed in Chicago in March 2026, during the second day of the Republican National Committee midterm convention at the American Airlines Center in Dallas, Texas on Sept. 10, 2026. (Patrick T. Fallon / AFP via Getty Images)
Conley responded to them first, "My heart absolutely breaks, and what happened to Sheridan is inexcusable. Government failed her. And for that, we have to make sure that that doesn't happen again."
WATCH: ANGEL MOM TURNS TABLES ON SANCTUARY POLITICIANS WITH BASIC QUESTION ABOUT THEIR PRIORITIES

"Immigration enforcement is essential," she said, though added, "What is happening under this administration, unfortunately, is not a focus on violent criminals, but what we're seeing is them rolling up people like grandmas and nurses, people in our communities."

Lawler then accused Conley of dodging the question, adding, "She does support Kathy Hochul's new law, and she would not support federal legislation to end sanctuary policies. Let me be very clear: I stand with you. I am against Kathy Hochul's disastrous new law, and I support any legislation that will end sanctuary jurisdictions in this country."
DHS BOSS REVEALS OVAL OFFICE PLAN TO 'WITHHOLD FUNDING' FROM SANCTUARY CITIES AFTER AGGRESSIVE NEW YORK BUST
It came weeks after the Gormans took the stage alongside Lawler at the GOP's 2026 midterm convention in Dallas, Texas.

"The Gormans have more courage than any Democrat member of Congress who voted against protecting our citizens from criminal illegals," Lawler said in introducing them. "They are not running for office, but their story — Sheridan's story — is the direct result of bad policy. Policies we cannot afford to get back to every again."
OUTGOING HOUSE DEMOCRAT BACKS INCUMBENT REPUBLICAN LAWMAKER FOR RE-ELECTION
The teenager's story again popped up in new ads released by Lawler's campaign on Wednesday.
In one of the spots, Gorman's mother tearfully tells the viewer, "He just shot her. Just shot her. Hunted her down. I thought I knew what sanctuary city policies are, I didn't."

Former U.S. Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg attends a rally for Cait Conley, who is challenging U.S. Representative Mike Lawler to represent New York’s 17th Congressional District, on Sept. 16, 2026 in Tarrytown, N.Y. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)
SHERIDAN GORMAN’S MOM SCORCHES DEM LAWMAKERS SHE SAYS REFUSED TO HEAR FAMILIES OF SLAIN AMERICANS
"The sanctuary policies being pushed by Kathy Hochul and Democrats killed our daughter," her father said. "I couldn't protect her from these policies."
Her mother added, "But Mike Lawler can."
Illegal immigration was one of the top issues in 2024, and Republicans are trying to harness the same backlash from voters who opposed the Biden administration's more lax border policies.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Fox News Digital reached out to Conley's campaign and to House Democrats' elections arm for a response.
Elizabeth Elkind is a politics reporter for Fox News Digital leading coverage of the House of Representatives. Previous digital bylines seen at Daily Mail and CBS News.

title: Election crime arrests keep piling up as Dems insist it 'just doesn't happen'
summary: New federal cases charge noncitizens with voter fraud across multiple states, clashing with Democrats who oppose the SAVE Act and deny it happens.
story: Congressman Chip Roy details the urgency for the Save America Act to secure federal elections. He highlights a "software glitch" in New Jersey, where 6,600 non-citizens registered to vote and hundreds actually voted. Roy stresses that this widespread issue validates the need for voter ID, a measure supported by 80% of Americans, urging the Senate to pass the bill.

Federal authorities made arrests in a string of election-related indictments against noncitizens in recent weeks, colliding with Democratic claims ranging from such voting being "extremely rare" to assertions that it simply "doesn’t happen."

The cases come amid a partisan fight over the SAVE Act, which would require proof of citizenship to register to vote in federal elections. Democrats argue the measure would make voting harder for eligible Americans.
"Let me be perfectly clear: This is a non-issue. Noncitizens do not vote in U.S. elections," Rep. Mary Gay Scanlon, D-Pa., declared in 2025 after voting 'no' on the bill at the time.
Three noncitizens were arrested this month in Philadelphia County, which Scanlon partially represents, and charged with election-related offenses.
BIDEN ADMINISTRATION GRANTED WOMAN GREEN CARD MONTHS BEFORE SHE ILLEGALLY VOTED IN 2024 ELECTION: DHS
Joshua Kofi Edzie of Ghana is pictured after his arrest on noncitizen voting-related charges. (DHS)

Trinidad and Tobago national Sade Guppy allegedly voted illegally in the 2022 midterms, while Haitian illegal immigrant Cliff Sanon was charged with submitting a fraudulent voter registration application prior to the 2026 Pennsylvania primary.
DHS also pointed Fox News Digital to Mauritanian illegal immigrant Mahady Sacko, who is accused of voting in seven federal elections since 2008.
Fox News Digital reached out to Scanlon for comment.
Rep. Mary Gay Scanlon, D-Pa., who represents Delaware County and part of Philadelphia, is seen during a hearing. (Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

On Wednesday, Attorney General Todd Blanche announced indictments of 10 foreign nationals accused of committing voter fraud in Minnesota alone, including during August's primary, saying the issue should not be a "partisan concept."
The alleged illegal voters captured are from Brazil, Ghana, Germany, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Liberia and Canada.
Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., has similarly called noncitizen voting "extremely rare" while denouncing the SAVE Act as "anti-voter" and claiming Trump is trying to "scapegoat immigrants."

When asked Wednesday by Fox News Digital about the spate of arrests, Padilla reaffirmed the crime is "already illegal and every legitimate study shows it is extremely rare, despite Donald Trump’s claim to the contrary."

"The Department of Justice’s arrest of a dozen people after investigating millions of the 174 million registered voters in America confirms that," he said, adding he wished the DOJ would instead focus on reported delays in voter-registration processing in states like Texas to ensure every eligible voter can vote.
DEMOCRAT NEW JERSEY GOVERNOR SAYS THOUSANDS OF NONCITIZENS DISCOVERED ON VOTER ROLLS, PURGED
Sen. Alex Padilla speaks during a press conference at the Federal Building on Wilshire Blvd. on Thursday, June 12, 2025, in Los Angeles. (Luke Johnson / Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)
Padilla called the recent announcement of 12 arrests a "desperate attempt by Republicans to distract from their record of rising costs, chaos, and corruption that are hurting the American people."
Rep. Joe Morelle, D-N.Y., has called the SAVE Act "extremely dangerous" and "voter suppression." His office responded to Fox News Digital but did not offer comment before press time.
Last month, Democratic Rep. James Walkinshaw of Fairfax County, Virginia, spoke out similarly on MS NOW.

"It is so rare that it's almost impossible to measure. It just doesn’t happen," Walkinshaw said, surmising that Trump is trying to resurrect the "Big Lie" and "whining about the fact that he lost the 2020 election" by posturing to make similar claims after Republicans lose the midterms.
Fox News Digital also sought comment from Walkinshaw and Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., who said in March that "noncitizens do not vote in American elections."
New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill also disclosed over the summer that roughly 400 noncitizens had voted in the state while resisting calls for additional federal scrutiny.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin speaks during a press conference at the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) New York field office on Sept. 1, 2026, in New York City, New York. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)
Three New Jersey residents were also charged this month with illegally voting and making false statements on citizenship applications. They hailed from Jamaica, Venezuela and Senegal.

Asked about the dynamic, a DHS spokesperson told Fox News Digital the agency could not comment on active investigations but remains committed to "rooting out and investigating election fraud wherever it can be found," demonstrating proof.
"Despite the media and Democrats denying it for decades, noncitizens continue to register and vote in federal elections," White House spokesperson Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital.

Attendees listen to Sen. Mike Lee (R-UT) speaking at an "Only Citizens Vote" bus tour rally on passing the SAVE Act at Upper Senate Park outside the U.S. Capitol on September 10, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Kent Nishimura/Getty Images)
"Only Americans should be electing America’s leaders," she said, as clamoring from both sides of the issue grows louder ahead of key midterm elections.
Fox News' William Mears Jr. contributed to this report.

title: Progressive lawmaker's baby bump photo sparks online firestorm as she faces prison time: 'Disgusting'
summary: Rep. LaMonica McIver's pregnancy announcement while facing 17 years in prison for allegedly assaulting law enforcement sparked fierce backlash online.
story: Rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., appeared in federal court Wednesday seeking dismissal of charges she argues are the result of President Donald Trump's alleged weaponization of the Justice Department.

Rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., caused an uproar on social media when she made a post defending her decision to get pregnant despite potentially facing nearly two decades in prison for allegedly assaulting law enforcement officers at Delaney Hall detention center protests.

"People might find it crazy that even though I’m facing 17 years in prison, I made the decision to get pregnant," McIver posted to X on Tuesday. "But, at the end of the day, this is something I couldn’t let be consumed by this administration. I refuse to let them take my joy or my future."

The New Jersey congresswoman is being charged on three counts of allegedly assaulting, impeding and interfering with law enforcement. The charges stem from McIver's May 2025 visit to Delaney Hall with other Democratic lawmakers. Prosecutors allege McIver physically interfered with federal officers as they attempted to arrest Newark Mayor Ras Baraka. McIver has denied wrongdoing and argued that she was performing congressional oversight.
EXCLUSIVE: DHS SECRETARY MULLIN SLAMS SANCTUARY POLITICIANS AS ATTACKS ON ICE OFFICERS SKYROCKET
Democrat Rep. LaMonica McIver. (Department of Homeland Security)

McIver's post prompted several conservative figures and social media users to accuse her of highlighting — or even timing — her pregnancy in hopes of receiving favorable treatment in her criminal case.
"When getting pregnant is a social media stunt to avoid prison time...," Rep. Nancy Mace, R-S.C., posted to X.

"You violently assaulted a law enforcement officer on camera, then somehow convinced a man to knock you up for political reasons so you could paint yourself as a victim," New Jersey Trump delegate Mike Crispi wrote. "Disgraceful. The poor child."
"Why is your pregnancy amid the criminal charges a social media stunt accompanied with a photoshoot?" conservative journalist Andy Ngo said. "Is anyone in your office normal?
"Getting pregnant to sway justice is a whole new level of sick," one X user posted.
"Why would I find it crazy?" another user said. "You are a cheater & a fraud and, true to character, you became pregnant in an attempt to sway the outcome of the court in your favor."
TRUMP ADMINISTRATION HAS LOST OR ABANDONED HUNDREDS OF LAWSUITS AGAINST ANTI-ICE PROTESTERS, MIGRANTS: REPORT

Rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., took to social media with a new pregnancy picture, defending her "decision" to get pregnant despite facing potential prison time for allegedly assaulting federal law enforcement officers at Delaney Hall detention center in New Jersey. (Rep. LaMonica Mciver via X)

"Facing 17 years, gets pregnant in hope of leniency," another user wrote. "‘I refuse to let them take my joy or my future.’ as the excuse. Congratulations on giving your child the best possible start to life. You are just a genuinely disgusting person."

The post comes about a month after a divided federal appeals court allowed two charges against McIver to proceed while sending a third back to the district court for further consideration of her legislative-immunity argument.
McIver argued that she should have immunity from prosecution because she was carrying out her duties as a congresswoman in her actions that led to her being charged, calling the charges "vindictive."
"Oh stop with the desperate need for sympathy," one posted to X. "YOU are not above the law."
"You are on camera assaulting law enforcement," another said. "You are not above the law, you swore to defend it and broke it."
One user left a screenshot of a past tweet from McIver where she posted saying, "No one is above the law! Full stop."
AOC DOCUMENTS EGG-FREEZING JOURNEY, TAKES AIM AT TRUMP ADMIN OVER WOMEN'S REPRODUCTIVE CHOICES
Congresswoman Rep. LaMonica McIver demands the release of Newark Mayor Ras Baraka after his arrest while protesting outside an ICE facility on May 9, in Newark, N.J. (AP/Angelina Katsanis)
McIver faces multiple felony charges and, if convicted, could face prison time.
McIver did not respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment.

Despite the charges, McIver is on the ballot for re-election to continue to represent New Jersey’s 10th Congressional District.
Hannah is a Production Assistant for the Politics team at Fox News Digital.

title: ICE arrests illegal alien accused of sexually assaulting children after Fairfax County release: DHS
summary: DHS says Fairfax County, Virginia, released Oscar Evaristo Nunez, a Honduran immigrant charged with child sex crimes, despite an ICE detainer.
story: Fairfax County, Virginia, officials face scrutiny as illegal immigrant crime, including child sexual offenses and murders, dramatically rises. A DHS report says 75% of all murders in Fairfax County are committed by illegal aliens, fueling intense debate over the county's controversial sanctuary city policies and their impact on public safety.

A Honduran illegal immigrant facing multiple child sex crime charges is back in federal custody after authorities in Fairfax County, Virginia, released him from an immigration detainer, according to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrested Oscar Evaristo Nunez Sept. 15 during a targeted enforcement operation, DHS announced Wednesday.
Nunez was initially arrested Aug. 27, 2025, on charges of aggravated sexual battery involving children and offenses related to the non-consensual filming of an undressed minor, according to DHS.
ICE lodged a detainer with the Fairfax County Adult Detention Center two days later, but DHS said local authorities did not honor it and released Nunez without notifying the agency.
GUATEMALAN MAN CHARGED WITH CHILD PORN POSSESSION RELEASED BY FAIRFAX COUNTY DESPITE ICE DETAINER, DHS SAYS
Oscar Evaristo Nunez, a Honduran national facing multiple child sex crime charges in Virginia. (Department of Homeland Security)
The case has become the latest point of contention between the Trump administration and Virginia officials over cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.

"Another criminal illegal alien has been taken off the streets by the brave men and women of ICE with no help from sanctuary politicians in Fairfax County," DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a news release.
"This illegal alien from Honduras had been arrested for child sex crimes in August last year, but Fairfax County refused to honor ICE’s detainer and let this creep back out onto the streets.

"Once again, ICE did the job that these heartless sanctuary politicians won’t do: enforce the law and protect American lives. DHS is calling on Gov. Abigail Spanberger and her fellow sanctuary politicians to stop putting the needs of illegal aliens over the safety of the American people."‘OUT OF CONTROL’ KILLINGS IN SPANBERGER’S VIRGINIA REACH ‘INSANE’ POINT AS MIGRANT CHARGED IN STABBING SPREE

The case has become the latest point of contention between the Trump administration and Virginia officials over cooperation with federal immigration enforcement. (Jaque Silva/NurPhoto via Getty Images, File)
Spanberger, a Democrat, was not governor when Nunez was arrested, and ICE filed the detainer in August 2025. She took office in January 2026.

Spanberger has moved Virginia away from some forms of state participation in federal immigration enforcement since taking office, including directing state agencies to terminate agreements with ICE under the federal 287(g) program.
A representative for Fairfax County did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.
Oscar Evaristo Nunez sits in a vehicle after his arrest by ICE Sept. 15. (Department of Homeland Security)
DHS said Nunez illegally entered the U.S. near Arizona around September 2003.

Nunez remains in ICE custody pending immigration proceedings.
Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.

title: Chinese AI model investigated after researcher says it provided instructions for bioweapons, assassinations
summary: Researcher Peter Garrigan says Moonshot AI's Kimi model was manipulated into providing instructions for biological weapons and assassination plans.
story: Fox News senior foreign policy correspondent Gillian Turner reports on researchers’ tests of a popular Chinese AI model and the concerns raised by its responses. She examines how the findings are fueling broader questions about rogue behavior in advanced AI systems on ‘Special Report.’

Chinese AI company Moonshot AI has launched an internal investigation after a researcher found that one of its models could be manipulated into providing instructions for developing biological weapons and carrying out assassinations, Fox News senior foreign policy correspondent Gillian Turner reported Thursday.

Researcher Peter Garrigan told Fox News Moonshot AI's Kimi model could also be manipulated to provide information on planning terrorist attacks using real-time data, creating sarin gas, developing malware and taking down aircraft.
"What we found is quite damaging and worrying," Garrigan said.
BIOWEAPON THREAT EXPOSED AS ANTHROPIC SOUNDS ALARM ON FOREIGN ACTORS PLOTTING VIRUS EXPERIMENTS
Moonshot AI's Kimi-K3 model is displayed at the Global Digital Trade Expo in Hangzhou, China, Sept. 23, 2026. (Costfoto/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
The findings are raising broader concerns about advanced AI models concealing capabilities or behaving in ways their developers did not intend.
"We've also seen these problems within the U.S. models as well. It's a fundamental flaw in the technology," Garrigan said.
Artificial intelligence is helping hackers write phishing emails, build malware and move faster through cyberattacks, according to Microsoft Threat Intelligence. (shapecharge/Getty Images)

title: Make unknown callers explain why they're calling
summary: iPhone, Google Pixel and Samsung Galaxy phones now offer call screening that asks unknown callers to identify themselves before your phone rings.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

You know the feeling. Your phone rings, you look down and see a number you do not recognize. Now you have to decide whether to answer or let it go to voicemail. That choice gets harder when you are expecting a call from a doctor, repair person or someone else who may not be in your contacts.

Fortunately, your phone can now help figure out who is on the other end before you get involved. With iOS 27, your iPhone can ask an unknown caller for their name and why they are calling. Google Pixel phones have their own Call Screen feature. Compatible Samsung Galaxy phones can also use AI-powered call screening. Here is how each one works on the latest software.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways AI can help you get better healthcare.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class Get Better Healthcare With AI has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com
ANDROID FAKE CALL DETECTION WARNS YOU ABOUT SCAMS
Call screening tools can help you decide whether an unknown caller deserves your attention before you answer. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How to screen unknown callers on iPhone

Apple's Call Screening feature can automatically answer calls from unknown numbers without interrupting you. The caller gets asked for their name and the reason for the call. After they respond, your iPhone rings and shows you what they said. That gives you a little more information before deciding whether to answer.
Open SettingsScroll down and tap AppsTap PhoneScroll to Screen Unknown CallersSelect Ask Reason for Calling
Open Settings
Scroll down and tap Apps
Tap Phone
Scroll to Screen Unknown Callers
Select Ask Reason for Calling

Once you turn it on, calls from unknown numbers are asked for more information before your iPhone rings. Apple also gives you two other options in the same section. Never turn Call Screening off. Silence sends calls from unsaved numbers directly to voicemail and keeps them in your Recents list. For many people, Ask Reason for Calling may offer a useful middle ground. You can still hear from someone important without immediately answering every unfamiliar number.

While you are in the Phone settings, you can also review Apple's call filtering options. Go to Settings → Apps → Phone, then scroll to the call filtering section. Turning on Spam lets your carrier identify potential spam or fraud calls. Those calls can then be silenced, sent to voicemail and moved into the Spam list. You can also turn on Unknown Callers. That moves calls from unknown numbers out of your main Recents list and into a separate Unknown Callers list.
FAKE VERIZON FRAUD CALL NEARLY STOLE HIS ACCOUNT
iOS 27 can ask callers from unsaved numbers why they are calling before your iPhone rings. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How Samsung Galaxy screens unknown calls

Samsung has also brought call screening to compatible Galaxy phones. Samsung says the feature is available on supported Galaxy phones running One UI 8.5 or later. However, feature availability can still vary by Galaxy model, carrier and region. Galaxy Call screening can answer the caller and ask why they are calling. You can then read the caller's response as a live transcription.
Open the Phone appTap the three vertical dotsTap SettingsTap Call screeningTurn on Call screeningTurn on Auto screen calls if you want unknown calls screened automatically
Open the Phone app
Tap the three vertical dots
Tap Settings
Tap Call screening
Turn on Call screening
Turn on Auto screen calls if you want unknown calls screened automatically

Samsung also lets you choose a transcription language and customize the assistant's voice. If you prefer to decide which calls get screened, you can do that manually. When an incoming call appears, tap Call assist, then tap Call screening. The AI assistant answers for you and asks the caller to state the purpose of the call. Their response then appears as text on your screen. If you do not see Call screening, check for the latest Galaxy software update. You should also make sure the Samsung Phone app is current. Some Galaxy models may not support the feature.
On compatible Samsung Galaxy phones, turn on Call screening and Auto screen calls to automatically screen suspected spam and scam calls. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How to screen unknown calls on a Google Pixel

Google Pixel phones take a slightly different approach with Call Screen. The feature can answer certain calls for you and ask the caller why they are calling. Depending on your Pixel and settings, Google can also screen some calls automatically.
Open the Phone appTap the three dotsTap SettingsTap Spam and Call Screen or Call ScreenTap Call ScreenTurn on Automatic Call ScreenChoose your preferred protection level
Open the Phone app
Tap the three dots
Tap Settings
Tap Spam and Call Screen or Call Screen
Tap Call Screen
Turn on Automatic Call Screen
Choose your preferred protection level

On newer Pixel phones, you may see Maximum protection, Medium protection and Basic protection. Medium protection is Google's recommended setting and screens suspicious calls while declining known spam. Maximum protection screens unknown numbers more aggressively, while Basic protection mainly declines known spam. You can still screen a call manually. When an unfamiliar number comes in, tap Screen call. Call Assist will ask who is calling and why while you watch the response appear as a live transcript. From there, you can answer the call, hang up or use one of the suggested responses.
Pixel’s Automatic Call Screen can screen suspicious calls and decline known spam before they reach you. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Why screening can beat automatically silencing every unknown caller

Sending every unfamiliar number straight to voicemail certainly cuts down on interruptions. However, it can also send legitimate callers there. Maybe you are waiting for a medical office to call from a number you have never seen. Perhaps a service technician needs to reach you from a work phone. Call screening gives that person a chance to explain why they are trying to reach you. You can then make the call about whether to answer.

There is also a security benefit. Scam callers often count on getting someone on the phone quickly. Screening puts another step between the caller and you. However, do not assume someone is legitimate simply because they answered the screening question. Scammers can still lie about who they are. Caller ID can also be spoofed.
Do not let a convincing answer lower your guard

Call screening gives you information. It does not verify someone's identity. If a caller claims to represent your bank or another company and suddenly asks for money or login information, end the call. The same advice applies if someone asks for a one-time security code. Instead, contact the organization yourself through its official app or website. For financial accounts, you can also use the phone number printed on your card or statement. This is especially important because phone scams continue to get more convincing. Scammers can spoof familiar numbers and create a sense of urgency to push you into acting quickly.
Kurt's key takeaways

I like the idea of making an unknown caller explain themselves before they get my attention. With iOS 27, iPhone owners can have unfamiliar callers provide a name and reason before the phone rings. Pixel owners can use Google's Call Screen, while compatible Galaxy phones offer their own call screening feature. For me, screening makes more sense than automatically silencing every unfamiliar number. There are plenty of legitimate reasons someone outside your contacts may need to reach you. Still, treat the screening response as information rather than proof. If the conversation turns to passwords, money or account access, hang up and contact the company yourself.

title: How to protect family photos and files from ransomware
summary: Ransomware can lock your irreplaceable photos and documents in seconds. A tested backup strategy and stronger cybersecurity habits are your best defense.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

Think about what you would be most upset to lose if something happened to your computer. For me, it would be the photos and videos you cannot replace. But your computer may also hold years of tax returns, medical records, scanned IDs, insurance paperwork, legal documents and other files you would hate to suddenly lose access to.

That is exactly what makes ransomware so damaging. It can lock or encrypt files so you can no longer open them, then the attacker demands money to give you access again. Even if you pay, there is no guarantee you will get everything back. By the time a ransom message appears on your screen, a lot of the damage may already be done.
The smarter move is to prepare before that ever happens. Here are the steps I would take to protect the files you care about most and make recovery a lot easier if ransomware ever hits.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways AI can help you get better healthcare.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class Get Better Healthcare With AI has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
153 MILLION DRIVER'S LICENSE SCANS MAY BE ON THE DARK WEB
Family photos, tax records and other important files can be difficult or impossible to replace if ransomware locks you out of them. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Start with the files you would hate to lose

Before choosing a backup method, make a short list of your most important files. You do not have to organize your entire computer in one afternoon. Start with family photos and videos, recent tax returns, medical and insurance records, passports or scanned IDs, mortgage or lease documents, wills, financial statements and work or creative projects. Include files stored in your Downloads, Desktop and Documents folders if they are important to you.

Give files clear names and place them in easy-to-find folders. For example, you might create folders called "Taxes," "Medical," "Home," "Family Photos" and "Important IDs." This makes it easier to back up the right material and find it later. Avoid keeping the only copy of a document in an email inbox, on a phone or inside a single computer folder. Those locations may be convenient, but they should not be your entire backup strategy.
Build backups before you need them

A backup is another copy of a file stored somewhere else. If your computer fails, is stolen or becomes infected, you have a way to recover your information. One commonly recommended approach is the 3-2-1 backup strategy: keep three copies of important data on two different types of storage, with at least one copy kept somewhere separate from your main device or location. For many households, a practical setup might include the files on your computer, a regularly updated external drive and a trusted cloud backup or storage service.

Keep an external backup drive disconnected when you are not using it. If it remains attached to an infected computer, ransomware may be able to reach files on that drive too. Cloud services can add another layer between your files and your computer. Before relying on one, check what it covers, how much storage is included and how file restoration works. Also remember that cloud storage and cloud backup are not always the same thing. A storage service may sync changes across devices, while a backup service may provide separate copies or previous versions that can help with recovery.
Make your backups useful, not just automatic

Automatic backups are helpful because you do not have to remember to run them every week. But an automatic backup does you little good if you cannot restore anything from it. Choose a few files occasionally and confirm that they appear in your backup location. Then try restoring a copy to a different folder. This can uncover problems with permissions, file selection or an expired account before you are dealing with an emergency. Protect backup and cloud-storage accounts with strong, unique passwords and multifactor authentication. Multifactor authentication requires another form of verification beyond your password and can make it harder for someone to get into your account if your password is compromised.

Pay attention to the date of your most recent successful backup. A backup that has not run for months may be missing your newest family photos, tax records or work. Also look at whether your service keeps previous versions of files. Version history can be useful if something is accidentally deleted, overwritten or encrypted. Check your provider's retention and recovery policies so you know how far back you can restore files.
SCAMMERS KNOW THE BEST TIME TO TEXT YOU
A disconnected external drive can give you a separate copy of important files that ransomware on your computer cannot easily reach. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Reduce the chance of ransomware getting in
Ransomware can start with a deceptive email, text message, website, attachment or download. A few habits can help reduce the chances of letting it onto your computer in the first place:

Be suspicious of unexpected messages. A scam may claim that a package is delayed, an account needs attention or an invoice is overdue. Pause before opening attachments or clicking links.Go directly to the source. If a message appears to come from a bank, tax service, medical provider or government agency, open the organization's official website or app yourself instead of following a link in the message.Download software from trusted sources. Stick with the developer's official website or a trusted app store. Be cautious with free screensavers, unexpected browser-update warnings, unofficial video players and software that asks you to turn off security protections before installing it.Keep your software updated. Install updates for your operating system, browser and commonly used applications. Turn on automatic updates where practical so known security holes are patched sooner.Use a standard account for everyday use. When possible, avoid using an administrator account for routine tasks. That can limit some of the changes an unwanted program is allowed to make.Give each person their own account. If several people share a computer, use separate accounts instead of sharing one login and password.
Be suspicious of unexpected messages. A scam may claim that a package is delayed, an account needs attention or an invoice is overdue. Pause before opening attachments or clicking links.

Go directly to the source. If a message appears to come from a bank, tax service, medical provider or government agency, open the organization's official website or app yourself instead of following a link in the message.

Download software from trusted sources. Stick with the developer's official website or a trusted app store. Be cautious with free screensavers, unexpected browser-update warnings, unofficial video players and software that asks you to turn off security protections before installing it.
Keep your software updated. Install updates for your operating system, browser and commonly used applications. Turn on automatic updates where practical so known security holes are patched sooner.
Use a standard account for everyday use. When possible, avoid using an administrator account for routine tasks. That can limit some of the changes an unwanted program is allowed to make.
Give each person their own account. If several people share a computer, use separate accounts instead of sharing one login and password.
What to do if files suddenly look encrypted

If files suddenly will not open, filenames or extensions have changed or a ransom message appears, act quickly. What you do next can help limit the damage and protect any clean backups you still have.

Disconnect the computer from Wi-Fi and unplug its Ethernet cable if one is connected. This can help stop ransomware from reaching shared drives, other computers or network resources. Also, disconnect external hard drives or other backup storage if you can do so safely. If you cannot disconnect the affected computer from the network, powering it down may help stop further spread. Disconnecting it first is preferable because shutting down the computer can erase information from memory that may be useful during an investigation.

Do not start deleting encrypted files or the ransom note. They may contain information that helps identify the ransomware involved. If a ransom message is displayed, take a photo of it with another device so you have a record of what appeared on the screen. Do not open additional suspicious files, install random recovery programs or follow instructions in the ransom note without first getting professional guidance.

Paying does not guarantee that you will receive a working decryption key or get your files back. The FBI does not support paying ransomware demands and recommends that victims report ransomware incidents.

If this is a personal computer, contact your security provider or a reputable computer-repair or cybersecurity professional. You can also report ransomware to the FBI through the Internet Crime Complaint Center at IC3.gov or contact your local FBI field office. If the affected computer belongs to your employer, stop using it and contact your IT or security department immediately. Do not attempt to clean or restore a work computer yourself unless your organization instructs you to do so.

Do not reconnect an external backup drive to an infected computer. The affected device should first be evaluated, cleaned or rebuilt so you do not accidentally expose a good backup to the same ransomware. Once the computer is clean, you can restore files from a backup created before the ransomware infection. If you do not have a usable backup, recovery can be much more difficult. Some ransomware variants have free decryption tools available, but there is no universal tool that can recover every encrypted file.
Safer online habits, software updates and security protection can help reduce the chances of ransomware getting onto your device. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Add another layer of protection against ransomware

Strong security software can add another layer between your important files and ransomware. Look for real-time protection that continuously monitors for malware, suspicious downloads and other threats instead of relying only on occasional manual scans.

A firewall can also help monitor network activity and block suspicious connections, while tools such as password managers and scam protection can help reduce other ways attackers may try to get into your accounts or devices.

Security software can lower your risk, but no product can guarantee that every threat will be stopped. That is why it should work alongside safer online habits and a separate, tested backup that gives you another way to recover your files if ransomware gets through.
Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.
A simple monthly protection routine
You do not need to spend hours managing your cybersecurity. Once a month, set aside a few minutes to check the protections you already have in place.

Confirm that your operating system, browser and security software are updated.Delete old downloads and remove software you no longer use.Review important accounts and turn on two-factor authentication (2FA) where it is available.
Confirm that your operating system, browser and security software are updated.
Delete old downloads and remove software you no longer use.
Review important accounts and turn on two-factor authentication (2FA) where it is available.

Check the date of your most recent successful backup and make sure it includes your newest important files.Open your backup and restore one backed-up file to a different folder so you know recovery works.If you use an external drive, disconnect it after the backup finishes instead of leaving it plugged in all the time.Keep at least one backup isolated from your main computer, such as on a disconnected external drive or in a separately protected backup service.If you use cloud backup, review its file-version history and recovery settings, so you know how far back you can restore files.
Check the date of your most recent successful backup and make sure it includes your newest important files.
Open your backup and restore one backed-up file to a different folder so you know recovery works.
If you use an external drive, disconnect it after the backup finishes instead of leaving it plugged in all the time.
Keep at least one backup isolated from your main computer, such as on a disconnected external drive or in a separately protected backup service.
If you use cloud backup, review its file-version history and recovery settings, so you know how far back you can restore files.
Make sure family members know not to click unexpected links, open suspicious attachments or approve unusual sign-in requests.
Make sure family members know not to click unexpected links, open suspicious attachments or approve unusual sign-in requests.

This routine is not complicated, and it does not require you to become a cybersecurity expert. The goal is to make sure that if ransomware, a device failure or another problem hits, you already have another copy of the files you care about and know how to get them back.
Kurt's key takeaways

Ransomware can turn years of family photos and important records into files you suddenly cannot open. For me, security software and safer online habits are only part of the protection I want in place. I also want a separate backup of anything I would be devastated to lose, and I want to know that backup actually works before I need it. Spending a few minutes each month checking updates, backups and account security can put you in a much better position if ransomware ever hits.
If ransomware locked your computer today, how confident are you that you could recover the photos and documents you care about most? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: FBI hack claim raises fears over sensitive personal data
summary: ShinyHunters claims it breached FBIJobs.gov and stole Social Security numbers, home addresses and sensitive assignment details of FBI personnel.
story: Following the arrest of an alleged leader in the Netherlands, a top FBI cyber official released an unusual public address urging the remaining cybercriminals to turn themselves in "while the choice is still yours."

If you have ever filled out a job application, handed over your Social Security number for a background check or trusted an organization with information about your family, pay attention to what happened at the FBI.

The cybercriminal group ShinyHunters claims it compromised FBIJobs.gov and stole highly sensitive information connected to current and former FBI personnel and people who applied for jobs at the bureau. The group says its haul reaches far beyond basic contact information.

On Sept. 23, the FBI acknowledged the group's claims and said it was "actively and aggressively investigating" the incident. The bureau said investigators had not yet determined whether the point of breach involved an FBI system or a third-party provider supporting FBIJobs.gov.

That uncertainty is important. At the same time, samples provided to journalists contain enough real-world information to make the situation difficult to dismiss. For anyone whose details may be included, the potential fallout goes well beyond having an email address leaked.
FBI SAYS SOURCE OF ITS JOBS PORTAL BREACH STILL UNKNOWN AS HACKERS ALLEGE EMPLOYEE DATA COMPROMISED

Since that statement, the FBI has struck back by announcing the arrest of an alleged ShinyHunters leader in the Netherlands after a joint operation with Dutch authorities. Dutch police said a 24-year-old Amsterdam man was arrested Sept. 15.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways AI can help you get better healthcare.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Get Better Healthcare With AI, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com
FBI investigators monitor digital threats as questions remain over how the FBIJobs.gov incident occurred and what information may have been exposed. (FBI)
What the FBI said about the FBIJobs.gov incident
In its Sept. 23 statement, the FBI addressed both the alleged compromise and the uncertainty surrounding where the attackers may have gained access.

"The FBI is aware of a cybercriminal enterprise group claiming a compromise of the fbijobs.gov portal," the bureau said. It added that the point of breach remained undetermined and said it was "actively and aggressively investigating this matter."

The FBI also said investigators were working closely with third-party providers that support FBIJobs.gov to reduce potential risk. The FBI confirmed the investigation and the unresolved question about where the breach occurred. It did not verify ShinyHunters' full account of what the group says it stole.

The FBI's Special Agent Applicant Portal also became unavailable as the incident unfolded. A notice posted Sept. 22 said FBIJobs.gov and the Special Agent Applicant Portal were unavailable. The applicant portal supports people who have progressed through portions of the special-agent hiring process, making the type of information potentially involved especially sensitive.

CyberGuy reached out to the FBI for an update on the incident, including whether employee or applicant data was accessed and whether affected individuals are being notified or offered identity protection. We did not hear back before our deadline.
The data sample raises much bigger concerns

ShinyHunters provided journalists with a spreadsheet containing about 5,000 alleged FBI personnel records. Reuters reported that the spreadsheet included names, home addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, Social Security numbers and emergency contact information. It also included information about field office assignments and, in some cases, sensitive intelligence or counterespionage work.

Reuters said it could not authenticate the entire spreadsheet. However, reporters independently verified details belonging to more than 22 people by comparing the information with credit records and earlier leaked data. Reuters also matched career information or job titles for eight people against court filings, news reports, public profiles and online posts.

That still does not establish where every record came from. Real information can appear in several databases or previous breaches. Yet the matches add credibility to at least portions of the sample. 404 Media separately reported that the 5,000-person sample contained names, home addresses, phone numbers and information involving FBI employees' spouses.
Sensitive FBI assignments reportedly appeared in the data

The personal information alone creates obvious privacy concerns. The reported job information raises another level of risk. Reuters found records identifying people connected to China-related investigations, Russian intelligence work, human intelligence operations and electronic surveillance. Other entries referenced covert access, clandestine technical operations and telecommunications interception. Reuters said it could not verify that every assignment was authentic or up to date.

On Sept. 23, 404 Media also reported that the data appeared to expose members of the FBI's Remote Operations Unit. The outlet describes the ROU as a secretive FBI team involved in developing and using hacking tools to gain access to target devices. Think about what that combination of information could provide to someone with bad intentions.

A name may lead to a home address. An emergency contact could identify a spouse or child. Job information might reveal the kind of investigations someone works on. For an FBI employee working in a sensitive position, that creates risks far beyond ordinary financial fraud.
IS YOUR SOCIAL SECURITY NUMBER ON THE DARK WEB?
FBI cyber personnel work at computer stations as the bureau investigates claims that hackers accessed sensitive data tied to employees and job applicants. (FBI)
What ShinyHunters claims happened

ShinyHunters says it breached the FBI and stole between 2 and 3 terabytes of information connected to FBI personnel and job applicants. The group has also claimed that Justice Department worker data was obtained. The hackers claim they exploited a previously unknown vulnerability involving Oracle PeopleSoft, software used for human resources and other enterprise functions.

FBI documents reportedly show its recruiting operation uses PeopleSoft and AWS GovCloud. However, that does not prove the hackers' claimed method of attack. The alleged PeopleSoft vulnerability, the claimed 2-to-3-terabyte haul and a broader compromise of FBI systems had not been independently verified.

Reuters also reported that ShinyHunters claimed to possess files involving employee and applicant vetting, contracted background investigations and sensitive medical information. Reuters said it could not verify what additional information the hackers actually possessed. That caveat is critical. ShinyHunters has an obvious interest in making its access sound as extensive as possible. For now, there are signs that portions of the information supplied by the hackers correspond to real people. Major questions about the source, scope and attack path remain unresolved in the FBI's public statement.
Why ShinyHunters says it targeted the FBI

ShinyHunters says retaliation, rather than a demand for money, motivated the attack. The group points to warnings the FBI issued about ShinyHunters-related cyber activity earlier in 2026. On May 15, the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center published an advisory describing ShinyHunters as a cybercriminal group specializing in large-scale data breaches and extortion.

The advisory warned that actors using the name may use real or exaggerated claims about stolen information to pressure victims. It also described threatening communications, harassment of family members and swatting among tactics associated with ShinyHunters actors. ShinyHunters disputes portions of the FBI's description of its activities. Reuters reported that the group said it targeted the FBI because of the May warning and said it was holding the allegedly stolen data while demanding that the bureau rescind the statement.
Why you should care even if you never worked for the FBI

You may read a headline about FBI employees and assume this has little to do with you. Yet the way the alleged data could be abused should feel familiar to anyone who has handed personal information to an employer, bank, health provider, insurance company or government agency. Organizations often collect far more than your name and email address. They may hold your home address, Social Security number, birthdate, employment history and emergency contacts. Job applications can contain years of background information.

You may have done everything right and still have that information exposed because the organization holding it or one of its technology providers was attacked. That third-party piece deserves attention here. In its Sept. 23 statement, the FBI specifically said investigators had not determined whether the breach point involved its own enterprise or a third party.

The same setup exists throughout everyday life. Your employer might use an outside payroll provider. Your doctor's office may rely on billing software from another company. Retailers routinely send information through outside payment systems. Once you hand over your personal data, you often have little visibility into how many systems eventually store or process it.
FBI headquarters in Washington, D.C. The bureau is investigating ShinyHunters’ claims that sensitive personnel and applicant data was stolen. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images)
Stolen personal details make scams much harder to spot

Suppose someone emails you and knows your full name, employer and home address. Then the person mentions your spouse or a job application you actually submitted. That message feels very different from a generic scam email. This is why personal data can be so useful to attackers. They can combine stolen records with information already available from data brokers, social media or previous breaches. The result can be a phishing message tailored closely enough to make you hesitate before questioning it.

Cybercriminals could pose as an FBI recruiter or someone from an employer's human resources department. They could even claim they are contacting you to help protect information exposed in the breach. The FBI's May advisory warned that stolen personal information can help attackers create targeted campaigns and pressure victims.
What FBI applicants, employees and families should do now
Even while investigators work to establish the full scope, anyone who believes their information may be involved can take precautions.

If you applied for an FBI job, be suspicious of calls, texts or emails claiming you need to reenter information because of the portal incident. Do not use a link or phone number contained in an unexpected message. Contact your existing applicant coordinator or reach the FBI through a channel you already know. The FBI's own ShinyHunters guidance recommends verifying unusual requests through another method before responding.

This step becomes particularly important because the reported sample included spouses and emergency contacts. Tell people listed on employment or application records to be cautious if someone suddenly knows their connection to you. Criminals may target a relative because they expect that person to have fewer security safeguards. If someone claims there is an urgent problem involving you, an employer or law enforcement, verify the story independently before sharing information or sending money.

A credit freeze can make it harder for someone to open a new credit account in your name. You need to place the freeze separately with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. The FTC says credit freezes are free and remain in place until you lift them. A freeze will not prevent every form of identity theft. Continue monitoring accounts you already have.

If your Social Security number may have been exposed, an IRS Identity Protection PIN can help protect you from tax identity theft. The six-digit IP PIN prevents someone else from filing a federal tax return using your Social Security number or Individual Taxpayer Identification Number. Anyone with an SSN or ITIN who can verify their identity can request one. Keep the number private. The IRS says it will never call, email or text you asking for your IP PIN.

Look for new accounts you do not recognize, unfamiliar charges or changes to existing accounts. Also pay attention to unexpected IRS notices, rejected tax filings and medical bills or insurance explanations of benefits for treatment you never received. These can signal types of identity theft that a credit freeze alone may not stop. If you discover identity theft, report it through IdentityTheft.gov and follow the recovery plan for the information that was compromised.

Neither Reuters nor the FBI's Sept. 23 statement said passwords were included in the 5,000-record sample. Still, exposed personal details can make attempts to steal your passwords much more convincing. Use a unique password for every important account. A password manager can help keep track of them. Turn on two-factor authentication (2FA) or passkeys wherever available. Also be cautious about unexpected password-reset requests.

A personalized phishing message can still contain a malicious link or infected attachment. Strong antivirus software can help detect known phishing websites, malicious downloads and malware before they compromise your device. That gives you another layer of protection if a convincing email or text gets through. Security software cannot replace careful clicking, but it can help when a scam looks unusually believable. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

If your home address, phone number and relatives already appear on people search sites, leaked records can give criminals even more information to work with. Search for yourself online and review what is publicly visible. You can request removal from many data broker and people search sites yourself or use a personal data removal service to handle recurring opt-out requests. Reducing what is publicly available gives a criminal fewer pieces to combine with information from a breach. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.

Dark web monitoring can alert you when information tied to your email address, phone number, Social Security number or other identifiers appears in known breach collections. Some identity theft companies include Dark Web Monitoring that searches for exposed personal information and alerts you when it is found. However, treat an alert as a warning rather than proof that someone has stolen your identity. Monitoring cannot prevent information from circulating once criminals obtain it. Its value comes from giving you an opportunity to secure affected accounts, watch for fraud and take action sooner. See my tips and best picks on best identity theft protection at CyberGuy.com.

The FBI's guidance involving ShinyHunters recommends against paying or engaging with threat actors making demands. Save threatening communications instead. Preserve screenshots, email addresses, phone numbers and other identifying information. You can report cybercrime through the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at IC3.gov. If someone appears to face an immediate physical threat, contact emergency services.

There are still major unanswered questions about the FBIJobs.gov incident. The FBI's Sept. 23 statement left the point of breach unresolved, and the bureau had not publicly validated ShinyHunters' claim that it stole between 2 and 3 terabytes of data. Still, the data samples deserve serious attention. Reuters verified details belonging to more than 22 people and reported that the spreadsheet contained Social Security numbers, home addresses, dates of birth, emergency contacts and information about sensitive assignments. What concerns me most is how useful those pieces become when they are connected.

A criminal who knows where you work, where you live and who your spouse is has a much easier time building a scam that feels authentic. For FBI personnel tied to intelligence or covert technical work, the exposure could create security concerns that reach well beyond financial fraud. The takeaway for the rest of us is practical. You cannot control the security of every employer, government agency or company holding your information. You can control how much information about you remains publicly available, how strongly your accounts are protected and how quickly you respond when something suspicious appears.

If information this sensitive can potentially be exposed through a system connected to the FBI, how confident are you about the employers, companies and government agencies holding your personal data? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.
