New account fraud can be difficult to detect because criminals may open credit cards, phone accounts or other services without touching accounts victims already monitor. (Thomas Fuller/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)
How new account fraud usually works

With fraud targeting an account you already use, you have a decent chance of spotting it quickly. A strange purchase shows up, your bank sends an alert or your card suddenly stops working. New account fraud can stay much quieter. A criminal applies for a new account using enough of your personal information to pose as you. If the application goes through, the account may be tied to an address, phone number or email account the criminal controls. As far as the lender or company knows, you opened it.

The first clue could be a hard inquiry on your credit report, a new account you do not recognize or mail welcoming you to a service you never signed up for. But there is an important catch. Not every type of account appears on all three credit reports, and some phone, utility or buy now, pay later activity may not appear there. That is why checking your credit reports helps, but it should not be the only thing you watch.
Why new account fraud keeps growing

Criminals have more stolen personal information to work with than ever. Years of data breaches have exposed names, Social Security numbers, birthdates, addresses, email addresses and other details that can help someone impersonate you. A criminal may also combine information from multiple breaches, phishing attacks or data broker records to build a much fuller picture of your identity.

At the same time, opening financial and other accounts online has become incredibly convenient. You can apply from your couch and sometimes get a decision within minutes. That convenience works in our favor when we are the ones applying. It can also give criminals more opportunities to try stolen identities without ever walking into a bank or store.

The Federal Reserve has also warned that digital account openings create new opportunities for fraudsters, especially as stolen personal information and more sophisticated technology become easier for criminals to use.
A closer look at how this can start

A criminal may not get everything needed to steal your identity from one breach. Your name and email could come from one leak. An older breach might expose other personal information. A people search site may help fill in an address or phone number. Put enough pieces together and a criminal may have what is needed to start testing your identity against lenders, retailers, phone carriers and other companies. That also helps explain why identity theft can seem to come out of nowhere. The information used against you may have been floating around for months or even years before someone decided to use it.
Where the evidence can show up
New account fraud can leave clues in several places, and some of them are easy to miss if you do not know where to look.

Your credit reports: Start here. Look for accounts and hard inquiries you do not recognize. Check Equifax, Experian and TransUnion because the information can differ from one bureau to another. You can currently get your reports from all three bureaus for free every week through AnnualCreditReport.com. Remember that a clean credit report does not rule out every kind of new account fraud. Some accounts may not be reported to the major credit bureaus.Mail and email you did not expect: Watch for welcome letters, account statements, verification messages, approval notices or rejection letters tied to applications you never submitted.Calls or letters from debt collectors: Do not automatically dismiss a collection attempt because you do not recognize the debt. Ask what company originated the account and investigate it.Phone, utility and buy now, pay later activity: These accounts can sometimes fly under the radar because they may not appear on a traditional credit report. Account-monitoring services may offer additional alerts for some of these categories.Addresses or other information you do not recognize: Your credit report can also contain addresses and other identifying details. An unfamiliar entry deserves a closer look, especially if it appears alongside an account or inquiry you do not recognize.

Your credit reports: Start here. Look for accounts and hard inquiries you do not recognize. Check Equifax, Experian and TransUnion because the information can differ from one bureau to another. You can currently get your reports from all three bureaus for free every week through AnnualCreditReport.com. Remember that a clean credit report does not rule out every kind of new account fraud. Some accounts may not be reported to the major credit bureaus.
Mail and email you did not expect: Watch for welcome letters, account statements, verification messages, approval notices or rejection letters tied to applications you never submitted.
Calls or letters from debt collectors: Do not automatically dismiss a collection attempt because you do not recognize the debt. Ask what company originated the account and investigate it.

Phone, utility and buy now, pay later activity: These accounts can sometimes fly under the radar because they may not appear on a traditional credit report. Account-monitoring services may offer additional alerts for some of these categories.

Addresses or other information you do not recognize: Your credit report can also contain addresses and other identifying details. An unfamiliar entry deserves a closer look, especially if it appears alongside an account or inquiry you do not recognize.
5 steps to check right now
You do not need to wait for a strange bill or collection call to find out something is wrong. A few quick checks can help you spot signs of new account fraud before it turns into a bigger problem.

Go to AnnualCreditReport.com and review your Equifax, Experian and TransUnion reports. Free reports are currently available weekly, so you can check all three at once or stagger your reviews throughout the year.
Pay close attention to accounts, hard inquiries, addresses and other information you do not recognize. If something looks strange, do not assume it is harmless.

A credit freeze can make it much harder for someone to open a new credit account in your name because lenders generally cannot access your frozen credit report. Freezes are free to place and lift, they do not hurt your credit score and they stay in place until you remove them. You need to contact Equifax, Experian and TransUnion separately to freeze all three files.
Look for messages about accounts you never opened, especially welcome notices, bills, password-reset messages and application updates.

Your bank and credit card companies may offer account alerts at no charge. Identity theft monitoring can go further by watching for certain credit inquiries, new accounts and other signs that someone may be using your information. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at Cyberguy.com. The faster you know something has changed, the faster you can investigate it.
IS YOUR SOCIAL SECURITY NUMBER ON THE DARK WEB?
Identity thieves can use stolen personal information to open new accounts, leaving victims unaware until an unfamiliar bill, credit inquiry or collection notice appears. (Anna Barclay/Getty Images)
What to do if you find a fraudulent account
If you spot an account you do not recognize, act quickly. These six steps can help you shut down the fraud, limit the damage and start cleaning up your records.
Call the company's fraud department. Explain that you did not open the account and ask them to close or freeze it. Keep any confirmation they send you.
Go to IdentityTheft.gov and create an FTC Identity Theft Report and recovery plan. That report can also help when you dispute fraudulent information.

A fraud alert tells businesses to take extra steps to verify your identity before opening new credit. An initial fraud alert is free, lasts one year and requires you to contact only one of the three major credit bureaus. That bureau must notify the other two. A credit freeze goes further by restricting access to your credit report. To freeze all three reports, contact each bureau separately.

Contact any credit bureau showing the fraudulent account and ask it to block the identity theft information from your report. To use the FTC's blocking process, send the bureau a copy of your FTC Identity Theft Report, proof of your identity and a letter identifying the fraudulent information. You can also dispute inaccurate information directly with the credit bureau.

Your bank and credit card companies may offer account alerts at no charge, so turn those on first. Identity theft monitoring can add another layer by watching for certain credit inquiries, newly opened accounts and other signs that someone may be using your personal information. That can be especially helpful with new account fraud because the criminal may never touch the accounts you already check. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at CyberGuy.com.

Write down who you contacted, when you contacted them and what they told you. Save letters, emails, case numbers and copies of anything you submit. Those records can save you a lot of frustration if you need to follow up later.
9 WARNING SIGNS OF IDENTITY THEFT YOU SHOULD NEVER IGNORE

Checking all three credit reports can help consumers spot unfamiliar accounts, hard inquiries and other warning signs tied to identity theft. (Michael Siluk/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)
Kurt's key takeaways

New account fraud can be especially tough to spot because the criminal may never touch the bank accounts or credit cards you already watch. That is exactly why I want you to check all three of your credit reports instead of waiting for a strange bill or collection call to show up. You can pull your reports for free, look for unfamiliar accounts or inquiries and consider freezing your credit when you are not applying for anything new.

Then add alerts or identity monitoring if you want another set of eyes watching for activity you might otherwise miss. The big takeaway here is speed. A fraudulent account that sits unnoticed for months can turn into damaged credit, collections and a much bigger cleanup job. Catch it early, and you have a far better chance of shutting it down before things snowball.

title: Delivery drones could be waiting before you even order
summary: Flytrex says its AI-powered Rooftop Dock system in Dallas-Fort Worth positions drones at restaurants before orders arrive, cutting delivery costs by 60%.
story: FOX Business correspondent Madison Alworth reports on drone food delivery services launching in New Jersey on ‘America Reports.’

Your next food delivery could start moving before you even place the order. Flytrex is rolling out a system in Dallas-Fort Worth that sends drones to restaurant rooftops ahead of expected demand. AI predicts which locations are likely to get busy, then positions an aircraft nearby.

If the prediction is right, the drone is already waiting when your food is ready. Flytrex says its new Rooftop Dock and predictive fleet positioning can cut its own delivery costs by 60%. The company also says customer delivery times can drop by half.

The idea makes a lot of sense. Stop wasting time sending a drone to the restaurant after the food is ready. So, how does Flytrex know where to put a drone before anyone orders, and how could this expand beyond Texas?
PILOTLESS CARGO AIRCRAFT COULD CHANGE HOW PACKAGES MOVE
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Get Better Healthcare With AI replay

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class Get Better Healthcare With AI has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay now at CyberGuyLive.com
Flytrex is rolling out AI-powered drone positioning in Dallas-Fort Worth, sending aircraft to restaurant rooftops before customers place orders. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
AI tries to figure out where the next order will come from

Flytrex uses machine-learning models to study past demand, location and the time of day. The software also looks at other activity across its delivery network. It then predicts which restaurants are most likely to receive upcoming orders. Instead of leaving every available drone at a central location, Flytrex can send aircraft closer to restaurants before customers order anything.

That could make a big difference during busy meal periods. A pizza restaurant that usually sees a rush around dinner time could already have a drone waiting nearby. Once an order comes through and the kitchen finishes the food, the aircraft can get moving quickly. The current process can take longer. An operator may have to send a drone from another location after the restaurant has the order. The aircraft then flies to the restaurant before it can start the customer delivery. Flytrex wants to cut out that extra trip.
The drone waits on the restaurant rooftop

Once Flytrex decides where a drone should wait, the aircraft lands on its Rooftop Dock. The company says the system can go on an existing rooftop or another elevated area near the restaurant. According to Flytrex, the setup does not require additional real estate or structural changes. The company also says it can operate without placing a Flytrex employee at each restaurant. After the drone lands, it shuts down its motors and waits. When the food is ready, the aircraft lowers a hook into position.

A restaurant employee clips the packaged order onto it without handling the drone. Then the aircraft takes off and heads directly toward the customer. That also removes the need for someone to carry the food to a separate drone launch site. Flytrex co-founder and CEO Amit Regev says those last few hundred feet between the restaurant kitchen and the aircraft have been one of the harder parts of drone delivery.
"The truly challenging part has never been the flight; it's the last few hundred feet between the kitchen and the aircraft," Regev said.
Why Flytrex thinks this could slash delivery costs

Sending a drone to a restaurant before an order arrives could save more than time. Flytrex says its new setup cuts its cost per delivery by 60%. The company also says it can reduce customer delivery times by half. The drone no longer has to make a separate pickup flight from a central location. Meanwhile, restaurant workers can load the order without a dedicated Flytrex employee standing there.

That could let each aircraft handle more deliveries over the course of a day. There is one big variable, though. The AI needs to put the drone in the right place. Customer demand can change quickly. Weather can shift ordering patterns. A local event could suddenly make one restaurant much busier than expected. If a drone ends up waiting at the wrong location, Flytrex may have to move it again.
Dallas-Fort Worth is becoming a drone delivery testing ground

Flytrex is launching the technology at active merchant locations across Dallas-Fort Worth. The company says it is also installing the system at more than 100 additional sites. That makes North Texas an important test for something Flytrex wants to expand much further. The company says it has completed more than 250,000 U.S. deliveries.

It has also been building relationships with some of the biggest names in food delivery. In 2025, Uber invested in Flytrex through a partnership focused on Uber Eats orders. We covered that move when Uber Eats began preparing for drone deliveries.

Flytrex also partnered with DoorDash in Dallas-Fort Worth. DoorDash has since expanded its own drone ambitions. We recently covered how DoorDash received FAA approval for its commercial drone delivery operation.
CLEVELAND CLINIC LAUNCHES PRESCRIPTION DRONE DELIVERY
Flytrex says its Rooftop Dock system could cut its delivery costs by 60% and customer delivery times by half. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
FAA approval could help Flytrex reach many more cities

Flytrex has another important piece in place as it looks beyond Texas. The company received Federal Aviation Administration approval for beyond visual line of sight operations, also known as BVLOS. That allows Flytrex to conduct approved flights without requiring a visual observer to keep each aircraft in direct sight throughout the trip.

Instead, Flytrex can monitor multiple drones remotely from an operations center under the conditions of its authorization. Flytrex says the approval gives it a path toward expanding into the 37 largest U.S. metropolitan areas. That does not mean rooftop drone delivery will appear across all 37 markets at once. Flytrex still has to build out its network as it expands. The new rooftop system gives the company a setup it hopes to repeat from one market to the next.
Flytrex has been building toward bigger food deliveries

The rooftop system comes after several other moves from Flytrex. In April 2026, the company introduced its Sky2 delivery drone through a partnership with Little Caesars. The aircraft can carry up to 8.8 pounds, enough to handle two large pizzas. Flytrex also opened a manufacturing facility in Pilot Point, Texas.

The company says the site can produce about 1,000 drones per year. Now Flytrex is tackling the next problem. Building more drones only gets you so far if those aircraft spend too much time traveling to pickup locations. Putting them closer to the restaurants before orders arrive could keep more of that fleet moving toward customers.
What this means to you

If Flytrex gets this right, you could spend less time staring at a delivery timer. The drone may already be waiting at the restaurant when your food is ready, so it can head toward your home almost immediately. That could also mean your meal spends less time sitting around before pickup. Then there is the cost. Flytrex says the system cuts its own delivery costs by 60%.

The company has not said whether those savings will eventually lead to lower fees for customers, but a cheaper delivery model could make drone delivery easier to expand. Don't expect a drone hovering over your takeout spot tomorrow. Flytrex is starting in Dallas-Fort Worth, and expanding this kind of service will take time. The bigger takeaway is what happens before the drone ever takes off. If AI can put the aircraft where the next order is likely to happen, Flytrex could make the whole process faster without asking customers to do anything differently.
CHINA’S GRIP ON RARE-EARTH MAGNETS COULD CRUSH US DRONE INDUSTRY BEFORE IT GROWS
AI predicts which restaurants are likely to get orders, allowing Flytrex drones to wait nearby before food is ready for pickup. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Kurt's key takeaways

What gets my attention here is how simple the problem sounds once Flytrex points it out. The drone may be fast in the air, but that does not help much if it has to spend part of the delivery flying to the restaurant first. Moving drones ahead of demand could change that. The AI looks for where orders are likely to come from, while the rooftop dock gives the aircraft somewhere to wait. If Flytrex can get those predictions right consistently, it could cut a lot of wasted time out of each delivery.

Dallas-Fort Worth should give us a good sense of whether this works beyond a handful of restaurants. Flytrex says more than 100 additional installations are underway, which should give the company plenty of chances to prove whether those big claims about speed and cost hold up.

Would faster food delivery be worth having drones waiting on restaurant rooftops around your community, or would you rather keep all that buzzing out of your neighborhood? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Lawyers, experts urge Tennessee governor to commute Christa Pike’s sentence after botched execution
summary: Christa Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital in a botched Tennessee execution, and her lawyers now urge Gov. Bill Lee to commute her death sentence.
story: Death Penalty Information Center Executive Director Robin Maher urged Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee to commute Christa Pike's sentence to life in prison after her "unprecedented" failed execution, pointing to her "torturous experience" in the execution chamber.

Christa Pike's lawyers are calling on Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee to commute her death sentence to life in prison after she remained alive following two doses of lethal injection drugs in what one death penalty expert described as an unprecedented event.

Pike, who was sentenced to death for a 1995 murder of a classmate, was rushed to a hospital Wednesday night after surviving her planned execution. Her lawyers said on Thursday that she remains in critical condition and is receiving "lifesaving medical care."
"We don’t have a sense of her prognosis or much update on her health at the moment," attorney Randy Spivey said during a news conference. "But we know she is alive right now."

The botched execution prompted Lee to halt any further efforts to carry out Pike's execution and the state’s other execution scheduled this year. He also ordered a third-party review into Pike's execution, which he called "deeply disturbing."
CHRISTA PIKE'S ATTORNEYS SAY SHE'S IN CRITICAL CONDITION AFTER BOTCHED LETHAL INJECTIONS
Christa Gail Pike is seen during her trial for the murder of Colleen A. Slemmer. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)
Pike's lawyers are now calling for her death sentence to be commuted.

Her lawyers filed an emergency motion with the Tennessee Supreme Court seeking to immediately halt and stay the execution, noting that she was in "unnecessary agony" and arguing that putting her through another attempted execution violated her right to be put to death without cruel and unusual punishment.
Death Penalty Information Center Executive Director Robin Maher, who called the failed execution "completely unprecedented," also urged the governor to commute Pike's sentence.

"Given the experience that Christa Pike went through last night, after a childhood and young adulthood that was full of gender based violence and abuse, it would be irresponsible for state officials to put her through another attempt at execution. I really hope that in light of what she's experienced, that the governor will decide to commute her sentence to a life in prison and not put her through another torturous experience in the execution chamber," Maher told Fox News Digital.
Before the planned execution, about 25,000 people had signed a petition to Lee asking him to commute Pike's death sentence to life in prison.
An appeals court had halted her execution early on Wednesday, but the U.S. Supreme Court overturned that stay hours later to clear the way for her to be put to death.

Pike, 50, would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. She would have been the 30th person executed in the U.S. this year, driven largely by Florida's record increase in inmates put to death since 2025.
Since the Supreme Court resumed the death penalty in 1976, only 18 women have been executed in the U.S., making up about 1% of all executions in the country.

This was the second time this year that Tennessee had a failed execution. In May, Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and murdering three people in 1994, was not executed because officials could not find a suitable vein for an IV line, so the drugs were not administered. Multiple states have previously paused executions after cases of officials being unable to find a suitable vein for an IV line.
Christa Pike's lawyers are calling on Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee to commute her death sentence to life in prison after she survived an attempted execution. (Tennessee Department of Correction via AP)

In 2024, Tennessee switched from a three-drug series to a single drug, pentobarbital, for lethal injections. About two years earlier, the state abruptly halted the execution of Oscar Smith, who was convicted of first-degree murder, and acknowledged it had failed to ensure its lethal injection drugs had been tested properly. He was eventually put to death by lethal injection last year.
Several others have survived medical problems linked to a failure to access a vein to administer lethal injection drugs, but no one had stayed alive after receiving the drugs until Pike on Wednesday.

"This, unfortunately, is not the first time that Tennessee officials have botched an execution. There is really a quite shameful history in Tennessee of executions going wrong, although Christa Pikes really stands out. There's never been someone who has received lethal doses of execution drugs and survived until last night. This is a completely unprecedented event, even in the context of Tennessee's other botched executions," Maher said.
The Death Penalty Information Center lists 65 botched executions across the U.S. in the modern era.
In the execution chamber, Pike said she was at peace and "ready to be free."
"This is a happy day," she said.
But she remained awake, and even complained about a feeling in her arm. Witnesses reported that Pike complained of pain in her arm and remained conscious after the first dose.

An hour after officials first raised the curtains, witnesses said that a second dose of pentobarbital was administered. Pike could still be heard snoring behind a closed curtain until the microphone was cut off nearly 30 minutes later.
WHAT TO KNOW ABOUT PENTOBARBITAL AFTER DEATH ROW INMATE SURVIVES 2 LETHAL INJECTION DOSES
The botched execution prompted Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee to halt Christa Pike's execution and the state’s other execution scheduled this year. (Mark Zaleski/AP)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Pike, who was 18 at the time of the crime, and her then-17-year-old boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp, were convicted of the fatal stabbing of a classmate, 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. Shipp was sentenced to life in prison with the possibility of parole, as he was a minor and not eligible for the death penalty.
The third defendant, then-18-year-old Shadolla Peterson, who acted as a lookout while her two friends carried out the attack, testified for the state and avoided the death penalty.

Pike did not dispute that she helped kill Slemmer, but supporters argued that her mental illness and allegations of severe sexual abuse when she was young should be considered. She was diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder after the killing.

"I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid. It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done," she previously said. "It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime."
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Christa Pike's attorneys say she's in critical condition after botched lethal injections
summary: Christa Pike is in critical condition after two botched lethal injection attempts, and her attorneys said the needle may have pierced her veins.
story: Christa Pike's attorneys Randy Spivey and Stephen Ferrell give an update on her condition after a chaotic failed execution attempt in the 1995 murder of Knoxville teen Colleen Slemmer.

title: Loyal dog fetches police to help owner who fell at Kansas home

story: The Leawood Police Department in Kansas said a "loyal companion" dog was able to find help for a homeowner who had fallen. (Credit: Leawood Police Department)
A Kansas dog is being hailed by police as a "loyal companion" after it sought help for its owner who had fallen and was unable to get up.

title: Ole Miss students died near drug listing newly illegal ingredient, ex-prosecutor says selling it is 'unlawful'
summary: Two Ole Miss students were found dead near tablets listing an ingredient the DEA recently made illegal, and the brand's site no longer shows it.
story: Former prosecutor Neama Rahmani says anyone in the supply chain can face liability for a Schedule I drug, but DOJ must prove intent. Two Ole Miss students were found dead near tablets listing a DEA-banned ingredient.

OXFORD, Miss. – Two Ole Miss students were found dead near tablets whose labels list an ingredient the federal government recently made illegal, and the product is nowhere to be found on the brand's website.

According to court documents, Ole Miss students Aidan Hamilton, 18, and Robert Strang, 20, were discovered dead on Sept. 21, each found near similar packages of kratom or synthetic kratom. Officials noted that Hamilton "could have died due to a Pulmonary Edema," a finding consistent with a drug overdose. When first responders reached Strang's house near campus, he was found "cold to the touch."

Packaging found near both students bears the name Modus, according to court documents. The affidavit describes the tablets as Smax Pseudo-DHM, and lists pseudoindoxyl and MGM-15(DHM) among the ingredients on the pack found near Hamilton.

In a statement Wednesday, Lafayette County Metro Narcotics, a department in the sheriff's office, stopped short of declaring that investigators found kratom itself near either student. "During the investigations, packaging associated with kratom-related products was discovered at both locations," part of the statement read. The Sept. 25 affidavit reported toxicology results from the medical examiner were still pending.
OXFORD MAYOR WARNS KRATOM IS 'ROLLING THE DICE ON DEATH' AS FEARS LINGER OVER OLE MISS DEATHS
Robert Strang and Aidan Hamilton in a split image provided by their families. (Strang family | Kathleen Hamilton/Facebook)

American Kratom Association Senior Fellow on Public Policy Mac Haddow said Wednesday during a press conference that the specific drug found near both students is illegal.Haddow pointed out the sale and possession of kratom has been illegal federally as of August and illegal to sell or possess in Oxford, Mississippi since 2019, and illegal in Lafayette County, where Oxford is located, since 2021.

The Drug Enforcement Administration temporarily placed mitragynine pseudoindoxyl in Schedule I on Aug. 26, which bars its sale. A Mississippi law enforcement agent investigating the Ole Miss students' deaths said he believes "pseudoindoxyl" refers to that compound, and lab results confirming the tablets' contents are pending, court documents say.
Toxicology results, which are still pending, could help determine how Hamilton and Strang died, according to the affidavit.

Modus Brand, which has offices in Florida and California, doesn't list the Smax Pseudo Tablets on its website, but says the product is a "next-generation approach to botanical supplements, offering a carefully formulated, high-quality product in a convenient chewable format."
While it's unclear if the Smax Pseudo Tablets were once on the Modus website, they're not listed at the moment.

In September, Hamilton made multiple purchases at Puffs Vape, Tobacco and Beer Store in Oxford. Two employees at that store, Yahya Mohamed Mosleh, 51, and Islam Mohamed, 18, were arrested and face a charge of possession of a controlled substance with intent to distribute, according to court documents. They were handed bonds of $100,000 each. Officials have said they do not believe there is any connection between the arrests and Hamilton's death.

Officials said the synthetic kratom-derived product Strang had bought was purchased at a gas station about 30 minutes away from Oxford, Mississippi.
OLE MISS NAMES STUDENTS FOUND DEAD AS OFFICIAL ADDRESSES POTENTIAL FOR FOUL PLAY
Packages of synthetic kratom products, including Smax Pseudo-DHM and Smax Pseudo tablets, that authorities say were found at the scene where Robert Strang was discovered dead. (Court records)

The owner of that gas station told Fox News Digital that the Smax tablets found near Strang did not come from his store. He said he does not put price stickers on his packages, unlike the one on the pack by Strang's nightstand. He didn't dispute that his store sold Smax Pseudo Tablets.
He said that federal agents seized all of his kratom inventory on Friday.
SEND US A TIP
Former federal prosecutor Neama Rahmani told Fox News Digital it's illegal for anyone to sell products containing MGM-15 after the DEA rescheduled it, but prosecuting it is trickier.
GOT A TIP?

"It would be unlawful for anyone, whether it's a drug dealer or a gas station convenience store owner, to sell MGM-15 after it was categorized as Schedule I," Rahmani said. "Now, to be prosecuted, the Department of Justice would have to prove intent."
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Stewart Hall, a dorm building on the University of Mississippi campus where an 18-year-old student is believed to have died on Monday. Dispatch records show first responders arrived within a minute of being sent to the address. (Adam Sabes/Fox News Digital)
Kratom is a plant, but MGM-15 and related chemicals are synthetic versions of it, and the two are "certainly not an apples-to-apples comparison," he said.
GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL
Modus, the company whose name appears on the packaging, could face civil and even criminal liability if its product is found to contain a Schedule I substance, Rahmani said.

"There's no doubt that Modus and any company that distributed this drug can face civil, even criminal, liability. If you put out a dangerous product, doesn't matter if it's a pharmaceutical, street drug, or really, frankly, anything else. It could be a vehicle, it could be social media. Products liability law does hold the company responsible," Rahmani said.

"Now, in the case of something that's outright illegal in Schedule I, there's no question that criminal liability for the distributors can attach as well, and it can be the manufacturer, it can be the street level dealer, the wholesaler, anyone in the supply chain that distributes a Schedule I drug can absolutely be held responsible."

title: Lindsay Clancy lawyer pushes back on claims he shifted strategy after mistrial in new interview
summary: Kevin Reddington argued a Rule 25 motion claiming prosecutors failed to prove Lindsay Clancy killed her three children beyond a reasonable doubt.
story: The Fox News contributor and 'Hot Mics' podcast host says Tuesday's hearing yielded "no satisfaction" and argues the defense lawyer has become the face of Clancy's fight.

PLYMOUTH, Mass. — Lindsay Clancy's defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, is pushing back on claims that he changed strategies in court Tuesday when he raised doubts over whether prosecutors proved his client killed her three children, insisting he has attacked the strength of the Commonwealth’s case from the beginning.

Reddington, speaking with Fox News contributor Billy Bush on his "Hot Mics" podcast, called the investigation into his client "horrific" and "atrocious" after arguing in court that prosecutors hadn't presented enough evidence in their case to prove his client guilty beyond a reasonable doubt.

"That’s exactly what I was saying," Reddington said in the interview — right after Clancy's return to court for the first time since her mistrial. "I’ve been arguing that from the very beginning. I argued it in a closing argument to the jury. I argued in our motions."
LINDSAY CLANCY LAWYER RAISES EXPLOSIVE DOUBT OVER WHO KILLED HER CHILDREN

Lindsay Clancy and her attorney, Kevin Reddington, attend a status hearing for the Clancy case at the Plymouth County Superior Court in Plymouth, Massachusetts, on September 29, 2026. Lindsay Clancy is appearing in court for the first time since the judge declared a mistrial on September 4, after a jury was unable to reach a unanimous verdict in the high-profile case of Clancy, an American woman who killed her three young children. (Greg Derr / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)
Reddington was arguing a Rule 25 motion for a required finding of not guilty, in which he is seeking to convince the court that the evidence given at trial wasn’t good enough to support a conviction.

"Where’s the evidence that she did this?" Reddington asked Judge William Sullivan in court Tuesday, before running down a list of what he painted as insufficient evidence and faulty statements. "Where is the evidence she did this?"
LINDSAY CLANCY'S LAWYER REVEALS POST-MISTRIAL STRATEGY AS RETRIAL LOOMS

Although Reddington's comments on his motion for a required finding of not guilty garnered national headlines, Sullivan made no rulings and pushed oral arguments on other pending motions back to Nov. 2, leaving many who are following the case, including Bush, disappointed with the lack of answers.
WATCH: Kevin Reddington describes Lindsay Clancy's demeanor as she fights murder charges

"He didn't get any answers on the insufficiency of evidence," Bush told Fox News Digital Wednesday. "He wanted, immediately, her to be declared not criminally responsible because of that. I think that was a stretch. He probably knew it. He brought in his double jeopardy expert, Martin Weinberg. That was punted to Nov. 2. That wasn't immediately successful. And the alleged juror misconduct, we didn't get anything on that because Judge Sullivan, Reddington told us, impounded that information. We want to see the jury questionnaire. Everybody wants to see it."
Callan, left, Dawson and Cora Clancy. The three children were killed at their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home in January 2023. (Lindsay Marie Clancy/Facebook)
LINDSAY CLANCY JUDGE INDEFINITELY IMPOUNDS JUROR NAMES, CITING SAFETY AND 'DIVISIVE' ATTENTION
Sullivan declared a mistrial on Sept. 4 after jurors could not agree on a verdict following roughly a week of deliberations.
Rule 25 motions are routine but seldom successful, according to Carol Erskine, a retired Massachusetts judge and child welfare advocate who has been following the case closely.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X
WATCH: Clancy attorney questions ‘where is the evidence’ that she killed children
LINDSAY CLANCY PROSECUTORS FACE DILEMMA: RETRIAL OR PLEA DEAL IN CASE INVOLVING 3 STRANGLED CHILDREN

"He is arguing that [they] did not prove each and every element as required by law," she told Fox News Digital. "I understand why people don’t get this, but he had to argue sufficiency of evidence under Rule 25(b)(2) case law. He told the judge he asked for a Bowden instruction and was denied, which meant he was challenging the poor investigation/search at the home by police. It’s a very nuanced argument."

Plymouth County prosecutors had a tougher take on Reddington, calling it "a laughable argument" and asking the judge to deny his motion.

Patrick Clancy exits Plymouth Superior Court, Plymouth, Mass., Monday, July27, 2026. (David McGlynn for Fox News Digital)
Clancy is due back in court on Nov. 2 for a motions hearing. A date for a potential retrial has not yet been scheduled.

While Clancy's future remains uncertain, Reddington has developed a following of his own outside the courthouse, where Bush said the well-known Massachusetts defense lawyer regularly mingles with people covering the trial and has garnered a national reputation, including nicknames like "Big Red" and "Shreddington."

Lindsay Clancy's defense lawyer Kevin J. Reddington poses for a photo with a supporter outside of Plymouth Superior Court, Wednesday, August 26, 2026. (David McGlynn for Fox News Digital)

summary: A medevac helicopter crashed off Catalina Island in California with five aboard, leaving one person missing as search and rescue operations continue.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A medevac helicopter crashed into the water off Catalina Island in California on Wednesday night, with one of the five people aboard reported missing and the other four taken to hospitals, according to officials.
The Los Angeles County Fire Department received reports of the crash shortly before 8 p.m.
Search and rescue operations are ongoing, with the fire department dispatching helicopters and divers shortly after learning of the crash.

County Fire, Sheriff, Coast Guard, and Avalon Fire are on the scene," Los Angeles County Supervisor Janice Hahn said on X. "Search and rescue operations are underway, and I am praying for everyone who was on board."

At least one of the five people aboard the helicopter remains unaccounted for as of late Wednesday night. Two others were transported to hospitals in stable condition and the remaining two were transported in unknown condition, according to KTLA.
At least one of the five people aboard the helicopter remains unaccounted for as of late Wednesday night. (Photo by Qian Weizhong/VCG via Getty Images)
The Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department said two people were taken to a hospital on Catalina Island, while two others were transported to the Ronald Reagan Medical Center at UCLA.
The fire department said the helicopter's flight plan was unclear, according to CBS LA. Deputies said the helicopter belonged to Reach Air Medical Services.

title: Arizona sheriff's helicopter crew rescues man stranded atop overturned truck in rapidly rising floodwaters
summary: Video captures a Maricopa County sheriff's helicopter crew hoisting a man from his overturned truck as flash flooding surged in Tonopah, Arizona.
story: Maricopa County Sheriff’s Office aviation crews rescued a man stranded atop his overturned vehicle in rapidly moving floodwaters in Tonopah, Arizona, lowering a rescue specialist by helicopter before carrying him to safety on the riverbank (Credit: Facebook/Maricopa County Sheriff’s Office).
Dramatic video shows an Arizona sheriff's helicopter crew rescuing a man stranded on top of his overturned truck as rapidly moving floodwaters surrounded the vehicle.

The Maricopa County Sheriff's Office said its Fox 1 aviation crew responded Tuesday morning to a flooded wash in Tonopah, where deputies found the man sitting atop the overturned vehicle with water rushing around him.
Video released by authorities shows the man perched on the truck as muddy floodwaters rush past him.
Because of the dangerous conditions, first responders determined that directly reaching the man was too risky and decided a "hoist rescue" would be the safest option.
TRAGEDY AT SEA LEAVES TEEN STRANDED ON OVERTURNED BOAT FOR NEARLY 3 DAYS IN FRIGID WATERS
The Maricopa County Sheriff’s Office Fox 1 aviation crew carries out a hoist rescue after a driver became stranded in rapidly moving floodwaters. (Maricopa County Sheriff's Office)
The video shows a Fox 1 crew member being lowered to the vehicle to secure the man in a rescue harness before both are hoisted to safety.
The man was taken to the riverbank, where fire personnel were waiting, according to the sheriff's office.
The helicopter's pilot, Rich Dickner, told CBS News that the water was quickly rising around the vehicle.
"We didn't waste much time," Dickner said.
"As opposed to when we first got there, you can see the water line on the video — it's below the window — and it had risen up to the top of the window," he continued. "So there was that urgency."
HELICOPTER RESCUE CREW CAUGHT ON CAMERA SAVING 2 CLIMBERS TRAPPED ALONG POPULAR CALIFORNIA BEACH CLIFF
A Maricopa County Sheriff’s Office helicopter crew responds to rescue a man stranded on an overturned truck in Arizona floodwaters. (Maricopa County Sheriff's Office)
People magazine reported that Deputy Lindsey Smith was lowered approximately 80 feet from the helicopter toward the overturned truck.
She initially struggled to get her footing before securing herself to the vehicle, according to the report.
The entire rescue took less than five minutes, authorities said.
The Maricopa County Sheriff's Office credited the crew's swift response with getting the man to safety.
"Thanks to the skill and quick response of our aviation crew, the subject was safely brought to shore," the sheriff's office said.
"Excellent work, Fox 1!"
DEADLY GRAND CANYON FLOODING KNOCKS OUT CRITICAL WATER LINE AMID RACE TO FIND MISSING HIKERS
A stranded driver is hoisted from his overturned truck as floodwaters continue rushing around the vehicle in Tonopah. (Maricopa County Sheriff's Office)
The Weather Channel reported that remnants of Hurricane Polo brought historic rainfall to parts of the Desert Southwest, contributing to dangerous flash flooding.
The Flood Control District of Maricopa County warned drivers not to attempt to cross flooded roads.
"Remember: Conditions can change fast. If you encounter a flooded roadway, Turn Around, Don't Drown."

story: Dakota Harper and his partner, Felicity Eatmon, have been accused of starting a fire that destroyed an abandoned home, damaging a nearby church (Credit: WCHS).
A TikTok couple was arrested Tuesday for allegedly setting an abandoned West Virginia home on fire, possibly causing more than $10,000 in damage to a nearby church.

Dakota Harper, 21, and Felicity Eatmon, 22, were each charged with first-degree arson and one count of conspiring to commit an offense that carries a potential life sentence, according to the Kanawha County Magistrate Court.
The pair is known for posting videos together on social media and have amassed 28,000 followers on TikTok.

Dakota Harper appears at an arraignment in Kanawha County, West Virginia, on Tuesday after being charged with arson. (WCHS)
A video showing Harper at his arraignment has since gone viral for highlighting his stature. According to court records, Harper stands at 3 feet, 9 inches tall and weighs 43 pounds.
At the Kanawha County courtroom, Harper took a seat before an officer approached from behind and tucked his chair closer to the table, leaving his head barely above the desk.
Eatmon, who referred to herself as Harper’s fiancée in their social media videos, also appeared alongside him. She stands at 5 feet, 1 inch tall, records indicated.
According to WCHS-TV, the fire was reported at 11:15 p.m. Sunday in the West Side of Charleston.
The couple was arrested after surveillance footage allegedly showed them placing a lit piece of paper inside the home. (Kanawha County Magistrate Court)
SURVEILLANCE VIDEO SHOWS OFFICERS TACKLE 'ANTI-AMERICAN' SUSPECT AFTER FEDERAL BUILDING FIREBOMBING
Surveillance footage captured Eatmon giving Harper what appeared to be a piece of paper that was then lit on fire and placed inside the home, the outlet reported, citing a complaint.

An abandoned home in Charleston, West Virginia, was reportedly set ablaze Sunday night, causing significant damage to a nearby church. (Google Maps)

A Texas man was arrested Wednesday after allegedly planning to attack the Texas State Capitol, according to officials.

The Texas Department of Public Safety said in a news release it received "credible information" Tuesday about someone plotting a "violent attack" for Thursday on the Capitol.
WOMAN’S ALLEGED ISIS RADICALIZATION UNFOLDED ONLINE BEFORE CAPITOL BOMB PLOT: COURT DOCS
Benny Caldera Jr. was charged with felony terroristic threat against a public servant. (Bexar County Jail; Getty Images)

title: Georgia college student miraculously survives 8-story plunge after metal bench breaks her fall
summary: A University of Georgia student fell eight stories at Rambler Athens after dancing near an open window, but a metal bench may have broken her fall.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A 21-year-old University of Georgia student survived an eight-story fall from an apartment window after apparently falling through a screen while dancing near an open window, according to a police report obtained by Fox News Digital.
Kristin Sargent fell from an eighth-floor window at the Rambler Athens apartment complex on West Broad Street around 7:37 p.m. Saturday.

Witnesses told police Sargent had been dancing on a couch or air mattress near the open window when she apparently fell through the screen. She landed near a pool in a courtyard on the building's second floor, according to the report.
Police found evidence that Sargent struck a metal bench during the fall. An officer noted blood on the bench's cushion and that one of its armrests had broken off.
WOMAN DIES AFTER PLUNGING INTO UNCOVERED MANHOLE OUTSIDE LUXURY STORES

A University of Georgia senior survived an eight-story plunge from an apartment window in Athens, Georgia, after police say she fell through a screen while dancing near an open window. (Instagram/_kristinsargent; Google Maps)

Lt. Katie Jenkins, a spokesperson for the Athens-Clarke County Police Department, told Fox News Digital that investigators believe the bench helped break Sargent's fall. She said the incident is not being investigated as a criminal matter and that police understand Sargent is alert and conscious.
Emergency 911 audio obtained by FOX 5 Atlanta captured the frantic moments after Sargent fell.
"We’re on the eighth floor. My friend just fell out of the window," a caller told dispatchers. "She's on the ground. She fell out of the window. We were dancing, and she just fell out of the window."
A dispatcher asked whether Sargent was moving.
MAN ACCUSED OF LURING UGA STUDENT WITH ‘WALK HOME’ RUSE BEFORE BRUTAL ASSAULT: POLICE
University of Georgia student Kristin Sargent, 21, survived an eight-story fall from an Athens apartment window while dancing on a couch, according to police. (Instagram/_kristinsargent)
"Is she moving? Is she moving? No, she's not," the caller responded.
The caller later told the dispatcher she could see Sargent below but could not determine whether her eyes were open.
"No, I don't know. I'm looking down at her on the floor. She's not moving," the caller said.
Emergency responders transported Sargent to a hospital, where police investigators interviewed her and witnesses while forensic personnel investigated, according to the police report.
LAKEN RILEY MURDER EXPOSED GLARING SECURITY LAPSES ON COLLEGE CAMPUSES, NEED FOR EMERGENCY BLUE LIGHTS
The Rambler Athens apartment complex on West Broad Street in Athens, Ga., where a University of Georgia student fell from an eighth-floor window. (Google Maps)
A responding officer wrote that information gathered at the time suggested the fall was an accident. Jenkins told Fox News Digital police are not investigating the incident as a criminal matter.
The report identifies Sargent as a resident of the apartment where the fall occurred.
Police could not address the window or what safety measures may or may not have been in place.

Sargent is a student at the University of Georgia in Athens. (Jeffrey Greenberg/Universal Images Group via Getty Images, File)

title: Fetal tissue supplier billed $765 procurement fee per organ, warns records could imply illegal sales: records
summary: Records obtained by David Daleiden’s Center for Medical Progress show UCLA purchase orders tied $765 procurement service fees to individual liver and thymus specimens
story: Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and HHS decertified Kentucky's Network for Hope organ donation nonprofit after shocking allegations of harvesting organs from living patients. Dr. Marc Siegel joins hosts Sandra Smith and John Roberts to break down the federal investigation, which uncovered 73 instances of premature harvesting, including a 2021 incident where a patient woke up during surgery.

FIRST ON FOX: Newly obtained public records show Cercle Allocation Services billed a UCLA research operation a $765 procurement service fee tied to each individual liver and thymus specimen, while warning in internal correspondence that certain billing language could improperly imply the tissue itself was being sold.

The records, obtained from UCLA through a California Public Records Act request made on behalf of Center for Medical Progress founder David Daleiden, include purchase orders and correspondence between the university and Cercle Allocation Services.

An internal UCLA order form identifies the purchasing operation as part of the David Geffen School of Medicine’s Division of Hematology-Oncology and references the "Mouse Core." UCLA redacted the names and other identifying information of researchers from the record.
The records reviewed by Fox News Digital do not establish that UCLA or its researchers, procurement personnel or other employees engaged in illegal or unethical conduct with the transactions.
'DRUG-DEALING' NETWORK SHIELDED BY BLUE STATES TARGETED IN SCOTUS CHALLENGE
Cercle supplies human fetal tissue for biomedical research. (Shane Collins/Northwestern University/File)

One UCLA purchase order lists seven individually numbered liver and thymus specimens at a $765 unit amount apiece, totaling $5,355. Another lists five specimens from Aug. 18, 2023, each carrying the same $765 amount, for a total of $3,825. Additional purchase orders reflect the same per-specimen amount.

Cercle objected to the purchase orders’ tax treatment and asked UCLA to reissue them, telling the university that the charges reflected procurement services and that sales tax should not be applied. Cercle said tax language could improperly imply that the specimens themselves were being sold.

Cercle does supply human fetal tissue for biomedical research. Peer-reviewed scientific literature has identified the company as the source of human fetal liver tissue used by researchers, providing independent evidence of the type of procurement business described by CMP.
SUPREME COURT UNANIMOUSLY SLAPS DOWN BLUE STATE TARGETING PRO-LIFE GROUP
UCLA redacted the names and other identifying information of researchers from the record. (Myung J. Chun/Los Angeles Times/File)

CMP identified the liver and thymus specimens in the UCLA purchase orders as fetal tissue. Fox News Digital has not independently verified that the tissue associated with these specific purchase orders was fetal. The purchase orders identify the organs by type, sample number and date but do not describe them as fetal.
The records do not establish that the payments were illegal. Cercle characterized the money as fees for procurement services rather than payments for the tissue itself.
But correspondence shows the company was particularly concerned about how those payments were described.

"The overriding issue is the use of terminology that we must not use due to their improper implication that we are selling taxable items, which we are not," a Cercle accounts manager wrote in September 2023. "Due to the nature of our business, we must be very careful and clear that we invoice fees for our procurement services."

The same email said notations referring to sales tax would imply Cercle was "selling the items received," which the company said were "illegal to sell." Cercle instead instructed UCLA that purchase orders should authorize payment for its services while tying individual sample numbers and dates to a unit amount of $765.
The correspondence shows UCLA subsequently prepared revised purchase orders after Cercle objected to the tax language.
David Daleiden, a defendant in an indictment stemming from a secret investigation of his undercover videos of Planned Parenthood, stands in a Houston courtroom Feb. 4, 2016. (David J. Phillip/AP)

One Cercle email said a July invoice totaling $5,355 for procurements on three dates had already been "processed and paid." The company also asked UCLA to replace other purchase orders containing tax language, including one covering five procurements from Aug. 18 worth a combined $3,825.

Federal law prohibits knowingly acquiring, receiving or otherwise transferring human fetal tissue for "valuable consideration," if the transfer affects interstate commerce, while allowing "reasonable payments" associated with transportation, implantation, processing, preservation, quality control or storage.
The records reviewed by Fox News Digital do not establish that Cercle or UCLA violated that prohibition.
Daleiden contends the documents raise questions about whether the uniform $765 charges represented permissible reimbursement for procurement-related costs.
HAWLEY SENDS CRIMINAL REFERRAL OF 'LEFT-WING DARK-MONEY' GROUP OVER MAILED ABORTION DRUGS

He pointed to the uniform $765 amount UCLA assigned to individual specimens on the purchase orders, including multiple organs listed on the same date. Daleiden told Fox News Digital he believes the structure raises questions about whether the payments reflected the procurement-related costs permitted under federal law.
Documents reviewed by Fox News Digital do not contain Cercle’s invoices or underlying cost calculations and do not establish whether the $765 amount exceeded reasonable procurement-related expenses.
Daleiden also said UCLA did not produce Cercle’s invoices in response to the public records request.

The May 2025 request sought the original and most recent materials associated with UCLA IRB No. 11-002504 and records and communications from 2023 forward between the authors of a specified UCLA study and Advanced Bioscience Resources or Cercle. The request covered records, including emails, text messages, notes and fetal tissue logs.

UCLA later said its departments had completed their search and that the September 2026 production represented the final batch of non-exempt responsive records. The university said it redacted certain researcher identities because of concerns about threats and harassment involving sensitive research.
Records also show the UCLA-Cercle relationship continued into 2025.

A February 2025 Cercle ticket involving UCLA was titled "Liver and brain." Cercle responded March 3 that it had been "unable to fulfill your request today" and canceled the ticket. The records do not specify that the requested tissue was fetal or establish that any brain tissue was ultimately procured or transferred.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Daleiden has spent years investigating fetal tissue procurement after CMP released undercover videos involving Planned Parenthood officials in 2015. His recording operation later became the subject of a California criminal case.

Kamala Harris’ office opened the investigation while she was California attorney general. Charges were later filed under Attorney General Xavier Becerra. In April 2026, a California judge dismissed the final charge and expunged the case.

The records reviewed by Fox News Digital do not establish that the UCLA-Cercle transactions violated federal law. UCLA and Cercle have not been accused or charged by authorities with illegal conduct in the transactions reflected in the public records obtained by CMP.
UCLA and Cercle Allocation Services did not respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.
Jasmine Baehr is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital, where she covers politics, the military, legal debates surrounding life and family policy, as well as faith and culture.

title: South Carolina mom accused of knife attack on young children; 6-year-old may lose arm: sheriff's office

story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A South Carolina boy’s call to his grandmother saying he was hungry led authorities to a home where investigators say his mother had stabbed him and his younger sibling dozens of times, leaving both children with severe injuries.

Taylor Gosnell, 35, was charged with two counts of attempted murder after allegedly attacking her children, ages 6 and 3, inside their Spartanburg County home during the overnight hours before they were discovered Saturday, according to authorities.
The 6-year-old called his grandmother Sept. 26, and told her his mother was not home and that he and his 3-year-old sibling were hungry, according to the Spartanburg County Sheriff’s Office.
ACCUSED NC KILLER MOM PLANS INSANITY DEFENSE — AS RETIRED JUDGE SAYS MORE MAY FOLLOW LINDSAY CLANCY STRATEGY
Taylor Gosnell, 35, was charged with two counts of attempted murder and two counts of possession of a weapon during a violent crime in Spartanburg County, S.C. (Spartanburg County Sheriff's Office)
The grandmother contacted a friend of Gosnell, and the two went to the residence. They found both children suffering from severe injuries and immediately dialed 911.
Deputies responding shortly after 2:30 p.m. found the residence in disarray, with numerous items damaged or broken, authorities said.

Investigators said the children had approximately 50 stab wounds between them, including injuries that penetrated to the bone. Both were initially taken to Spartanburg Regional Medical Center before being transferred to Prisma Health Children’s Hospital in Greenville, where they remained hospitalized and were expected to undergo additional surgeries.
SUBURBAN ILLINOIS BOY DIES IN SUSPECTED DOMESTIC HOMICIDE AS NEIGHBORS FEAR ANOTHER LINDSAY CLANCY CASE

Taylor Gosnell, 35, was charged with two counts of attempted murder after authorities say she attacked her two young children. The children were hospitalized at Prisma Health Children’s Hospital in Greenville, S.C. (Google Maps/Spartanburg County Sheriff's Office)

Arrest warrants reviewed by Fox News Digital provide additional details about the alleged attack. The warrants allege Gosnell struck the children with a baseball bat and a circular knife, causing severe injuries with intent to kill them.

Gosnell returned to the home while deputies were still there, according to the sheriff’s office. Deputies transported her to Spartanburg Regional Medical Center for an evaluation after observing behavior that raised concerns about her immediate well-being.
Authorities said Gosnell attempted to run from the ambulance before being transported and had to be restrained. She was medically cleared and released from the hospital shortly afterward.
DAYS AFTER LINDSAY CLANCY MISTRIAL, ANOTHER MASSACHUSETTS MOM ACCUSED OF KILLING HER CHILDREN SEEKS FREEDOM
Gosnell returned to the home while deputies were still there. (Getty Images, File)
Investigators attempted to interview Gosnell, but no interview was conducted after she requested an attorney, according to the sheriff’s office.
Gosnell was booked into the Spartanburg County Detention Facility shortly before midnight Sept. 26 and was denied bond on both attempted murder charges.

Investigators later obtained two additional warrants charging Gosnell with possession of a weapon during a violent crime. Those warrants, also reviewed by Fox News Digital, allege she possessed the weapons during the attempted murders.

The investigation remains active and ongoing.

title: EXCLUSIVE: State Department revokes over 250,000 visas in broad immigration vetting crackdown
summary: The State Department has revoked over 250,000 visas under Trump for criminal activity, fraud, birth tourism and national security threats.
story: Tommy Pigott sat down at the White House with Fox News Digital to discuss the department's crackdown on visas, including birth tourism.

EXCLUSIVE: The State Department has revoked more than 250,000 visas since President Donald Trump took office, as the administration continues to crack down on unlawful immigration and increase vetting of who is allowed to visit the United States.

The revocations were for a variety of violations, including visa holders who violated the terms of their visas, committed crimes, called for violence against the U.S. or Americans, defrauded Americans, abused the immigration system, and endangered national security, a State Department official told Fox News Digital.

Among the visas revoked were 2,300 in connection with birth tourism, the practice of pregnant foreign nationals traveling to the U.S. specifically to give birth so their child automatically receives citizenship.
BIRTH TOURISM SCAMS DRAW SWEEPING CRACKDOWN AS VISA REVOCATIONS CLIMB

The Trump administration has been aggressive about revoking visas of foreign nationals, yanking thousands of visas of those who have committed a range of offenses and violated the terms of their stay in the United States, the State Department said. (Harry Hamburg/NY Daily News Archive via Getty Images; Aaron Schwartz / AFP via Getty Images)

"Under President Trump and Secretary Rubio, the State Department has now revoked more than 250,000 visas — a historic milestone that reflects our unwavering commitment to protecting the American people," State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said.

"Every visa decision is a national security decision. Through continuous vetting on a scale never seen before, we are identifying and removing those who commit crimes, support terrorism, defraud Americans, or abuse our immigration system," Pigott added. "A U.S. visa is a privilege, not a right — and if you violate the terms of that privilege, you will lose it. We will not stop until every foreign national who threatens the safety of our communities is held accountable."

On Monday, the State Department revoked the visas of 27 Latin American officials, former officials, and their families over accusations of corruption. The officials are from Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru.
Over the summer, the Trump administration began preparing to revoke business and tourist visas held by as many as 200,000 foreigners who have applied for asylum in the U.S.
DHS' TOP LAWYER THREATENS PENALTIES FOR ATTORNEYS CLOGGING ASYLUM SYSTEM
Over the summer, the Trump administration began preparing to revoke business and tourist visas held by as many as 200,000 people. (iStock)

The effort would target B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026 to foreigners who later sought asylum. At the time, Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau said Americans were "fed up" with "bogus asylum claims."

"Asylum isn’t supposed to be a loophole to circumvent immigration laws; rather, it’s supposed to provide a narrow safe harbor for persons persecuted because of their ‘race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion,’" he wrote on X at the time.
TRUMP ADMIN PAUSES VISA APPOINTMENTS WORLDWIDE AMID HEIGHTENED SCREENING FOR APPLICANTS
The State Department under Secretary of State Marco Rubio has yanked thousands of visas for overstays and law violations — including support for terrorism. (Reuters)
He noted that frivolous claims have swamped the system, which could take years to adjudicate whether applicants are entitled to asylum in the U.S.

In August, the State Department also revoked more than 175,000 visas. The majority of those were revoked due to law enforcement encounters for a range of criminal activity, with assault, driving under the influence, theft and drug crimes being the leading causes.

A significant share of visas were revoked for reckless driving, sexual assault, child abuse, fraud and embezzlement and other crimes, the agency said.

title: Penn State cocaine ring suspect’s attorney warns of ‘foolish’ move in alleged frat drug operation
summary: Five men accused in a cocaine distribution ring at Penn State indicated a plan to plead not guilty, with three requesting jury trials as the Centre County case advances.
story: A massive drug bust at Penn State is drawing attention to a dangerous new reality facing college campuses: party drugs are no longer just party drugs. Following the dismantling of a student-led dealing operation in State College, Centre County drug and alcohol specialist Cathy Arbogast speaks out on the surge of synthetic stimulants flooding rural communities across Pennsylvania.

Five men accused of being part of a cocaine distribution ring at Penn State filed court documents in Centre County, Pennsylvania, signaling plans to fight the charges against them, while one defense attorney told Fox News Digital it would be "foolish" to rush to judgment.
Agostino Abbatiello, Mohammed Huraibi, Robert Zanolla, Thomas Robinson and Paul Robinson have each indicated they intend to plead not guilty as their cases move forward in Centre County court.
"Pre-judging the evidence would be foolish," Korey Leslie, who represents Zanolla, told Fox News Digital.
PENN STATE FRAT COCAINE RING SUSPECTS ALLEGEDLY USED CASH APP, SNAPCHAT TO ARRANGE DRUG DEALS

Leslie confirmed Zanolla has entered a formal not-guilty plea and requested a jury trial. He said the defense has requested all evidence the Commonwealth intends to use at trial and will review it as the team prepares for potential pretrial litigation.

Agostino Abbatiello arrives at Centre County Courthouse in Bellefonte, Pa., on Wednesday, Sept. 2, 2026. Abbatiello is accused of masterminding a cocaine ring at Penn State University. (Kamil Krzaczynski for Fox News Digital)
The latest filings come after testimony detailed kilogram-sized cocaine deals and a drug-packaging operation inside a fraternity house.

The Office of the Court Administrator said the five defendants waived their formal arraignments scheduled for Wednesday and will not appear at the Centre County Courthouse. Their next court appearance is scheduled for Nov. 16 for a pretrial conference.

Abbatiello and Thomas Robinson also requested jury trials on their waiver forms. Huraibi and Paul Robinson indicated they intend to plead not guilty but did not select either a jury or non-jury trial.
PENN STATE FRAT COCAINE BUST BLOWS LID OFF WIDER STIMULANT SCOURGE HITTING COLLEGE CAMPUSES — AND BEYOND

The five are among 14 people charged in the alleged operation, which prosecutors say used fraternity connections to move cocaine into State College before it was packaged and sold to Penn State students.
Thomas Robinson, 22, is facing felony charges for his alleged involvement in the downstream logistics of the operation. (Pennsylvania Office of the Attorney General Dave Sunday)
THE FRAT OMERTÀ: WHISTLEBLOWER WARNS OF ‘CODE OF SILENCE’ AFTER OLE MISS DEATHS, ALLEGED PENN STATE COKE RING
Thomas Robinson, a former Delta Upsilon fraternity member, testified that he and Huraibi began buying cocaine from Abbatiello in 2023, starting with about 100 grams for roughly $4,000.
Robinson said the cocaine was stored in his fraternity room, where he and Huraibi broke it into half-gram bags and sold them for about $80 each.
JEANINE PIRRO CALLS OUT 'DIRTBAGS' AFTER 14 CHARGED IN ALLEGED COCAINE RING OPERATING FEET FROM A SCHOOLYARD
Robert Zanolla, 24, is accused of helping transport cocaine from New York City to State College, Pennsylvania. (Pennsylvania Office of the Attorney General Dave Sunday)
The quantities later grew to kilogram-sized purchases, Robinson testified. He said he eventually began buying directly from Abbatiello through Snapchat, where messages disappeared after 24 hours.

title: Tennessee death row inmate survives 2 lethal injection doses in failed execution attempt
summary: Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike remained alive after two doses of a lethal injection drug, prompting Gov. Bill Lee to halt the state’s remaining execution this year and order an outside review
story: An 'Outnumbered' panel discusses convicted murderer Christa Pike surviving two lethal injection attempts in Tennessee, prompting an investigation ordered by the governor into the failed execution.

Tennessee officials were unable to execute death row inmate Christa Pike on Wednesday night after she remained alive following two doses of a lethal injection drug, according to court filings from her attorneys.

The failed execution prompted Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee to halt the state’s remaining scheduled execution this year and order "a comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred." Pike was taken to a hospital by ambulance for treatment, her attorneys said.

"Carrying out a lawfully imposed sentence is among the State's most serious responsibilities, and the people of Tennessee expect it to be done in a manner that is not only legal and constitutional, but is effective," Lee said in a statement.

The Tennessee Department of Correction said it "followed every step of the State's lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General's Office."MULTIPLE DEATH SENTENCES IN DIFFERENT STATES ARE SET TO BE CARRIED OUT WITHIN 24 HOURS: 'NOT VERY COMMON'
An undated portrait photograph of Colleen Slemmer provided by her mother. (May Martinez/Special to the News Sentinel)
Witnesses said Pike was strapped to a gurney when the curtains to the execution chamber were raised at 7:27 p.m. local time. In what were expected to be her final words, Pike said she was "at peace."
But the execution did not proceed as expected. Pike remained awake and at one point raised her head, asking prison officials whether her arm was supposed to feel that way.

At 8:26 p.m. local time, witnesses said the executioners had "injected both syringes of lethal injection chemicals and Pike is still alive and snoring," her lawyers said in a federal court filing, according to The Associated Press.
Pike’s attorneys said in emergency court filings that she "has not lost consciousness and still has a heartbeat," arguing that the attempted execution was causing "unnecessary agony."
At 8:53 p.m., media witnesses were escorted from the area after Pike could still be heard snoring behind the closed curtain.

The state’s protocol calls for a secondary set of drug syringes to be administered "if the inmate is not deceased" after the first set. The protocol does not specify what should happen if the inmate remains alive after the second set.
This comes after the U.S. Supreme Court late Wednesday vacated a last-minute stay that had temporarily spared her from becoming the first woman executed in the state since the early 1800s.
Emergency vehicles arrive at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution after the execution of Christa Pike was halted Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026, in Nashville, Tennessee. (AP Photo/George Walker IV)
The Supreme Court granted Tennessee's application to vacate the stay issued Wednesday morning by the U.S. Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals, clearing the way for the state to carry out Pike's execution.
In a 2-1 split decision, the Sixth Circuit issued a stay "until further notice" as the court weighed motions filed by Pike's attorneys and the Tennessee Attorney General's Office.
The state immediately appealed to the Supreme Court, seeking to have the stay lifted.

Justice Sonia Sotomayor dissented from the Supreme Court's decision, joined by Justices Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson.Sotomayor argued that the Sixth Circuit should have been given time to consider Pike's pending legal challenge before the execution proceeded.
Read the Court of Appeals order:
"In capital cases, "[a]ppreciation of our own fallibility, and respect for the judgment of an appellate tribunal," demand caution before "acting irretrievably.""
She added that the Supreme Court "chooses to overlook that principle precisely when it matters most."

Pike, 50, was 18 in 1995 when she, her boyfriend and another person beat, kicked and stabbed their 19-year-old classmate Colleen Slemmer to death in a brutal "satanic" attack that Pike claimed took between 30 minutes and an hour, according to court documents.
Pike and Slemmer knew each other through a vocational program in Knoxville called the Job Corps Center, the documents state.

Pike had accused Slemmer of "trying to get [her] boyfriend" and "running her mouth," the case file shows. A day before the killing, she told another classmate she wanted to kill Slemmer because she "just felt mean that day," according to the records. She was armed with a box cutter and a meat cleaver.
Pike and her accomplices lured Slemmer out, telling her they wanted to go to a music store and pick up some marijuana they'd hidden in a park nearby.
Pike attacked her, knocked her to the ground and hit her in the face with her knee and foot, according to court documents.
Christa Gail Pike is seen during her trial for the murder of Colleen A. Slemmer on March 18, 1996, in Knox County Criminal Court. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)

At one point, Slemmer broke away from Pike and tried to flee, but Pike's boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, grabbed her and held her down while Pike slashed her with the box cutter. The victim begged for her life, but the attackers kept going. At some point, they gagged her with a hair tie.

At trial, forensic psychiatrist Dr. William Bernet testified that the crime had "satanic elements" but also appeared to involve "the phenomenon of collective aggression, in which a group of people become emotionally aroused and 'the end result is that they engage in some kind of violent, extremely violent activity,'" court records show.
SOUTH CAROLINA INMATE WHO BELIEVES HE IS IMMORTAL CANNOT BE EXECUTED DUE TO MENTAL ILLNESS, JUDGE RULES

Dr. Eric Engum testified that Pike had been diagnosed with "very severe borderline personality disorder" in addition to showing signs of cannabis dependence and depression. However, he said, she had no symptoms of brain damage or insanity.
NEW HAMPSHIRE RESENTENCING GIVES DARTMOUTH KILLER ROBERT TULLOCH A PAROLE PATH AFTER SUPREME COURT RULING

University of Tennessee forensic anthropologist Dr. Murray Marks testifies about the wounds to Colleen A. Slemmer's skull during Christa Gail Pike's murder trial in Knox County Criminal Court on March 25, 1996. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)

Pike took a piece of the victim's crushed skull as a trophy and later showed it off in school, recounting that Slemmer had begged the trio to stop, according to court records. Pike told the friend she'd cut Slemmer's throat a half-dozen times and then smashed her head with a rock. She showed off her bloodstained sneakers to another classmate and brought Slemmer's skull fragment to breakfast the next morning.

Neither Shipp nor the third attacker, Shadolla Peterson, received death sentences. Shipp was under 18 at the time and not eligible for capital punishment. Peterson testified for the state.

Pike's supporters counter that her defense did a poor job presenting mitigating factors before her sentencing, including untreated bipolar disorder and PTSD stemming from repeated domestic violence and sexual assaults. summary: Lindsay Clancy's defense lawyer Kevin Reddington faces a bar complaint from attorneys for the holdout juror who blocked her acquittal at trial.
story: Edward Paltzik and Tyler Cox, attorneys for the Lindsay Clancy holdout juror, discuss comments from defense attorney Kevin Reddington and argue their client followed the law during the trial on ‘Hannity.’
