"No one ever has the right based on laboratory algorithms to decide the life of a given embryo or elderly person. Medicine must never become the servant of programmed death," he said.
Assisted suicide is legal in many Western countries, including France.
MICHIGAN DEMOCRATS PROPOSE PACKAGE SEEKING TO LEGALIZE ASSISTED SUICIDE
Pope Leo XIV is set to visit Lourdes as part of his visit to France. ( )
The practice has come under heavy criticism, particularly in Canada where it has seen widespread use.

Last week, the family of an 83-year-old Canadian woman demanded answers after she died through the country's medical assistance in dying program despite allegedly becoming distraught when told the procedure would end her life.
ASSISTED LIVING CENTER SENT RESIDENT TO DOCTOR'S APPOINTMENT AFTER GIVING HIM 18 SHOTS, 5 AM BEER: OFFICIALS
The Daily Mail reported that 83-year-old Christian grandmother Brigitte Stegemann was killed under Canada’s physician-assisted suicide program, called Medical Assistance in Dying (MAID), on July 10.
Brigitte Kranendonk sits with her grandmother Brigitte Stegemann. ( )

Her granddaughter, Brigitte Kranendonk, said that she was her grandmother’s primary caregiver and that her family had decided to place Stegemann at The Pearl care home in Cannifton due to physical and mental decline.
ORGAN HARVESTING BEGAN WHILE PATIENTS STILL SHOWED ‘SIGNS OF LIFE,’ FEDERAL INVESTIGATION FINDS
But according to Kranendonk, her grandmother still had a good appetite even following a stomach cancer diagnosis, and rejected the idea of using MAID when it was presented as an option.
Kranendonk said she was present for Stegemann's second MAID assessment, and said that the doctor used "really loose terms, never using the words death or dying."
NEW YORK NUNS' CHALLENGE TO ASSISTED SUICIDE LAW IS ABOUT PROTECTING FREEDOM, LAWYER SAYS
"She explains MAID to my grandmother by saying: 'We’re going to give you medicine, you’re going to feel at peace. And I just want you to know that you won’t have a bowel movement,'" Kranendonk said.
When Kranendonk interjected and said, "She doesn’t understand what you’re saying," the doctor allegedly looked at Stegemann and said, "We’re going to make sure you won’t have any more pain."
CAN FAITH HELP PATIENTS HEAL? VETERAN DOCTOR REVEALS WHAT HE'S WITNESSED FIRSTHAND
According to a doctor, Stegemann was "deemed fit for MAID, and we're going to proceed," The Daily Mail reported.
Kranendonk said that two days before Stegemann's death, she asked her grandmother directly whether she understood that the scheduled procedure meant she would die.

Disability campaigners from "Distant Voices and Not Dead" hold a demonstration outside Westminster Hall in central London, on April 29, 2024, protesting against proposals to legalise assisted suicide in the UK. (Ben Stansall / AFP via Getty Images)
According to Kranendonk's account to the outlet, Stegemann began crying and said she had "made a mistake."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Stegemann was allegedly told by the doctor her grandmother could "deny" MAID on the day of the procedure, but Stegemann was already unsure if her grandmother had actually consented to it, did not want to cause her more stress, and wanted to enjoy what could be the last few days she had left with her grandmother.
Anders Hagstrom is a reporter with Fox News Digital covering national politics and major breaking news events.

title: Four American tourists among 6 killed after explosion levels building near Athens’ Acropolis
summary: A suspected gas leak caused an explosions that leveled a residential building in Athens' Plaka district near the Acropolis, killing four American tourists and two residents.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
Four American tourists were among six people killed in Greece when a devastating explosion leveled a residential building near Athens’ famed Acropolis, according to officials.

The four Americans — two men and two women believed to be two couples — were staying in the two-story building in the historic Plaka district, the historic neighborhood at the foot of the Acropolis and close to some of Athens’ most heavily visited landmarks, when the blast struck Friday.

The two couples had been expected to catch a flight from Athens airport at 3 p.m. Friday but never showed up, a police source told Reuters. Documents and belongings recovered with the four victims indicated they were U.S. citizens, according to Greek state broadcaster ERT and other local media.
AMERICAN TOURISTS STABBED OUTSIDE ATHENS' ACROPOLIS AS POLICE DETAIN SUSPECT IN APPARENT RANDOM ATTACK
Firefighters work at the scene following Friday's powerful blast in Athens' Plaka district, Saturday, Sept. 26, 2026. (AP Photo/Yorgos Karahalis)
U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle mourned the victims in a post on X.
"I am deeply saddened to learn of the death of four American citizens in yesterday’s explosion in central Athens," Guilfoyle wrote.
Emergency crews searching through the rubble recovered six bodies from the collapsed building Saturday, authorities said.

Firefighters had been searching for an elderly couple who lived in one apartment and four tourists staying in another as crews painstakingly removed debris, fire brigade spokesman Vassilis Vathrakogiannis said in a televised briefing.
EXPLOSION NEAR GERMAN TRAIN STATION INJURES 2 UKRAINIAN CITIZENS
The explosion was believed to have been caused by a major gas leak, Athens Mayor Haris Doukas said. Authorities were investigating the cause after reports of a gas smell in the area.
Firefighters work at the scene following Friday's powerful blast in Athens' Plaka district, Saturday, Sept. 26, 2026. (AP Photo/Yorgos Karahalis)
The powerful blast destroyed the building and damaged nearby homes, shops and vehicles, sending rubble and shattered glass as far as three blocks away, Reuters reported.

Video from the scene showed debris strewn across the street and parked cars crushed beneath falling rubble. The destroyed building was reduced to twisted metal, broken tiles and concrete, with clothing and household belongings scattered among the wreckage.
Rescuers work at the scene following Friday's powerful blast in Athens' Plaka district, Saturday, Sept. 26, 2026. (AP Photo/Yorgos Karahalis)
The search-and-rescue operation involved 30 firefighters and three dogs, while crews also used cameras and sensors to comb through the debris.

Two women were injured in an adjacent building on Lysikratous Street, according to the fire department. Resident Andreas Martzaklis told the Associated Press that all those rescued from the neighboring building were tourists.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The damage extended to a nearby church, where the pastor said Sunday services would be held outdoors because the building had been damaged in the explosion.
The Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report.

title: UK police arrest 'explosive' suspects near US airbase, key to Iran war
summary: Multiple suspects were arrested under the Explosives Act near RAF Fairford, prompting evacuations as explosive ordnance disposal teams examined vehicles.
story: Fox News' Lucas Tomlinson reports the latest on the threat from Iranian hackers targeting U.S. infrastructure.
U.K. police say they arrested multiple suspects for offenses under the "Explosives Act" near a U.S. airbase in southwest England on Sunday.
Gloucestershire Police say the arrests took place just two miles from RAF Fairford, which hosts U.S. Air Force assets. The U.S. has recently used the base in operations relating to the war in Iran.

"A number of properties are currently being evacuated in the Whelford area following the declaration of a major incident," Gloucestershire Police said in a statement. "It follows the arrest of several men on suspicion of offenses under the explosives act."
ANDY BURNHAM TAKES OVER AS UK PRIME MINISTER, CALLS FOR 'NEW POLITICAL MODEL'

Police at a road block on the road to RAF Fairford after a major incident has been declared, with armed police manning a cordon near the village of Whelford in Gloucestershire, near RAF Fairford which is used by the United States Air Force (USAF). Picture date: Sunday, September 27, 2026. (Photo by Ben Birchall/PA Images via Getty Images)
"The Army's specialist explosive ordnance disposal team are currently examining a number of vehicles," police added.
President Donald Trump responded to news of the arrests while talking to the press later Sunday.

"The arrest in the UK was fantastic. Working with Britain. It was an amazing job. We had them under investigation," Trump said of the suspects. "They, they were looking to do big damage to our fort and working with the British worked out great."
A reporter then asked if the suspects were migrants, and Trump demurred.
"It may have been Scotland Yard. I don't know that we worked with a lot of them. We had them under review for a long time and we got them," Trump said.
Authorities did not name the suspects or detail exactly how many were arrested.
British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting wrote on X that the situation is "being dealt with."
UK PINS STRING OF ANTISEMITIC ATTACKS ON IRAN-LINKED GROUP, BANS IRGC

A B1 Bomber at RAF Fairford on July 25, 2026, in Fairford, England. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has declared RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire a "legitimate target" after U.S. Air Force B-1B Lancer bombers used the British base to launch defensive bombing missions against Iranian military targets. (Photo by Matthew Horwood/Getty Images)
Prime Minister Andy Burnham also released a statement on the arrests.

"I know today's incident near RAF Fairford will be deeply concerning for local residents and for many people following developments across the country. My thanks go to Gloucestershire Police, Counter Terrorism Policing, our Armed Forces and all those working to keep the public safe," he said.

"The safety and security of the public is our first priority, and I want people to know that we will always take every step necessary to protect our communities and keep our country safe. The investigation remains ongoing, and I would urge people not to speculate while the authorities establish the full facts," he added.
WATER CYBERATTACK HITS AT LEAST 7 STATES
The incident comes roughly a month after Iran-linked hackers were suspected of forcing a small British power generator offline for several days this summer.

The British shutdown came weeks after hackers struck more than 30 community water systems in Minnesota, accessing technology used to remotely monitor and control pumps and other equipment. Minnesota officials have not publicly attributed the attacks. Several news outlets, citing U.S. officials and a leaked industry threat-sharing memo, reported that Iran was the likely culprit.

Members of the US military offload equipment from a US Air Force C-5 Galaxy at RAF Fairford in Southwest England on March 6, 2026. Britain's Prime Minister Keir Starmer has given approval for Washington to use the bases of Diego Garcia in the Indian Ocean and RAF Fairford in Southwest England to bomb Iranian missile sites, after several Gulf countries were targeted by Iranian retaliations.  (Justin Tallis/AFP via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Federal agencies have also warned that Iranian-affiliated actors have targeted similar industrial devices across water, energy and government sectors, seeking access to the software used to control them. That activity has already caused operational disruptions and financial losses.
Anders Hagstrom is a reporter with Fox News Digital covering national politics and major breaking news events.

title: Finland's Stubb credits Trump for pushing Ukraine peace talks while dismissing Russian invasion fears
summary: Finnish President Alexander Stubb credits Trump with pushing for Russia-Ukraine war peace and says Finland is fully prepared for any Moscow threat.
story: In a Fox News Digital exclusive, Finnish President Alexander Stubb discusses efforts to end the war in Ukraine, pushes back on fears of a Russian attack on Finland and addresses growing military cooperation between Moscow and Tehran.

UNITED NATIONS — As Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warns that Russia could take its war beyond Ukraine, Finnish President Alexander Stubb is striking a markedly calmer tone — saying Finland is prepared for Moscow and crediting President Donald Trump with pushing harder for a negotiated end to the war.

"I think we're certainly in a better place than we were before President Trump started," Stubb told Fox News Digital in an on-camera interview on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York. "He's doubled down in the past year and a half to try to find a solution for peace with negotiators such as Steve Witkoff, Jared Kushner and many others."

Stubb, who has been closely involved in the diplomatic effort, said he and Norway’s prime minister have worked largely "in the back office," relaying information among Ukraine, the United States and European governments.
KUSHNER, WITKOFF SET FOR KYIV TALKS AFTER PUTIN MEETING IN US PUSH FOR PEACE

US President Donald Trump meets with Finnish President Alexander Stubb in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, DC, on October 9, 2025. (Photo by Jim WATSON / AFP) (Photo by JIM WATSON/AFP via Getty Images) (Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images)
"I think he's really working hard and hopefully we'll get a solution," Stubb said.
The interview came during an intense diplomatic week in New York focused heavily on the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East.

Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met in New York during UNGA week as Washington continued its effort to revive negotiations with Moscow. Zelenskyy said peace remained Ukraine's priority and thanked Trump for sending the two envoys to Kyiv after they had also held talks in Moscow.
Zelenskyy was asked by Fox News Digital after the meeting about the possibility that Russia could invade or attack another European country in the near future.
BATTLE-TESTED ZELENSKYY SOUNDS CHILLING ALARM ON WHERE PUTIN’S WAR COULD HEAD NEXT

Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukraine's president, left, and Alexander Stubb, Finland's president, right, during a news conference in Helsinki, Finland, on Wednesday, March 19, 2025. (Roni Rekomaa/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
"That's why the risk of offensive by drones, missiles or land operation is very high against other countries who are bordering Russia or Belarus," Zelenskyy said.

The Ukrainian leader argued that Russian President Vladimir Putin, unable to achieve his military objectives in Ukraine, could seek to create instability elsewhere in Europe to pressure Western governments into reducing their support for Kyiv. He pointed to drone incursions and disruptions affecting several European countries, arguing that Moscow is already attempting to intimidate European societies and test their response.
Asked by Fox News Digital what European countries should do in response to the growing threat, Zelenskyy offered a direct answer.
"Respond. Always respond. It's not about the war. If you don't respond, Russians, they will go further," he said.

But Stubb struck a notably calmer tone when asked about Zelenskyy’s warnings that Russia could eventually attack other European countries, including Finland, which shares the longest border with Russia.
"As commander-in-chief in Finland, I sit on all the relevant information and I just don't see a factual basis for it," Stubb said.
RUSSIA'S SHADOW WAR IS PUTTING EUROPE ON EDGE AS GERMANY CONFRONTS A GROWING THREAT

Commander of the Finnish Army Lieutenant General Pasi Valimaki addresses Finnish conscript soldiers after a military exercise at Pori Brigade in Niinisalo, Finland, Dec. 9, 2025. (Anne Kauranen/Reuters)
That does not mean, he stressed, that Moscow has stopped targeting Europe.

Stubb distinguished between the "kinetic" war Russia is fighting in Ukraine and what he described as a broader "hybrid" campaign in Europe, pointing to cyberattacks, sabotage and damage to undersea cables in the Baltic Sea.
"We have to see this as a campaign," he said. "Russia tries to intimidate Europe, scare us and get into our heads."
His prescription was characteristically Finnish: "cool, calm and collected, take a sauna and a nice bath and deal with it."
Stubb said Finland, a country with a population of 5.6 million, can afford that attitude precisely because it has spent decades preparing for a potential threat from its eastern neighbor.
"We are calm because we are prepared," he said.
Finnish President Alexander Stubb answers questions during an exclusive Fox News Digital interview in New York City. (Brooke Curto / Fox News Digital)

He pointed to Finland’s mandatory military service, reserve force, artillery, long-range capabilities and extensive network of civilian shelters. The Finnish Defence Forces puts Finland’s wartime military strength at 280,000 personnel, with additional reservists available if needed.

That deterrent received another boost just days before Stubb traveled to New York. Finland is acquiring 64 F-35A fighter jets to replace its F/A-18 Hornet fleet under a procurement decision announced by the Finnish government.
The first two F-35s intended for operations inside Finland arrived at the Lapland Air Wing in Rovaniemi on Sept. 18, according to a Finnish Defence Forces press release.

"We have obligatory military service. I did mine, my son did his. We have women who do it voluntarily. We have over 60 F-18s. We just bought 64 F-35s, the two first of which arrived. We have long-range missiles, air, land and sea. We have the capability to mobilize 280,000 troops within days in a conflictual situation. On top of that, we have land mines. And we have the biggest artillery in Europe together with Poland… On top of that, we have civilian shelters for over 4.4 million people out of 5.6."
FINLAND'S PARLIAMENT VOTES TO LIFT DECADES-OLD BAN ON NUCLEAR WEAPONS IN HISTORIC NATO DEFENSE SHIFT

Security cameras overlook the Niirala Border Crossing Station along Finland's eastern border with Russia in Nov. 2023 after Finland closed the checkpoint amid heightened border security concerns. (Brooke Curto/Fox News Digital)
"We don't have them because we're worried about Sweden," Stubb joked of Finland’s military capabilities. "We have them because we see a security threat coming from Russia."

He said that level of preparedness, combined with Finland’s NATO membership, makes a direct Russian attack unlikely. Finland became NATO's 31st member on April 4, 2023, after abandoning its longstanding military non-alignment following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

"We feel that we're very prepared, and that gives us a strong enough … deterrent that we don't believe that Russia is going to test a country like Finland," Stubb said. "And of course the icing on the cake is that we are now security providers in the Alliance NATO."

Stubb also used his Sept. 22 address to the U.N. General Assembly to advocate for continued support for Kyiv, calling the "Coalition of the Willing" supporting Ukraine "particularly close to my heart." He said the coalition was working toward a "just and lasting peace in Ukraine in accordance with the U.N. Charter."

Stubb made additional news on Ukraine during UNGA week, when he urged SpaceX owner Elon Musk to extend Starlink coverage so Ukrainian forces could use the satellite network in areas containing Russian ballistic missile launchers, including inside Russia. He argued that doing so could help Ukraine target launchers firing missiles at Ukrainian cities.
Yet Ukraine was only one piece of what Stubb described as an increasingly interconnected global security crisis.
WORLD LEADERS DESCEND ON NEW YORK FOR UNGA — BUT WHO REALLY HAS AMERICA’S EAR?
Finland's President Alexander Stubb addresses the 81st United Nations General Assembly at UN headquarters in New York City, US, September 22, 2026. (Brendan McDermid/Reuters)
Asked about Trump’s call at the U.N. for countries to support efforts to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon, Stubb was unequivocal.
"I agree, Iran should not obtain nuclear weapons," he told Fox News Digital, adding that Tehran should not use proxies or be able to produce missiles.

Stubb also argued that the conflicts involving Russia and Iran can no longer be viewed in isolation, alleging that Moscow is providing intelligence to Tehran that Iran has used against U.S. military bases in the Gulf, while Iranian weapons have been supplied to Russia for use against Ukraine.
"We're going in this merry-go-round where every bit of the conflict is linked to another," Stubb said. "The sooner we can end both, the better."
Iran conducts joint military exercises with Russia in the Strait of Hormuz after the U.S. deployed surveillance drones. (Iranian Army/Handout/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Trump used his Sept. 22 U.N. General Assembly address to call for Iran's economic isolation and reiterate that Tehran should not obtain a nuclear weapon, while warning of further US military action if a peace agreement is not reached, according to Reuters.
For Stubb, the proliferation of conflicts — from Ukraine and Iran to Gaza, Yemen and Sudan — is testing a diplomatic system already struggling to keep pace.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"It's not a zero-sum game," he said. "We have to deal with a multiplicity of conflicts right now, unfortunately."
And for Trump, he added, that means "working around the clock."

Efrat (Effie) Lachter is a reporter for Fox News Digital with more than 15 years of experience covering conflict, global affairs, human rights and political accountability. She has directed and produced more than 200 documentary segments across more than 40 countries, documenting conflicts, humanitarian crises, corruption, human trafficking, gender-based violence and the human stories behind major world events.

Lachter’s reporting has taken her into conflict zones and crisis areas across the Middle East, Europe, Asia and Africa. Her work has included uncovering human trafficking networks, revealing an ISIS underground torture prison in Syria, documenting the war in Ukraine and interviewing senior political figures and world leaders. She was also among the Western journalists who entered Russia after the war began to bring testimonies from Putin’s opposition. Lachter is the recipient of the 2022 Peres Center for Peace Award and was a 2023–2024 Knight-Wallace Journalism Fellow at the University of Michigan. She also won two Rockower Awards for Excellence in Reporting. She holds a bachelor's degree in communication and a master's degree in political science.

title: Vance talks 2028, Ted Cruz and a tough midterm climate that could affect his future
summary: Vice President JD Vance said the GOP faces an “uphill climb” in the midterms — and that the results may be a data point he reviews as he decides his 2028 plans.
story: JOINT BASE ANDREWS, Md. — Vice President JD Vance acknowledged Thursday that Republicans face an “uphill climb” in next month’s midterm elections — and that the results may be a data point he reviews as he decides whether to run for president in 2028.

“Historically there’s always a bit of an uphill climb, and I think you definitely sense that,” Vance said in an interview with NBC News. “I also think you can sense a sense of cautious optimism, in the sense that, you know, people feel like the numbers are sort of moving, maybe in our direction.”
He added: “Politically, there’s just a recognition that it’s always going to be hard to win a midterm when you have the White House, the Senate and the House.”

Vance spoke aboard Air Force Two shortly after it landed on a return trip from Lakeland, Florida, where he campaigned for Sen. Ashley Moody and Rep. Byron Donalds, the Republican nominee for governor. It was his latest headlining gig at a rally meant to boost support for the party’s candidates in what is expected to be a challenging year for the GOP.

Aside from the historical trends Vance mentioned, polls have shown President Donald Trump and the war in Iran highly unpopular among voters. A related rise in gas prices has added to a cascade of affordability concerns. And Americans are growing more skeptical of artificial intelligence and the large, power-hungry data centers being built to accommodate the technology. All of those issues could factor into voters’ choices in this fall’s key races for the House, the Senate and governor.

Vance, 42, has said consistently that his focus is on his job as vice president and on helping his party through the midterms — and that any decision about running to succeed Trump in 2028 won’t come until after then.

Asked Thursday whether a poor showing for Republicans on Nov. 3 would factor into his thinking, Vance replied: “You make these decisions by collecting as much information and trying to make a wise decision. And yeah, I mean, regardless of what happens over the next 35 days, there will be new information, new things you have to make a decision over.”
Could substantial GOP losses convince him that the climate might not be favorable for him to run for president? Vance was noncommittal.

“Right now, I try not to think too much in hypotheticals,” he said. “I’m just going to try to do as well as I can and encourage people to elect the candidates that I think are good. The American people make that decision, and when they do, then yeah, I’ll have some new information to consider.”

Vance was more eager to assess a prospective rival: Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas. Cruz said in a recent interview with MS NOW that Vance does not have a lock on the 2028 nomination and spoke of wanting to “certainly be part of the discussion.” He also has framed the future of the party as a choice between being a “small-government, free-market conservative party” or a “big-government, nanny state party.”
Add to Google
Add to Google
Vance said Cruz’s efforts to engineer a clash don’t bother him.

“It is really obvious to me that, at this very moment, Ted Cruz is running for president,” Vance added. “At this moment, I’m not. I’m trying to help elect Republicans. That’s what I’m going to keep on doing.”

Cruz, who is not up for re-election to the Senate this year, has been raising money and campaigning for midterm candidates — not only in Texas but also in states like Iowa and South Carolina. Both are traditionally placed early on the GOP’s presidential caucus and primary calendar.
Cruz also is expected to campaign this month for Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, as well as Republican Senate candidates Ken Paxton in Texas and Michael Whatley in North Carolina.

“Senator Cruz has been focused on electing Republicans up and down the ballot this November, and he will continue campaigning vigorously over the next several weeks to help make that happen,” a spokesperson said in a statement to NBC News.

In the interview, Vance tackled several of the issues that have become central to the midterm elections. He acknowledged frustration over high gas prices and said it was a topic he and Donalds discussed backstage at Thursday’s rally in Florida.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

Vance also reiterated a message he has been delivering on Capitol Hill and across the country. Republicans, he said, can’t pretend things are perfect, but they can highlight their successes while they accuse the past Democratic administration of leaving them a mess and arguing that the next wave of Democrats would be worse.

“I think people recognize that the message is starting to penetrate a little bit — that we are solving problems the Democrats created and the Democrats are running a lot of crazy people,” Vance said. “I do get a sense that message is penetrating. Obviously, we’re going to find out in about 35 days whether that carries the day.”
Asked whether blame targeted at the Trump administration — which has now been in office for more than a year and a half — is justified, Vance acknowledged that such frustrations may exist.

“Voters are impatient, right? They ultimately make the decision,” he said. “We have to make the argument as best as we can. And what I honestly think is that we inherited a remarkably tough situation. … But I think that our approach is to brag about the victories, talk about the great accomplishments.”
Vance also wrestled with two of the hottest-button issues this campaign season: data centers and AI.
On data centers, Vance took something of a middle-ground stance.

“I certainly think that there are local apprehensions,” he said. “I think in some cases the companies building the data centers have done a good job of ensuring the community shares the benefits and ensuring prices don’t go — power, electricity prices don’t go up. And then in some communities, obviously, you don’t see that happening, and you see more of a pushback.”

His stance is more nuanced and tonally different than Trump’s. In an August post on Truth Social, the president likened data centers to a “Golden Goose” and charged that people opposing their construction “want to end up being backwards and poor.”

On AI, Vance has been both enthusiastic and cautious, having recently raised concerns about cybersecurity and its use in war. In the interview, the vice president noted recent alarm over how fast the technology is advancing and the fear that it will bring the end of human existence, drawing comparisons to the early days of the Covid pandemic.

“Actually, I felt a little bit like I did with Covid, where it seemed like there was a significant panic. The risk is real, just like it was with Covid, but the remedy was not necessarily appropriate or tailored to the risk,” Vance said. “And specifically, when I see people who quite literally have developed models that are good at hacking into other people’s software coming and saying, ‘Oh, my God, we’ve unleashed Frankenstein into the wild; the government should help us’ — well, one of the ways the government has to help is by ensuring that people who release Frankenstein into the wild suffer some consequences for it.”

He added a moment later: “My fear with AI right now is that we respond not by forcing more responsibility on the companies that are creating the products but by creating a regulatory regime that actually shields them from liability and in the process doesn’t deal with the real risk.”

title: How 16 undecided voters are weighing their 2026 election options
summary: The voters, who participated in a recent NBC News poll and spoke to reporters afterward, are laser-focused on high prices and largely disappointed with both parties.
story: James Morton isn’t sure which party he’s going to support in November’s elections, and he doesn’t like his options.

Morton, a 67-year-old retired truck driver in Colorado, said Democrats have “gone too far to the left towards socialism,” while Republicans are “globalists” who “don’t care about the working-class people in this country.”

Morton, an independent who voted for Donald Trump in 2024, is leaning toward backing third-party candidates in races for the House and the Senate this year. But he said his decision will come down to the high cost of living.

“The No. 1 thing is getting the cost of things back down, inflation under control, and pretty much that’s it,” Morton said. He noted that he and his wife have been buying different groceries as they navigate high prices.

Morton is among the 5% of voters surveyed last month in a national NBC News poll who said they weren’t sure which party they wanted to see controlling Congress after this year’s elections. NBC News spoke with 16 of those undecided voters as they weigh their votes this fall, some of whom declined to share their full names discussing politics.

These voters feel little loyalty to either party — and many of them said that’s in part because they aren’t sure either party understands what’s important to them. Almost every one said high costs are top of mind.

In the NBC News poll, 50% of voters said they wanted Democrats to win control of Congress in the midterms, while 45% said they wanted Republicans to have control. How the undecided voters in between resolve their strong, sometimes conflicting feelings could ultimately decide what Congress looks like in 2027, from who controls the majority to how many seats that party holds.
Costs dominate

Voters’ focus on making ends meet has been standing out in recent polling. In the latest NBC News survey, voters ranked cost of living and inflation as the most important issues facing the country, followed by government corruption and threats to democracy.

“I don’t like how expensive things are, and I don’t think anyone does,” said Aidan Valenzuela, a 19-year-old security worker in Texas, who said he hasn’t decided whom to support in his state’s hotly contested races for governor and the Senate.
Joanne, a 72-year-old Vermont independent who works for a heating company, said she plans to sit out her state’s governor’s race, and she hasn’t decided whom she’ll support farther down the ballot.

“I just want somebody to bring some of these prices back down,” she said. Joanne said her husband relies on multiple medications, including insulin. “It’s pretty expensive and leaves nothing for anything else.”
Luke Melanson, 49, of Louisiana, who is retired from construction work, said the rising cost of groceries has changed how he shops.
“I’m not eating as much. I’m eating less food because I can only afford so much,” he said.

Melanson doesn’t identify with either political party, instead considering himself a libertarian, and he declined to say where he was leaning in the midterm election. But he is frustrated with both parties and wants to see new candidates emerge who can personally relate to his financial position.

“I want a plumber. I want someone that ran a smaller business, like a Kroger’s,” he said. “A teacher. I take anybody that isn’t a lawyer or someone so ultra-rich that the pay gap is so far they would never understand what I’m going through.”
Meanwhile, South Carolinian Darien Thompson, a 25-year-old unarmed security guard at a mall, sees gas as the biggest financial woe of the moment. The cost of his commute is only going up.
“It does take a mental load when it’s like, well, it’s going to cost this much to get to work and back, and I’m only making this much,” Thompson said.
It doesn’t bode well for his long-term hopes of owning a home, and he doesn’t see any current politicians stepping up to tackle the issues in a way that has earned his support.
“Politicians are getting into these petty squabbles,” he said. “But it’s, like, none of us can afford houses.”

Thompson doesn’t see himself voting for a Republican in November, but he’s still undecided. He has leaned Democratic before, voting for then-Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024, but his vote this year will depend entirely on the specific candidate Democrats run in his area.

Ibraham, a 42-year-old truck driver in Ohio who isn’t registered with either party, said he plans to back Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown in the Senate race in his state. Ibraham supported Harris in 2024 and said his vote this year is driven almost entirely by the surging price of diesel and a higher cost of living.

“I’ve been driving for nine years. I’ve never seen anything like it. Never. Never, ever. Even during Covid, it didn’t get that high,” Ibraham said, noting that his weekly diesel costs have jumped from $2,000 to $3,500 or $3,700.
“I’m spending an extra $1,500 on diesel every week. Just think about it — it’s a fortune,” he said.
Down on both parties and Trump
Ibraham described his support for Brown as more about opposing Republicans than endorsing Democrats, blaming the GOP-controlled White House and Congress for the current economic struggles.
“It’s not about Brown,” Ibraham said of his Senate vote. “It’s just voting against the Republicans for what they’re doing. That’s it.”

Other voters who were undecided but leaning toward Democrats expressed similar views, expressing caution and saying their potential support for Democrats was motivated more by reining in Trump and Republicans.
For Subscribers
Several voters — including those who backed Trump two years ago — specifically voiced concerns about Trump’s handling of the economy and the war in Iran.
For Subscribers

“I will probably support [a] Democrat this time around just so there’s some check and balances in place,” said Aaron L., a 30-year-old California independent who works in tech. He didn’t vote in 2024 while he was moving, but he said he most likely would have voted for Trump. But nearly two years into Trump’s second term, Aaron said, the economy is “a mess.”
“It seems like the party, the Republican Party, just follow whatever Donald Trump says,” Aaron said.
Like other undecided voters, Aaron said the economy and the war in Iran were among his top issues. Dissatisfaction with the war was high, including among Trump voters.

“One of his platforms was no more useless wars, and here we are — we’re back,” said Kevin, a 35-year-old civil engineer in Massachusetts. Kevin, a Democrat, voted for Trump in 2024 hoping he would boost the economy.

This year, he said, he is leaning toward supporting Republican Mike Minogue in the Massachusetts governor’s race, hoping he could shake up the state, and leaning toward backing Democratic Sen. Ed Markey for re-election.
“It goes back to the checks and balances,” Kevin said of the possibility that he could split his ticket, saying he wants to see a Democratic-controlled Congress end the war in Iran.

Kaleb Saracino, 21, of Nevada, doesn’t like how many resources are being poured into the Iran war or the idea that the U.S. is fighting there in behalf of Israel. He said he wants the government to cut off support for Israel, bring down costs and refocus on issues affecting everyday Americans.
“The cost of groceries, the cost of gas, the cost of living have all gone up because of these endless wars,” Saracino said.
Saracino knows he doesn’t want to support Trump, so he’s leaning toward the Democrats this year. But he doesn’t have warm feelings for either party.
“They’re looking out for themselves, their careers, because they’re career politicians, not so much the betterment of the American people,” Saracino said about both Republicans and Democrats.
Alexis, a 20-year-old college student in Florida, also expressed frustration with both parties in Washington.
“They’ve made a bunch of promises that haven’t been fulfilled, and you know why? It’s because people cannot talk to each other these days. Congress is so divided,” she said.

Alexis, an independent who voted for Harris in 2024, isn’t sure whom she’ll support in the Florida Senate race. She said more could get done “when we start allowing younger candidates who are more open-minded to vouching for the American people as a whole, rather than their own specific party.”

Essen Zali, a 46-year-old IT consultant from Texas, voted for Joe Biden in 2020 but backed Trump in 2024 after he became frustrated with Biden during the conflict in Gaza. Now, the Iran war has again left him frustrated.
“He went two steps forward with the whole war thing, and now we are all over the place,” he said. On top of that, Zali said, Trump seems focused on the wrong things.

“All the construction work that was going on in Washington, that was not ever required. All the beautifications and everything, that’s secondary. The tariff war without a reason,” Zali said. “It seems like he is burning all the ships.”
Connor Woodring, a 22-year-old independent from Colorado, also supported Trump in 2024. He was another voter who felt disdain for both parties.

“They’re one on the same side of the same coin, basically. Republicans are the warmongering side of it. Democrats are the side that try to pull at your heartstrings,” he said. “Either way, they’re going to vote and do the same thing they’ve done for the last 50 years, so it doesn’t matter which side you vote in.”
Woodring is a registered independent and doesn’t like any candidates in his area. His preference is to vote for someone not in either major party.
But, he said, “there’s a lot that can happen between now and November.”

title: What we know about the pilot hailed as a hero for averting crash of Israel-bound plane
summary: He is being hailed around the world as a hero for helping stop a passenger plane bound for Israel from plunging into the ground, despite his own severe injuries.
story: He is being hailed around the world as a hero for helping stop a passenger plane bound for Israel from plunging into the ground, despite his own severe injuries.

Images of Capt. Smit Machchhar covered in blood have gone viral after he fought his fellow pilot, who, according to Israeli officials, stabbed him and attempted to nosedive the plane carrying 174 people from Dubai to Tel Aviv.

While bleeding profusely, Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door, allowing other passengers and the Emirati crew to overpower the other pilot and take control of the aircraft. The flight was diverted to an airport in Saudi Arabia, where it landed safely.

The Mumbai native’s actions have “shown the world the highest form of courage” and “prevented another 9/11-like attack from happening,” Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said Thursday, after speaking with Machchhar’s family. “The whole world is proud of him,” he added.
Machchhar spoke previously of getting the “aviation bug” at 19 while pursuing a management course to grow his family’s textile business.
He worked for years at a low-cost Indian airline before joining Flydubai and had nearly 10,000 hours of flying experience before Wednesday’s incident.

Machchhar is being treated in a hospital in Tabuk city in northwest Saudi Arabia, with his condition described as “stable” on Wednesday by the Indian Embassy in Riyadh. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told Fox News he was “very badly wounded.”

Deepak Mittal, India’s ambassador to the United Arab Emirates, said on X he met with Machchhar’s family on Thursday in Dubai and “conveyed full support of the Government of India in ensuring welfare and wellbeing of the Indian Hero.”
Netanyahu called Machchhar “a true hero.”

“Despite being stabbed and seriously injured, he fought back, resisted, opened the cockpit door and enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker — preventing a catastrophic midair disaster,” he said.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

Machchhar’s former employer, the Indian budget carrier SpiceJet, said on X that he flew for the airline for 10 years. According to his LinkedIn profile, Machchhar joined the Emirati low-cost carrier Flydubai in 2022 after flying for SpiceJet since 2011.

On Wednesday, the veteran captain was flying a Boeing 737 Max 8, the newer variant of the 737 plane that Machchhar had nearly 10,000 hours of experience flying, according to his profile and a YouTube podcast interview he gave last year.
“My first aircraft was a Boeing, and it’s always been that aircraft all my life,” he said.
Machchhar said he had flown challenging routes, dodged bad weather and handled medical emergencies in the air before.
His mother was “scared” when he first told her of his plan to become a pilot, he said in the 2025 interview, but his supportive father agreed to cover the steep fees for aviation training.

Between 2008 and 2009, Machchhar trained for 18 months at an aviation college in New Zealand. It was the first time he had been outside India, he said, and he had been on only a “couple of flights” as a passenger before learning to fly.
He “stood out” among those training and did well with his studies, Mainland Air chief executive Philip Kean told New Zealand’s 1News, adding: “We’re all very proud of him here.”
In his early days as a qualified pilot, he took whatever flight routes he was assigned.
“When I started flying ... the only thing I wanted to do then was fly,” Machchhar told the podcast. “I didn’t want to sleep, I didn’t want to go anywhere, and they loved me for it.”
“For a pilot to gain that experience and to refine your skills is what a pilot is,” he added.
But his attitude changed when he got married and started a family, he said.
“Now I would say I try when I get out of the cockpit or the aircraft, I don’t want the other guy to know that I’m a pilot. I don’t want to discuss aviation,” he said.
“Now the kids are there,” he said. “They want to play with you.”
In the interview, Machchhar also spoke about the “rigorous training” that pilots and cabin crew undergo, which includes safety and emergency procedures.
“When we are up there and if something happens, who is going to save you? You’ll be lucky enough to have a doctor on board,” he said.
“They can save your life,” he said, referring to the cabin crew.

title: Screaming, panicking, blood: Passengers detail horrifying Israel-bound flight
summary: It was too early to say why a pilot stabbed another on the flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv, according to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
story: TEL AVIV — A stabbing, an emergency alert, a terrifying midair plunge.
Details are still emerging after an Israel-bound flight carrying 180 people emitted a distress signal Wednesday, raising fears of a possible hijacking when one pilot stabbed the other in the cockpit.
Aviatar Alevi, who was on the Flydubai flight Wednesday, described people “screaming, running, panicking, blood.”
“At the start, I thought it was a plane malfunction, but then I started hearing screaming about the stabbings,” Alevi, 17, told NBC News. “Then I understood the weight of the actual situation.”
“We didn’t know what was going to happen,” he said, adding that the possibility of death “was definitely an option.”
The plane made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, one of its rudders damaged, apparently by the force of its descent.
The passengers, who had been flying from Dubai, were mobbed by media and flag-waving fellow Israelis after they finally arrived at Ben Gurion Airport near Tel Aviv.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
They said they feared for their lives after the plane plunged more than 14,000 feet in 29 seconds at one point, according to FlightRadar24.
“Imagine sitting on the plane, all scared after you fell down five kilometers. You don’t understand anything,” 16-year-old Peleg Itali told NBC News.

Capt. Smit Machchhar, an Indian national, was recovering in a hospital in Saudi Arabia on Thursday as the other pilot, so far identified only as an Omani citizen, was being interrogated elsewhere in the country. Machchhar was widely praised for his efforts to prevent the plane from crashing, opening the cockpit door and allowing passengers and crewmembers to rush in.

Machchhar and the pilot who initiated the attack were transferred to Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, on Thursday, the Saudi Arabian Interior Ministry said in a statement, citing an unnamed “official source” at the ministry.

“The source indicated that initial investigations conducted by the competent authorities in the Kingdom, with the participation of a security team from the sisterly United Arab Emirates, revealed an assault on the pilot by his co-pilot, resulting in both sustaining various injuries,” the ministry said. “The source confirmed that the pilot and his co-pilot, after their health improved and the medical team cleared them, departed the Kingdom for Abu Dhabi this morning.”
Few details had emerged about the pilot Thursday morning. Questions about a possible motive, including whether it was terrorism-related, hang over the attack.

“I don’t think it was a hijacking. It looks like a suicide attempt, simply because of what this hero, Yaniv, has described,” Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on “CBS Evening News” as he praised Yaniv Hayun, who rushed into the cockpit and subdued the attacker.
Hayun, who was pictured with his shirt spattered with blood sitting next to Netanyahu, said he confronted the pilot who initiated the attack, according to the Israeli government press office.
“I grabbed the attacker and choked him, pulled him out first,” Hayun said. “I started pulling the controls.”
“Thank God, we pulled it off. We really put our heads together and worked as a team,” Hayun said, adding: “It was between fear and a sense of a do-or-die situation.”
“We had to win. We had to pull through and come out on top,” he said. Hayun told Netanyahu that he acted based on what he had seen on a TV show and helped stabilize the plane.
Flydubai said on-duty crewmembers on the flight were able to land the plane.
Motive under investigation
Netanyahu said it was still too early to determine why the pilot apparently stabbed his colleague and appeared to try to take over the Flydubai flight and whether Iran was involved.

“We’ve had signs that Iran, in particular through its proxies, was intending to heighten terrorist attacks against Israel and Israeli nationals abroad,” he said. “But I think it’s too early to say whether there was Iranian collusion here.”
Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz branded the incident a “jihadist terrorist attack attempt,” without expanding on how he had reached that conclusion.
President Donald Trump also weighed in, calling it “an incredible story.”
“It seems as though the co-pilot was perhaps a terrorist or perhaps a whack job, and he stabbed the pilot,” Trump told reporters.
On Thursday, Trump told reporters at the White House that the pilot who initiated the attack could be linked to Iran.
“I would say the answer, based on what I’m hearing, is yes. But we’re working on it right now,” he said.
Asked whether the pilot could have been radicalized or working with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, Trump replied, “Could have been, yeah.”
Trump also told reporters Thursday that there would be renewed strikes against Iran if it was behind the attack.
“Oh, they’ll be hit very hard, don’t worry,” he said.
“You just ask them,” he added. “They know what happened. They’ll be hit very hard.”
All the passengers were Israeli, according to Netanyahu’s office. Four were dual American-Israeli citizens, two U.S. officials told NBC News.

With few details about the suspect or any potential motive surrounding the incident, Doron Spielman, a spokesperson for Netanyahu’s office, said there was a “strong opinion” that the incident was a terrorist attack, “but we can’t be sure until we debrief everybody.”
An investigation by Saudi authorities is ongoing, David Mencer, a spokesperson for the Israeli Prime Minister’s Office, said separately.
A senior U.S. official and a Saudi official who were both briefed on the Israeli investigation said the stabbing increasingly looked like an act of terrorism based on early findings.
The United Arab Emirates’ attorney general, Hamad Saif Al Shamsi, separately ordered an investigation.

His office said the probe would seek to “gather information and evidence, establish the facts and circumstances of the incident, and determine the underlying motives,” in addition to examining “whether the incident was linked to any terrorist activity or purpose, or involved any prior planning or direction.”

Hessa Alyahya, spokesperson for the Saudi Embassy in the U.S., said authorities were waiting to determine whether the attack was a dispute between the pilots or whether it was an act sponsored by Iran or the Houthis.
Israel and Saudi Arabia do not have official diplomatic relations.

title: For the same ticket on StubHub, different prices for different people
summary: NBC News volunteers saw eight different prices for the exact same Harry Styles ticket on StubHub. The company said it’s running random price experiments.
story: The same seat at an upcoming Harry Styles concert at Madison Square Garden could cost $455. Or it could cost $517.
The difference comes from the fees that ticket broker StubHub adds. But how much those fees are — and why they can vary — is unclear.

NBC News gathered nine volunteers to check the same StubHub ticket at the same time for Styles’ Oct. 30 concert. They saw eight different prices. The ticket’s base price, set by the seller, was the same for everybody.
The big differences came from the fees StubHub added. One person was charged $72 in fees, while another was charged nearly twice as much, $134.

When the volunteers looked up the same ticket using incognito mode in Google’s Chrome web browser, a private session that doesn’t use cookies, saved logins or site storage, the price discrepancy declined to $19 between the highest- and lowest-priced ticket. When they checked on StubHub’s phone app without being logged in, almost everybody saw the same price, with the exception of just one person who would have been charged $3 more.

The days of a single, transparent price tag are fading. In the digital era, prices can change by the minute, without warning or explanation. Companies can run price experiments, in which shoppers are given a range of prices at random to determine the optimal price for profitability. Some companies use surveillance or personalized pricing, in which they charge individualized prices based on a customer’s data.

StubHub, one of the largest online ticket resale platforms, has recently faced scrutiny over its business practices, including advertising ticket prices without clearly disclosing mandatory fees, leading to a $10 million Federal Trade Commission settlement, and listing “ghost tickets” from a seller who didn’t actually have them.
The company said it does not use personal information in setting prices but confirmed that ticket prices can vary.

In a statement, StubHub said it “regularly runs randomized tests on pricing — a standard e-commerce practice across retail and marketplace platforms. The fee variations observed in your experiment reflect that testing, not personalization based on individual user data.” The company also said that differences in incognito mode were due to the “natural randomness of a small sample, not a signal that cookie or browsing data drives fee differences.”

Lindsay Owens, author of the new book “Gouged: The End of a Fair Price — and What That Means for Your Wallet,” said price experiments are a way for companies to maximize profit by helping to identify the upper limits of what customers are willing to pay. Even if it is random, it’s still unfair, she said.

“It’s not the resale ticket holder who’s getting that money,” Owens told NBC News. “It’s StubHub, who’s just charging some parents more, some ticket holders more, concertgoers more, just to see their favorite show.”
Owens said it was notable that without access to users’ data trails, the company appeared to have a harder time determining what to charge users.

Mark Tremblay, an economics professor at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, noted that if the price experiments are random, consumers could take advantage of this by checking multiple ways. “As a consumer, you should shop around on different mediums,” he said.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

It’s not just StubHub, Owens said: More and more companies are charging different consumers different prices for the same products. Last year, Owens’ think tank, Groundwork Collaborative, and Consumer Reports found that some Instacart shoppers were shown different prices for the same grocery items. The company said it was price testing and later ended the program.

Companies also have the technology to go a step further, using personal data to determine what a customer is willing to pay and tailor prices to each individual, a practice called surveillance or personalized pricing.

There is no federal ban on personalized pricing, but some states have passed laws regulating the practice. In August, the FTC proposed a policy that would require companies to disclose their use of personalized pricing.

Bob Hedges, a digital fellow at the MIT Initiative on the Digital Economy, said new technology, more powerful algorithms and the explosion of online shopping have made it easier than ever for companies to do this. “Even five years ago, the compute power and real-time processing was not adequate to support some of the real-time pricing algorithms in place today,” he noted.

As companies increasingly use sophisticated algorithms to calculate and change prices in an instant, it’s becoming harder for consumers to know when the price they’re seeing is based on their personal data.
To find out what companies are thinking, Owens said look to their patents. She pointed to DoorDash as an example.

The delivery platform has filed a patent for technology that it says predicts how hungry users are based on things like “a low battery” and “fast scrolling,” suggesting you could be “searching urgently for something to order.”
In a statement, DoorDash said the patent was “never used and has been withdrawn” and was meant to “help people find support if they were struggling on the app.”

The company acknowledged that customers may receive “personalized promotions” for the same order based on “past orders and favorite stores” but said that this practice does not amount to “surveillance pricing.”

title: Vance talks 2028, Ted Cruz and a tough midterm climate that could affect his future
summary: Vice President JD Vance said the GOP faces an “uphill climb” in the midterms — and that the results may be a data point he reviews as he decides his 2028 plans.
story: JOINT BASE ANDREWS, Md. — Vice President JD Vance acknowledged Thursday that Republicans face an “uphill climb” in next month’s midterm elections — and that the results may be a data point he reviews as he decides whether to run for president in 2028.

“Historically there’s always a bit of an uphill climb, and I think you definitely sense that,” Vance said in an interview with NBC News. “I also think you can sense a sense of cautious optimism, in the sense that, you know, people feel like the numbers are sort of moving, maybe in our direction.”
He added: “Politically, there’s just a recognition that it’s always going to be hard to win a midterm when you have the White House, the Senate and the House.”

Vance spoke aboard Air Force Two shortly after it landed on a return trip from Lakeland, Florida, where he campaigned for Sen. Ashley Moody and Rep. Byron Donalds, the Republican nominee for governor. It was his latest headlining gig at a rally meant to boost support for the party’s candidates in what is expected to be a challenging year for the GOP.

Aside from the historical trends Vance mentioned, polls have shown President Donald Trump and the war in Iran highly unpopular among voters. A related rise in gas prices has added to a cascade of affordability concerns. And Americans are growing more skeptical of artificial intelligence and the large, power-hungry data centers being built to accommodate the technology. All of those issues could factor into voters’ choices in this fall’s key races for the House, the Senate and governor.

Vance, 42, has said consistently that his focus is on his job as vice president and on helping his party through the midterms — and that any decision about running to succeed Trump in 2028 won’t come until after then.

Asked Thursday whether a poor showing for Republicans on Nov. 3 would factor into his thinking, Vance replied: “You make these decisions by collecting as much information and trying to make a wise decision. And yeah, I mean, regardless of what happens over the next 35 days, there will be new information, new things you have to make a decision over.”
Could substantial GOP losses convince him that the climate might not be favorable for him to run for president? Vance was noncommittal.

“Right now, I try not to think too much in hypotheticals,” he said. “I’m just going to try to do as well as I can and encourage people to elect the candidates that I think are good. The American people make that decision, and when they do, then yeah, I’ll have some new information to consider.”

Vance was more eager to assess a prospective rival: Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas. Cruz said in a recent interview with MS NOW that Vance does not have a lock on the 2028 nomination and spoke of wanting to “certainly be part of the discussion.” He also has framed the future of the party as a choice between being a “small-government, free-market conservative party” or a “big-government, nanny state party.”
Add to Google
Add to Google
Vance said Cruz’s efforts to engineer a clash don’t bother him.

“It is really obvious to me that, at this very moment, Ted Cruz is running for president,” Vance added. “At this moment, I’m not. I’m trying to help elect Republicans. That’s what I’m going to keep on doing.”

Cruz, who is not up for re-election to the Senate this year, has been raising money and campaigning for midterm candidates — not only in Texas but also in states like Iowa and South Carolina. Both are traditionally placed early on the GOP’s presidential caucus and primary calendar.
Cruz also is expected to campaign this month for Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, as well as Republican Senate candidates Ken Paxton in Texas and Michael Whatley in North Carolina.

“Senator Cruz has been focused on electing Republicans up and down the ballot this November, and he will continue campaigning vigorously over the next several weeks to help make that happen,” a spokesperson said in a statement to NBC News.

In the interview, Vance tackled several of the issues that have become central to the midterm elections. He acknowledged frustration over high gas prices and said it was a topic he and Donalds discussed backstage at Thursday’s rally in Florida.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

Vance also reiterated a message he has been delivering on Capitol Hill and across the country. Republicans, he said, can’t pretend things are perfect, but they can highlight their successes while they accuse the past Democratic administration of leaving them a mess and arguing that the next wave of Democrats would be worse.

“I think people recognize that the message is starting to penetrate a little bit — that we are solving problems the Democrats created and the Democrats are running a lot of crazy people,” Vance said. “I do get a sense that message is penetrating. Obviously, we’re going to find out in about 35 days whether that carries the day.”
Asked whether blame targeted at the Trump administration — which has now been in office for more than a year and a half — is justified, Vance acknowledged that such frustrations may exist.

“Voters are impatient, right? They ultimately make the decision,” he said. “We have to make the argument as best as we can. And what I honestly think is that we inherited a remarkably tough situation. … But I think that our approach is to brag about the victories, talk about the great accomplishments.”
Vance also wrestled with two of the hottest-button issues this campaign season: data centers and AI.
On data centers, Vance took something of a middle-ground stance.

“I certainly think that there are local apprehensions,” he said. “I think in some cases the companies building the data centers have done a good job of ensuring the community shares the benefits and ensuring prices don’t go — power, electricity prices don’t go up. And then in some communities, obviously, you don’t see that happening, and you see more of a pushback.”

His stance is more nuanced and tonally different than Trump’s. In an August post on Truth Social, the president likened data centers to a “Golden Goose” and charged that people opposing their construction “want to end up being backwards and poor.”

On AI, Vance has been both enthusiastic and cautious, having recently raised concerns about cybersecurity and its use in war. In the interview, the vice president noted recent alarm over how fast the technology is advancing and the fear that it will bring the end of human existence, drawing comparisons to the early days of the Covid pandemic.

“Actually, I felt a little bit like I did with Covid, where it seemed like there was a significant panic. The risk is real, just like it was with Covid, but the remedy was not necessarily appropriate or tailored to the risk,” Vance said. “And specifically, when I see people who quite literally have developed models that are good at hacking into other people’s software coming and saying, ‘Oh, my God, we’ve unleashed Frankenstein into the wild; the government should help us’ — well, one of the ways the government has to help is by ensuring that people who release Frankenstein into the wild suffer some consequences for it.”

He added a moment later: “My fear with AI right now is that we respond not by forcing more responsibility on the companies that are creating the products but by creating a regulatory regime that actually shields them from liability and in the process doesn’t deal with the real risk.”

title: Governor replaces DA with New York AG Letitia James as special prosecutor in Cornell case
summary: Jane Doe, who has said she was raped and plied with drugs at a Cornell fraternity house in 2024, “deserves to know that every fact will be examined and justice pursued,” Gov. Kathy Hochul said.
story: New York Attorney General Letitia James has been appointed as special prosecutor in the Cornell University sexual assault investigation, Gov. Kathy Hochul announced Thursday, following increasing scrutiny and uproar over how university police and the local district attorney’s office handled the matter two years ago.
Hochul said in a statement that “newly released information continues to raise serious questions about the investigation,” which has in turn “undercut my faith, and the public’s faith.”

She said James, who has been attorney general since 2019, will take over the case of a former Cornell University student who alleged in a lawsuit last month that she was raped, sexually assaulted and plied with drugs by members of Chi Phi fraternity in 2024.
Add to Google
Add to Google

The student made a report to Cornell police about three weeks after the incident she alleges, and the matter was investigated by the Tompkins County district attorney, who said he found “insufficient evidence to support criminal charges” at the time. This week, District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said his office will look at the case again, but he defended its initial decision, saying the woman’s statement to police in 2024 “described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual.”
The woman, identified only as Jane Doe, sued the university, seven Chi Phi fraternity brothers and other defendants on Sept. 16. None of the seven was criminally charged.

The Chi Phi national fraternity said in a statement Sept. 18 that it could not discuss specific allegations during pending litigation. It called the allegations “deeply concerning,” and its local chapter has been barred from campus.

“As special prosecutor, the Attorney General will investigate this incident and, if warranted, prosecute any offenses arising from that investigation and present evidence to a grand jury,” Hochul said.
She said Jane Doe “deserves to know that every fact will be examined and justice pursued.”
Cornell rape allegation spotlights New York state consent laws
“This action will ensure that the matter is fully and thoroughly investigated without conflict or bias, and handled independently with the rigor that this matter demands,” she said.
Doe’s attorney, Thomas Guiffra, praised James’ appointment Thursday, saying he and Doe “had no faith in DA Van Houten’s ability or desire to actively investigate and prosecute this case.”

“We were dismayed that shortly after we agreed to give him all the assistance he needed, he published an announcement which questioned whether a crime was committed,” Guiffra said. “The most recent disclosure when he claimed that he never reviewed the transcript where Ms. Doe said “I am 100% certain I was raped” was the last straw.”

Guiffra’s remark was an apparent reference to the transcript of Doe’s interview with campus police in 2024, which was reported by CBS News earlier this week. Van Houten told NBC News on Wednesday that that specific allegation was not in the written statement his office received from Cornell police at the time. NBC News has not reviewed that transcript.
Guiffra said he intended to write a letter to Hochul requesting she appoint a special prosecutor, and said he and Doe “look forward to working with Attorney General James to finally obtain justice.”

James said in a statement Thursday evening: “Every New Yorker deserves to know that when they report a crime, it will be investigated fully and fairly. The Governor has entrusted my office with this investigation, and we do not take that responsibility lightly.”
“I stand ready to lead a process New Yorkers can trust, guided by the facts and the law,” she added.
The university confirmed Wednesday that it agreed to Hochul’s call for an independent investigation, and it backed James’ appointment Thursday night.
“Cornell supports Governor Hochul’s decision to assign this case to the New York Attorney General’s Office,” the university said in a statement.
Van Houten did not immediately respond Thursday night to emailed requests for comment.

title: FBI arrests man on charge of stalking conservative podcaster Katie Miller
summary: The defendant is accused of contacting Katie Miller, wife of White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, over 40 times during in less than two months.
story: The FBI on Thursday arrested a man on a charge of stalking former Trump administration adviser Katie Miller, an administration official familiar with the investigation told NBC News.

John Anthony Proia III, 41, was arrested and charged with stalking over allegations that he called, texted and left voicemails with “disturbing messages” about the victim, who was described as a former political adviser, and her husband, who is currently a high-level federal government employee, the Justice Department said in a news release.

The Justice Department did not name Katie Miller, though an administration official familiar with the investigation confirmed to NBC News that the victim is Miller, who is married to White House deputy chief of staff for policy Stephen Miller and hosts a popular conservative podcast.

“Thank you Todd Blanche, Leah Foley, and the FBI Washington Field Office for keeping me and my family safe. Good to see a Boston grand jury indict this man,” Miller wrote Thursday on X, referring to Attorney General Todd Blanche and U.S. Attorney Leah Foley.

Proia was indicted by a federal grand jury in Boston on Thursday on one count of cyberstalking after being arrested earlier in the day. He is alleged to have contacted the former political adviser more than 40 times in less than two months, according to the Justice Department.
The defendant is also accused of sending disturbing messages to Miller’s parents during the August-to-September time frame cited in court documents.

“As alleged in the Indictment, the defendant repeatedly and relentlessly targeted the victim, her husband and her family with deeply disturbing communications that profoundly disrupted their lives,” Foley said in a statement.

Ted Docks, special agent in charge of the FBI’s Boston Division, wrote in a statement on Thursday that Proia was arrested “for allegedly engaging in a sustained campaign of harassment to frighten this victim and her family, inflicting significant emotional distress.”
Proia made the calls, sent text messages and left voicemails from “an ever-changing series of unfamiliar phone numbers” to Miller, who lives in the Washington, D.C., area, the DOJ said.

The department added that those phone numbers were obtained through applications that provide free phone numbers for calling and messaging via Voice over Internet Protocol. The applications allow a user to hide their identity and easily generate new phone numbers, according to court filings.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

According to court documents, Miller sometimes received multiple communications from Proia in one day, including calls made late at night. Miller did answer some of the calls, but Proia also left voicemails, the DOJ said.
The calls “were allegedly made by what appeared to be a male caller employing a menacing tone and often using expletives,” the Justice Department said.
The Justice Department also detailed some text messages sent to phone numbers associated with Miller’s parents.

One message Proia is alleged to have written to Miller’s mother called Stephen Miller “evil” and Katie Miller a “creature.” Another message was said to feature a photo of Katie Miller, while another read, “My god, how can you be proud of this filth?”

In a text message to the victim’s father, Proia is alleged to have written, “Hey [first name of victim’s father], how goes it? Hope your daughter marrying a Jewish Nazi/white supremacist is working out for you and [first name of victim’s mother]. Did you raise her to be trash or did that just happen naturally?”

Proia’s arrest comes after Bloomberg reported over the weekend that two senior FBI officials in Washington were demoted and reassigned to FBI headquarters due to concerns that the agency was not moving efficiently enough to investigate threatening phone calls made to Miller, three people familiar with the matter told Bloomberg.

Darren Cox, assistant director in charge the FBI’s Washington Field Office, told Bloomberg in a statement that the move was a personnel decision made at the field office level based on “our constant evaluation of mission needs.”

title: Records give insight into how one Cornell student responded to rape accusation
summary: One of the seven Cornell University fraternity brothers named in a lawsuit alleging a gang rape in 2024 said he did not see the accuser in distress during his brief time in the room where she says she was sexually assaulted while she was under the influence of several substances.
story: One of the seven Cornell University fraternity brothers named in a lawsuit alleging a gang rape in 2024 said he did not see the accuser in distress during his brief time in the room where she says she was sexually assaulted while she was under the influence of several substances.

Scott Kretzschmar, now 22, said that after he saw a fraternity Snapchat post advertising “free p----y” upstairs, he went in the room already filled with several of his fraternity brothers — but that he never saw the woman naked, touched her or used ketamine.

Kretzschmar’s accounting of the evening was laid out in court documents he filed anonymously in Tompkins County, New York, Supreme Court in March in a last-ditch effort to annul Cornell’s decision to find him responsible for attempted sexual exploitation after its Title IX investigation. In the failed petition, Kretzschmar argued that the school improperly found him responsible for an offense that was not on his original list of violations — and then denied his appeal earlier this year.
Add to Google
Add to Google

The court records, together with text messages separately obtained by NBC News between Jane Doe and another Chi Phi fraternity member she later accused of assault, provide further context for the October 2024 incident and its immediate aftermath. The incident has reignited a national conversation about sexual assault and consent.

“My reputation is destroyed and i’m utterly ashamed,” Jane Doe texted another fraternity member, four days after she alleges she was raped while she was under the influence of ketamine, marijuana and alcohol. “I’m f------g pissed cause this many people shouldn’t know and i feel like i know who some of the rats in the room were,” she wrote. “if i ever find out i swear to god its in sight.”

During the dayslong text exchange, Jane Doe fluctuated between anger over being the subject of campus gossip and sending friendly messages before she ultimately cut off communication the day before she reported her allegations to campus police.

The report spurred a university investigation of seven Chi Phi members that culminated with a 12-day internal federal civil rights proceeding known as Title IX in May 2025, at which more than 30 witnesses testified following 50 investigative interviews, according to filings in Kretzschmar’s appeal. The investigation found that the night of the alleged assault, a photo of Jane Doe was shared among active Chi Phi members in a Snapchat group, the documents revealed. The nature of the photo is not made clear in the court documents.
“Are you guys at least naked?” a Snapchat message from an unknown user said after the photo was posted.

The Snapchat message thread, which was provided to campus investigators anonymously, “became a key exhibit in the resulting student conduct matter,” attorneys for the university argued in a July 17 memo filed in Kretzschmar’s case. Jane Doe’s lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, told NBC News she learned of the Snapchat messages only when they were leaked to her by another fraternity member who was outraged by what his fraternity brothers were said to have done to her.

Ultimately, the seven received differing penalties, ranging from writing a “reflection paper” to expulsion. The case went to the local district attorney’s office, which ultimately declined to bring criminal charges.

Cornell University police declined to comment on whether they had the photo when they conducted the November 2024 investigation into Jane Doe’s claims. The university did not respond to a request for comment on the photo and other details reported in this article.

Jane Doe told investigators that she did not specifically remember Kretzschmar’s directly taking part in her abuse. He was not expelled from Cornell and he graduated last year, but he faced several sanctions — including writing a “reflection paper” — at the conclusion of the Title IX process and was found responsible for attempted sexual exploitation.
Add to Google
Add to Google
Asked for comment on Kretzschmar’s state litigation, Giuffra simply called it “ridiculous.” On Thursday, Giuffra also revealed that Jane Doe completed a rape kit collection weeks after the incident.
Kretzschmar’s attorney, Jeremy Saland, stressed to NBC News on Thursday that his client was not involved in any criminal conduct alleged in the case.

“Rape allegations must be taken seriously, and the young woman at the center of this case is entitled to be heard. Nothing in our response is meant to diminish that or her,” Saland said in a statement. “However, Scott is not accused of rape and never has been. If  Scott had seen Doe in duress, he would have taken action but he was not present when her alleged victimization occurred.”

Saland added that his client “participated in a group chat whose content was ugly and reprehensible, and he regrets it.” The crude comments are “not the same as taking part in a rape,” and drug use allegations against Kretzschmar are also false, he said.

Last month, Jane Doe sued the university, Kretzschmar and six other current or former students, alleging that what began as a consensual encounter escalated into hours of nonconsensual sexual activity. She alleges that even after she reported the incident and endured the Title IX investigation, the school and other institutions failed to do enough to protect her. (Title IX is a federal civil rights law that prohibits gender-based discrimination in educational settings that involve federal funding. As a result, U.S. colleges and universities are required to have internal processes for adjudicating claims of Title IX violations brought by their students.)
